aspek.keterangan_umum: An authoritarian attitude tends to develop in people who were subjected to very strict parental control early in life, and who learned to bury their resentment and adopt an attitude of acquiescence. Often, experiences of this kind are forgotten, but the indirect effect of these childhood occurrences can be observed throughout life. As a result, in adulthood, these writers remain overly submissive to strong authority while at the same time directing their hidden hostilities toward weaker individuals who might be attacked without risk.

narasi.very_high:
With authoritarian very high, the writer often blames others for being overly combative. He refuses to accept the possibility that he, himself, might be the aggressive one. Instead, he projects such undesirable characteristics onto others. The traits that he despises in himself are the ones he attacks most fiercely in the people around him.

Important! When two people are authoritarian, real problems develop. Both will want their own way and neither of them is willing to compromise.
narasi.high:
The writer believes in, practices and advocates unquestioning obedience to authority rather than individual freedom of judgment and action. He is imbued with the ability to lay down the law and see that it is carried out. He is quite capable of throwing his weight about and insisting that others fulfill their obligations to the letter. He gives orders instead of asking; his instructions sound harsh and lacking in courtesy. He hardly praises but frequently criticizes and belittles. He tries too hard, most of the time, and creates his own resistance. No matter how unintentional such behavior may be on his part, it tends to offend those toward whom it is directed. People resent being forced and driven and dislike the person who tries to dominate their lives.

The writer will not adapt himself. Instead, he expects that others should conform to him. He wants the rules he has laid down to be followed. With his dictatorial attitude, he often antagonizes people and wounds the feelings of others. He lays down the law when compromise would be essential. When he senses he is not getting through, he will step up the pressure. He is determined that other people will do things his way, or else! It becomes an issue of will. Reasoning with him is not possible. He wants his own way and that is all that is on his mind. The minute he loses authority on the job or at home, he will turn moody and discontent or he may become totally disinterested. It is not his nature to submit.

The writer will take orders willingly from very few people because he believes very few people are superior to him. As an employer, he tends to be bossy. He will insist that his orders and instructions are carried out immediately and to the letter. He will not stand for disobedience or defiance and becomes angry when his discipline is thwarted. Others may find out the hard way that he does not like to be contradicted, especially in public.

The writer is power-oriented and sees the world divided into the weak and the strong. He, himself, identifies with authority figures. He is submissive toward superiors and contemptuous and dictatorial toward inferiors. He insists on strict obedience from subordinates. He may be hostile to members of minority groups.

The writer adheres strictly to conventional values. He finds it difficult to tolerate uncertainty.

The writer would function best in a position of management or command. He is a natural in sales, law enforcement or the military where force is right and necessary.
narasi.medium: The writer is a more cooperative individual. He follows regulations and laws and expects others to do the same.
narasi.low: The writer lacks an authoritarian demeanor. He has a live-and-let-live attitude and is more agreeable in communications and in positions of command.

aspek.keterangan_umum: This trait demonstrates the writer's need for being recognized, of being appreciated and noticed. A high score may explain many conflicts within the personality make-up. An introverted person may engage in extroverted activities which, in turn, will result in much tension and anxiety.

narasi.high:
The writer thrives on praise, acknowledgment and compliments as others show their approval of him. He is happier when he is talking about himself and his plans than about anything or anybody else. He needs constant ego boosts. His self esteem depends on outside approval and he can lose it instantly with direct reproach.

He worries very much what people are saying about him and how he appears to them. If they praise him, he will strive extra hard for a fine performance. With acknowledgment, his self-esteem is confirmed and he feels worthwhile. Flattery, adulation and compliments are all ways to his heart. (He has an inner desire to be noticed, and often, for instance, he puts five dollars in the collection plate, he wants everyone to know it is a five-dollar bill not a one-dollar bill.) Lacking praise and encouragement, the writer may withdraw from whatever he is involved in. He is afraid of making a poor showing and being ridiculed. Comparisons are especially aggravating to him. If he is criticized, particularly in front of a group, he becomes extremely distressed. Being criticized to him means losing face and destroys his image.

The writer prefers friends who have prestige and travel in the right social circles. He probably looks for a mate who enhances his position in life. He tends to seek the company of attractive, efficient people who can be a credit to him and build up his ego and status in life. (The writer most likely has two behaviors: a likable, personable one for company, especially if it includes new people to impress, and the other egocentric one for the family who may be left bewildered by his inconsistent attitude.) When his needs are not met, he can become destructive in words and attitude towards those receiving the acknowledgment.

The writer enjoys things that are impressive, like a stately home or a luxury car. He likes to own things that others don't have and he is pleased to show them off. He likes his name on his belongings and well-known store labels on the things he buys. For that reason, he is apt to splurge on things that others will feel are unneeded luxuries, but which are very necessary to him. Expensive items or high-priced clothes help him to feel his importance. (So important is prestige that he might be tempted to accept a job with a lower salary if it gives him a better office and a more impressive title.)

The writer lets others know of his accomplishments. Whatever happens to him is special. He speaks of what he is going to do and frequently puts himself on the spot so that he actually does have to accomplish remarkable things in order to save face.

He likes to feel that he has new ideas first. The best way to introduce a topic is to leave a few casual remarks with him to think about and later request his opinion on the subject.

The writer's love for an audience draws him into the entertainment world. He could perform as lecturer, receptionist, professional athlete or in sales.
narasi.medium: The writer enjoys recognition when it is earned but he has enough poise to get along without demonstrated approval.
narasi.low:
The writer relies on his accomplishments to speak for him. He enjoys recognition for what he has done, not for what he is. His feelings of self worth result from an inner satisfaction based on what he has accomplished. His pride is the job well done. It takes longer for him to build his own self worth, but once built, it is not easily destroyed by others’ criticism.

The writer is more content to remain in the background instead of demanding public acclaim. He often fails to put himself forward to gain his rightful reward. He is less exciting to be around but he is more likely to maintain a steady performance.

narasi.high:
The writer wants to be loved and accepted by everyone; he can be deeply hurt if others resist or are indifferent to his expectations. He prefers individuals who are warm and quick to demonstrate that they approve of him. Consideration, encouragement and acceptance are necessary for his well-being. When others demonstrate that they like him, he is relieved and receives a measure of security. He feels uncomfortable with people who are cold and detached because they do not fulfill his need for reassurance. If he cannot be accepted and liked, he wants people to feel at least sorry for him.

The writer wants someone to lean on and does not enjoy doing things by himself. He does not feel complete without someone else around. Since his need for acceptance is so great, he tries to accept everyone else around, too.

The writer defers to other people and is willing to let them have their way. In fact, so great is his desire to please and his fear of being rejected, that he is easily taken advantage of. He may frequently find himself doing things he really does not want to do just because he is afraid of upsetting another individual.

The writer tries to live up to the role others expect of him and goes to great lengths to avoid criticism and disapproval. When he encounters a rebuff in spite of all his efforts, he has little to fall back on and can be crushed. He is quick to misinterpret detachment as rejection, even when this is not the case.

Any sign of acceptance gives him superficial reassurance, but deep down it meets with disbelief and evokes feelings of distrust and fear. He can never really believe that he is liked and appreciated and he always feels inadequate. Basically, he runs the treadmill. He reaches out for affection, but the chances for satisfaction are slim. The insecurity that creates the need interferes with its gratification.

The writer's pattern of living has serious flaws. Firstly, his need is overpowering, requiring more and more people to satisfy it. Secondly, since he is constantly clamoring for approval from others, he is not living his own life. He has to do what will please others and ignore his own wishes, aspirations and desires. Consequently, his energies and resources are not used to develop his own potential.
narasi.medium: The writer enjoys being accepted by other people. He does not like doing things by himself and feels uncomfortable with people who are detached and cold. In order to get along, he tries to live up to the role that others expect of him.
narasi.low: With defenses low, the writer has a good sense of self and is independent enough not to require continuing demonstrations of approval.

aspek.keterangan_umum:
Aspirations are a conscious mental desire to attain for the sake of self. The writer longs to realize a goal to advance his own progress and fulfill his true potential.

High aspirations need to be reinforced by favorable scores in related areas, otherwise they may result in frustration and/or conflict.

Aspirations that are too low may be related to inhibition, fear of failure or lack of self confidence.

narasi.high:
The writer has an ardent desire for advancement. He longs for personal improvement, achievement or gain. His aspirations are expansive. He is strongly motivated to achieve something worthwhile that will gain him recognition and success. He is progressive in setting his goals. He is desirous of improvement, particularly self-improvement. He is alert to ways of advancing himself and to the opportunities which present themselves. He is willing to take chances, undertake the unfamiliar and sacrifice for his ambitions. He thinks in terms of advancing rather than adapting. He wants to achieve much in order to improve his position and raise his station in life. He thinks in bigger terms. He anticipates how what he is doing in the moment will relate itself to the fulfillment of his aims. He mentally envisions the fulfillment of his desires. For him, in a sense, the image of what he wants to create is his reality.

With self-esteem high, the writer has large ego demands and a strong need for recognition. He will strive hard for reinforcement of his self-esteem.

With self-esteem very high but without supportive traits, the writer has lofty aspirations but is unable to sustain such exalted goals. He procrastinates or avoids undertaking the unfamiliar. Through exaggeration he wants to cover up his lack of inner assurance.
narasi.medium: The writer's aspirations are modest; they are based on the level of success he had in the past. He does not try very hard to get ahead. He does not challenge himself to use his innate talents and abilities nor does he demand much of himself.
narasi.low:
The person seems satisfied with what he has achieved and where he is in life. He does not try to get ahead and ignores opportunities for advancement. His aspirations are probably too low for his abilities. He may be too aware of his alleged limitations and overly concerned about them. He seems to feel that since he is uncomfortable under pressure, he will be inadequate to deal with it.

The writer's lack of courage may hold him back from many possible advances. He may have decided that the best way to avoid failure is to tackle only those things for which success is assured in advance.

aspek.keterangan_umum: Conformity is a self-protective maneuver stemming from insecurity and fear. The writer goes along uncritically with the social and moral rules of society, or a group he identifies with. He depends instead on the guidance and direction of others. In most cases, the beneficial effect of the defense is only temporary. It alleviates immediate tension or anxiety. In the long run, however, it creates more problems than it solves. The individual conforms at the expense of renouncing a good deal of his own individuality. He is living out a false role for the sake of a mate, or friend, or a group. He wants to be approved of so much that he attempts to live up to other people's standards even when they do not coincide with his own wishes and views. By conforming to the tenets of the group, he buys into an implicit “I am not all right pattern” and forfeits his own unfoldment.

narasi.high:
The writer acts in accordance with established rules, customs and conventions. He conforms outwardly, even though he may not necessarily believe in the opinions expressed or the behavior displayed. He wants supportive identification with a group, however small. He has found this to be the easiest and most expedient way to approach life. He selects groups because they share his attitude. The group, in turn, helps develop and sustain his individual point of view. He adopts entirely the kind of personality that fits the opinions of the group because being isolated from a group creates anxiety.

The writer avoids stress by identifying with the group and by accepting their attitudes. He observes rules and regulations and follows fads and accepted trends in thinking, dress and behavior. He becomes exactly as all others are because he is afraid to do otherwise. He may want to be independent and do things on his own but his need for approval prevents him from doing so.

Proper performance and demeanor are important since the writer unconsciously rates himself by what others think of him. His self esteem rises or falls with their approval or disapproval. He wants to “do right” and “be right.” Behavior that is approved by the group gives him a sense of security. He pursues “in” activities and plays the role that is expected of him. He adapts himself to circumstances, situations and other people in order to fit in. And he conforms to these standards not only in his actions but even in his thoughts and feelings. He presumes that rules are more important than personalities and feels secure by not behaving in noticeably different ways. In the face of nonconforming behavior, he feels lost. He tends to consider less conforming individuals as rule breakers and when he sees others flaunting customs, he becomes upset.

The writer thinks in traditional ways. He holds on to ideas he has known before without making an effort to think in new patterns. He wants to perpetuate what is familiar and approved. His role in his reference group determines to a large extent his conception of himself. If he is fully accepted by everyone, he gains confidence and feels assured. If he is only partially accepted, he suffers self-doubt. If he is rejected, he may experience intense anxiety. In his aspirations, the writer stays with current opportunities. He is content with where he is as long as it offers a minimum of security. The stronger the evidence of conformity, the less willing he is to try the unfamiliar or meet somebody he does not know. So long as his relationships involve people who behave in familiar ways, he feels safe.

Important! The stronger the evidence of conformity, the less willing he is to try the unfamiliar or meet somebody he does not know. So long as his relationships involve people who behave in familiar ways, he feels safe.
narasi.medium:
The writer accepts conventional standards when they are convenient. Most of the time it is simpler and less complicated to do things in a conforming way. He adapts when no great issues are involved or when he knows that people will be hurt or embarrassed by less conventional behavior. He is quite content when he can blend new concepts with accepted methods or forms.

The writer rejects or modifies group standards when it is better for him to do so or when he is in the company of people who are less conforming themselves and do not expect or demand such behavior.

He neither timidly accepts everything that is being imposed upon him by his parents or society, nor does he have to reject all of those principles to prove his independence. He retains standards that are valuable and rejects those that are not. What remains are now his values; he can live with them and accept responsibility for them.
narasi.low:
In his thinking and his behavior, the writer is independent. His own ideas carry more weight with him than the opinions of others or the codes of the group. He likes doing things his own way and resents personal restrictions. While he may be willing to listen to advice, he usually ends up doing things in his own unique or individualistic manner. He does what is desirable and realistic from his own point of view.

The writer is more willing to heed a suggestion than an order. He wants to feel that what he is doing is the result of his own free choice. He is doing it because he wants to do it, and the consequences of his activities are valuable to him. He feels little obligation toward others or toward society at large.

The writer's approval comes from within. He sets his own standards and responds to his behavior in self-satisfied or self-critical ways. The anticipation of feelings of self-contempt prevents him from behavior that is not in accordance with his self-made rules.

narasi.high:
The writer applies conscious, directed thought. When working on a problem or task, he focuses all his mental energy without deviating from his thought processes.

He consciously processes new ideas or challenges through an active thought process. Whenever he is faced with a new situation, he is likely to take the time to think it through.

He is able to learn new concepts and finds pleasure and challenge in considering the theoretical aspects of a subject.

Mentally alert, he is able to resolve most situations through clear thinking. He is likely to be successful in any job where he has a chance to use his mind.

The writer will rarely be satisfied with routine work or with staying in a position that requires only average or less than average mental capacity.

With pressure in conspicuous places, the writer will make a special effort when he feels himself observed.

With sudden heavy pressure in middle zone downstrokes, the writer's mind will function irregularly, having surges of thought.
narasi.medium:
The writer can think when he has to, but is not one to seek theoretical pursuits. With a fair degree of mental focus, he makes no intensive effort to study the material or the situation at hand.

While he may have trouble rising to intellectual challenges, he may be able to acquire the skills to become an expert in his special area of interest. Most of the time, he is directing his mind to useful practical purposes.
narasi.low:
The writer is usually content to just let his mind wander undirected. He lacks mental discipline and quickly loses interest in anything that needs mental effort.

He does not probe into matters; he prefers to skim along, noticing only the most obvious facts. He examines matters cursorily, selecting only information he momentarily needs. He does not bother to weigh things, but accepts them as he sees them.

Easily bored with theory, the writer finds it difficult to keep his mind on intellectual matters.

The writer is usually content to stay with what he already knows. He may deal well with practical assignments where he can apply what has worked before.

On the other hand, he may resent being asked to think beyond what he is familiar with.

aspek.keterangan_umum: Orientation, either physical or mental, has a significant effect on the writer’s behavior, interpersonal relationships, his outlook and his attitudes. Mental orientation is no guarantee of mental accomplishment. It is positive or negative according to scores in related areas. Without outlet in other areas, intellectual orientation will be a problem in the writer’s life. He will be frustrated and mentally spinning his wheels.

narasi.high:
The writer is intellectually motivated and inclined to express himself in terms of mental activity. What he accomplishes is the result of thought. He thinks dynamically and prefers to work with his mind rather than his hands. It is essential to his health and well-being that he keep his mind engaged. He will rarely be satisfied with routine work or with staying in a position that requires only average or less than average mental capacity.

The writer enjoys intellectual subjects and thrives on mental challenges. He loves intelligent discussions. He has the ability to concentrate and to think innovatively. Abstract thinking and mental pursuits are natural for him and his mind can stretch beyond the normal horizons. Unless he has a mental challenge, he feels stifled and dull and without continual mental stimulation, he is likely to become nervous and irritable.

The writer is an energetic thinker. His mind is always busy and restless. He wants to explore beyond what he already knows and he is prepared to experiment mentally. He may be the propounder of new theories. High mental energy activates his mind. It gives him drive and increases astuteness. It makes him want to tackle a job and set high goals. Additionally, it gives him an optimistic and enthusiastic outlook on life.

By nature, the writer is more likely to think than act. He does not lack physical stamina, but he has to call it up consciously and sustain it by will. He is more a thinker than a doer and is not attracted to physical labor. Physical activity does not produce the same enjoyment as mental action. Sports, physical labor, dancing, swimming or running may be done out of obligation but are a chore. Satisfaction is in mental, not physical work. He spends so much time thinking that he is likely to activate his body less than he should. He is not the type to go in for regular exercise. He would prefer to sit behind his desk rather than take off on a brisk walk or play a regular game of tennis. As a result, he is inclined to have poorer health and his recuperative powers are generally weaker. It takes him much longer to recover from exertion because mental energy cannot be restored as quickly as it is taken out. It takes at least three times as long to replenish mental energy as it does to restore physical stamina.

The writer has enough intellectual pursuits to make him an interesting person to meet. Personally, he prefers intellectual fellowship and in a relationship, he requires mental companionship more than physical presence. He needs partners who are on the same mental wavelength with whom he can discuss a wide range of topics. Because he lives in a mental world, his behavior at times may seem high-brow to more down-to-earth associates.

To the writer, love is more an idea than an emotion. It is a mental thing and he can be in love with the idea of love. He becomes intellectually rather than emotionally involved and has to be deeply stirred to begin love in ordinary terms. He has to experience a total blending of the mind and the spirit before the physical passions catch up in intensity. He requires a mental stimulus to set him off. Since the same energy that is used for mental work is used for sex, he may show only infrequent interest in actual sexual activities. This may be especially true while he is working on mentally demanding jobs. He finds his enjoyments in the mind, not in physical sensations. The writer’s aim is probably to earn a living through mental pursuits. Physical routine and manual labor are anathema to him. He can be quite practical in certain areas but he works best in the mental field. He enjoys scientific studies. Research and planning give him a feeling of being in the right place. His scholarly nature may induce him to take up a career in education.

With organizational ability, the writer may take a special interest in scientific studies. He is probably competent at extracting ideas and organizing them into an applicable pattern.
narasi.medium: The writer starts from a position that is more balanced between mental and physical interests. He could function well in a position that requires an even output of both mental and physical energy. Nursing, geology, anthropology, or civil service jobs would be satisfying.
narasi.low:
The writer is a matter-of-fact individual and concerned with the realistic areas of life. He deals well with practical assignments and is good at applying what he knows has worked before. Usually, he simplifies complicated information in order to deal with it more effectively. He is not troubled by possibilities. He is concerned with the realities in the moment and he is willing to do what is needed “right now.” He may have trouble rising to intellectual challenges, but can always acquire the necessary skills to become an expert in a special area of interest.

Possibly the greatest disadvantage is the writer’s lack of interest to improve his level of knowledge. He is content to stay with what he already knows; he may even resent being asked to think beyond what he is familiar with.

The writer functions most satisfactorily in jobs requiring predominantly manual labor and physical energy. Lumbering, mining, carrying mail by foot, excavating, construction work, road building, or freight handling would be suitable.

Important! This is one of the most important traits in assessing compatibility. In a partnership, people should have similar orientation. Communication is difficult enough without added conflicts due to divergent scores. There must be a common meeting ground of intellects. Otherwise, the writer with mental orientation will accuse the partner of “not understanding” and will look down on the practical accomplishments of the “physical” writer. And the partner with physical orientation will accuse the “mental” one of “complicating everything” and may belittle the mate’s intellectual accomplishments.

narasi.very_high:
The writer has a strong desire for self-development and attainment of a personal goal. He has a powerful urge to succeed. Motivation energizes his behavior and gives it direction. He can visualize a goal with great accuracy and make it materialize.

The writer has an unusual sense of purpose and the desire to produce his best effort in following through with a specific plan. Long range aims guide shorter range objectives. When he thinks about concrete goals, he thinks about a series of specific projects that build one upon another and eventually lead to the accomplishment of his plans. Furthermore, achievement is always intertwined with self-development.

The writer is a self starter who manages his own development. He starts with the decision to excel. When he sees the chance for action, he moves. He values any skills he can acquire and takes steps to further develop his capabilities. He makes a personal commitment to achieve the best that he can be.

The writer feels most alive when engaged in purposeful activity. He feels that what he is doing is the result of his own free choice; he is doing it because of his inner decision to excel. He wants to stand out and succeed in something that is important to him. He keeps his motivation refreshed by achievement, aim for results and by managing himself. He sets his own standards of conduct or performance. He responds to his behavior in self-satisfied or self-critical ways, depending on how the behavior matches his standards.

The writer is willing to forego the things he would like to do in order to focus on what is necessary. He has the discipline to pursue what he sets out to do. No matter how difficult it gets, he trusts that in the end he will succeed. He refuses to accept preconceived limits and aspires to achieve satisfying results repeatedly and consistently. In the process, he can greatly exceed his previous levels of performance.

His belief in himself is based on experience. It allows him to keep on trying and not to let obstacles deter him. He applies himself to the number of opportunities he can create and knows how to act when suitable circumstances present themselves. He likes being effective. What gets him really irritated is spinning his wheels and not doing what he is good at.

The writer is willing to adapt to changing conditions. He has the mental agility and the flexibility to change perspective. He sees difficulties as challenges and mistakes as signals that it is time to correct course. Even during setbacks he remains optimistic. He assesses the problem situation and learns from it. Then he continues based on updated information.
narasi.high: The writer aims at a lower plateau of achievement. Moderate levels of performance are acceptable to him. He engages in activity less vigorously and less efficiently. Before making a move he frequently looks for direction and he needs encouragement and supervision on difficult or long-term jobs.
narasi.medium:
The writer aims at a low plateau of achievement. Low levels of performance are acceptable to him. He looks for direction every time he has to make a move and needs encouragement and supervision on most jobs.

He may work strictly to please a boss or feed the family. Short range goals are ends in themselves. He becomes immersed in them, forgetting where they originally were to take him and where they fit in the overall project. What he is doing has been imposed on him by others. The consequences of his activity will not be a source of pride to him. He quits forging ahead, feeling that there is nothing more that he can do. He feels that external forces determine his goals. He does not concern himself about what he himself can do to further his cause.

He sees his abilities and capabilities as limited and restricts himself by fear of failure. Self-doubt impedes purposeful action. His work offers little personal meaning or joy. He follows long-ingrained habits and tries to maintain the status quo. He seeks things that are familiar, unchallenging, but also less productive.

narasi.high:
The writer is mentally astute. He has a keen mind and quick perception. He is able to grasp facts instantly and immediately understands the nature of things and situations. His assessments are instantaneous. He acquires knowledge quickly and assimilates it with what he knows in order to put it to immediate and profitable use. Labored explanations are not necessary for him; he gets the point at once and frequently grasps the whole argument before the speaker has finished the preamble. Although he moves quickly from one topic to another, it is not in a superficial way.

The writer is able to “think on his feet” and moves from one subject to another with great speed. He can outthink others and concludes, almost before the facts are in. He sums up situations swiftly and seems to have the answers before the questions are asked. Lengthy explanations make him nervous and he is irritated by people who take longer to process their thoughts. He may second-guess or try to hurry them along. Because of his perceptive mind and his desire to get to the next item, he often interrupts slower people. One of his pet phrases will be “Get to the point.”

The writer functions to advantage where time is at a premium or where fast decisions are needed. He would do well in emergency surgery, transportation, fire fighting or communication. Fast paced work gives him the feeling of being in the right place research. He is suited to farming, accounting and computer work. The educational field is excellent for him. Occupations which involve forecasting and theory will offer satisfaction, as long as they provide enough time for preparation, research and thought.

The writer is able to create without precedent and to reach conclusions that are not the norm. He probably enjoys artistic work that stirs his imagination. Music, poetry, or painting may have more than the usual appeal.

The writer shows independent judgment and high mental maturity. He has an original approach and puts his personal stamp on whatever he does. He adds creative thinking to his work. He is challenged by problems. He looks for ingenious solutions and is willing to experiment with the unknown. His creativity may be expressed in small ways or on a larger scale. Beyond personal applications, he may think up progressive schemes to increase the company's profit or lower its overhead. He may originate new product designs, an architectural drawing or a new marketing strategy. He may present old or unused materials in new and innovative forms. He has much initiative and his imagination is triggered wherever the need for new applications exists.

The writer's ability may either be used as a hobby or it may be turned to commercial use. He would probably enjoy a career in some artistic field. His need for self-expression may find an outlet in painting, writing, or, perhaps, music. With his talent, the writer could create something for practical use. Interior decorating, designing clothes or jewelry, making up faces or styling hair, could hold appeal.

Whatever the writer does, it would be difficult for him to keep to a tight or uniform schedule, regardless of standard office procedure. His creative energy comes on at all hours, and it cannot be adjusted to fit someone's idea of the proper work schedule. Because of his own creative personality, the writer is more sympathetic with other artistic people. He understands they cannot turn on creativity like a light switch at nine in the morning and turn it off again at five in the afternoon.

If the writer is not engaged in the arts himself, his intuitive understanding of it would allow him to move easily in artistic circles, if he is so inclined. If he is tied down to a routine job, he should be encouraged to keep busy at something creative in his leisure time.
narasi.medium: The writer is more imitative. He utilizes the ideas of other people to generate his own solutions. He applies innovative concepts proposed by others and adapts them to a particular need or circumstance. His greatest satisfaction comes from improving on what went on before. And this is what he aims to do. He likes to develop new standards based on what has already been proven by experience.
narasi.low: The writer is a practical, matter-of-fact person. He follows a pattern of conformity and prefers traditional methods of getting ahead. He takes risks carefully and he functions best where no independent thinking is required. He cannot conceive of ways to alter present plans or designs. He thinks and acts in conformity with standards that are acceptable. His approach seldom varies since it was effective in the past. He clings to the known method and to “safe” procedures.

narasi.high:
The writer is assured and confident in the face of difficult circumstances. He is courageous and faces up to challenges as a matter of course. He assumes authority and inspires confidence in others. He is more self-sufficient and dismisses minor problems as unimportant in the moment. He knows he can handle them if he has to. His confidence is based on his ability to achieve and is in no way held up by, or dependent on, the opinion of others.

The writer is threatened only by very large responsibilities. There is practically nothing he will not tackle, if it is a challenge or just something he thinks he wants to do. He is literally unable to conceive that anything he believes in, including him, can fail. Because of this he works to advantage in situations that call for leadership. He brings out what is best in others. He encourages their self-expression; he gives them confidence in their ability. Where a lesser person would stifle, he stimulates.

The writer functions well in his job because he knows his own strength and potentials. He is released within himself. He has bigger concepts and thinks in bigger terms than most people.

The ability to communicate is influenced by confidence. The writer is not afraid to speak his mind. He is able to accept criticism or different opinions that others may offer. He contributes his own ideas to make his work more efficient and productive. He is willing to apply new techniques to new situations, and he accepts responsibility for the consequences.

The writer has the drive and the enthusiasm necessary to develop his talents. He is assured of his own capabilities. He is willing to take risks to get ahead and confident in his ability to achieve his goals. He has learned that there are few irremediable mistakes, and he regards mistakes as nothing more than a friendly invitation to keep trying, not a loss of approval and prestige, or as a humiliation to be avoided at any cost.

The writer likes strength in others, too, and looks for it. Self-sufficiency in a person is what he admires most.

The writer is not immune to fear. However, a situation has to be very threatening to bring forth a distress reaction from him. When he finally realizes the immensity of a certain challenge, he can be very much afraid. And since he has rarely encountered self-doubt before, he does not know how to handle it. He may be baffled, confused and completely frustrated.
narasi.medium:
The writer feels confident with people who are familiar and in situations where he knows what to expect. In strange circumstances he has periodic feelings of inadequacy. He is hesitant to extend himself too far or to commit himself. He is easily overwhelmed by challenges larger than he is accustomed to carry. Under stress, he may activate a number of self-protective defenses when forced to stay with a project despite the sensation of uneasiness, he is usually able to complete the job. The feeling of inadequacy passes as he moves forward step by step toward his goal. Little by little, he frees himself from his self-doubts. They give way to pleasure in his own accomplishment. Every time he stays with a task or in a situation that makes him anxious, he grows in confidence.

Much of the time, he does not feel as adequate as he projects outwardly, but he is generally able to conceal from others when he is ill at ease.
narasi.low:
The writer has little assurance and is ill equipped to command or lead others. He feels uncomfortable under pressure and therefore assumes that he is unable to deal with it. He is uneasy, sometimes to the point of being anxious, in interpersonal relationships. He cannot relax. He is aware of his alleged limitations and excessively concerned about them.

The writer often has negative feelings about himself. He appears hesitant and fearful much of the time. This limits his ability to express himself. It inhibits him in making social contacts easily. In any public appearance, he feels strained and ill at ease. It is difficult for him to deal directly with others as individuals. His conversation is composed mostly of agreements or silence. Until he develops a rapport of sympathy, he is hesitant to express his opinions. He is more inclined to listen to what other people are saying than to speak himself.

The writer is much more aware of, and affected by the world around him. He takes life in smaller doses. He is more apt to stay with what is familiar than to strike out into new areas. He is more likely to deal with small areas than large, especially when it comes to responsibility, authority and decisions.

The writer works well within the scope of his abilities but will not initiate innovative procedures on his job. He is an able follower. He functions better in support of other people rather than as the leader of an activity. He favors working behind the scenes. He is grateful to those he follows and he admires their strength and courage. He holds back from assuming bigger responsibilities because he feels there is always someone better qualified than he, himself, is. He is too willing to defer to the alleged superiority of others.

The writer is limited by the pressure around him. He feels himself thwarted by it, or inadequate to cope with it. Once he feels blocked, he tends to give up the project or assignment. Once he drops it, it is very difficult for him to return to it because of the knowledge that he failed before. He enjoys the immediate release from tension but on the other hand, every time he yields his responsibilities, he comes to doubt himself even more than he would naturally. When setting his goals, he needs support from others and encouragement that he can accomplish his aims.

The writer takes personally many comments that other people would not even notice. He depends upon an intricate defense system to keep his feelings of self worth intact. On the other hand, he is more compassionate toward the “underdog.” He is more considerate of the feelings of those close to him. He understands how deeply a slight can hurt and he wants to spare them the pain he knows so well.

While it is true that the writer appreciates help from others, he is often afraid to ask for assistance because this may show up his insecurities. Because of tension arising from his sense of inadequacy his ability to comprehend a given situation is limited. Under strain, the mind cannot operate as fully as in times of relaxation. Despite the tension he feels, the writer is eager to master new skills and acquire more information. Knowledge increases his sense of adequacy. He knows how much he has yet to learn. He is grateful to those who can teach him what he feels he needs to know. In his lifetime search for protection, he is prone to turn to education for the security it provides.

With self-esteem low, the writer feels the constant pressure to prove himself. He has few inner resources. He is at the mercy of others and the situations he finds himself in. He is afraid of derogation, ridicule and criticism by others.

Important! Other scores are very important here. If the writer does not have an acceptable outlet for continually proving his worth, he is a prime candidate for doing the unacceptable. He is susceptible to alcohol or drugs that would give him a temporary feeling of adequacy and well-being.

aspek.keterangan_umum: Self-esteem indicates the writer's general self-concept and discloses his feelings of self-worth. For genuine self-confidence and true self-respect, scores for self-confidence and self-esteem should be within one point of each other. With divergent scores, the writer suffers conflict. A much higher score for self-esteem means vanity as a defense. A much higher score for self-confidence means a facade of positiveness as a defense. In each case, the writer will manipulate people and situations to appear to his best advantage. The writer will stay with endeavors that enhance his abilities and avoids projects in areas where he scores low. Vanity leaves him open to feelings of failure and guilt. It increases tension, for he feels that he has to be right at all times. A facade of positiveness means that the writer will be too forceful and pushy.

narasi.high:
With self-confidence high, the writer is self-reliant, confident and positive. He is progressive, courageous and willing to chance failure in order to achieve success. He is resilient in the face of setbacks. He possesses well-developed leadership qualities.

With self-confidence low, the writer has an exaggerated opinion of himself. Inside himself, he feels that he is really unworthy. Consequently, he overcompensates for his feelings of inadequacy. By creating in his imagination a picture of himself that will impress others and that he can be proud of, he is able to ignore some of the reality of what he truly is. He is good at bluff, often promising more than he can deliver.

Most of the time, the writer gets off to a good start but, unfortunately the promising beginning does not always result in a good finish. He must succeed quickly and in a grand manner in carrying out whatever he has planned or he will suddenly lose interest in the project and decide that it was not “worthwhile.” He does not back up his promises with hard facts and prolonged, lasting effort and subsequently has to pay the price in irritation and embarrassment. He must continually rationalize and distort reality when events demonstrate that he is not, in fact, a superior human being. He becomes very annoyed when someone reminds him of his actions.

Due to his tremendous ego problems, the writer feels the need to always be on top. He is arrogant, patronizing, bossy and careless about the feeling of others. He has an inflated sense of pride in himself, his appearance and his achievements. He wants to be noticed and draw attention to himself. He wants recognition and the respect of others for little real effort on his part. When he does not receive the attention he wants he can become very destructive against those who are receiving the acclaim.

The writer is very interested in how other people's reaction will affect him, personally. He is overly concerned about what others are thinking and saying about him. He brags to cover up his failures or inadequacies. He will do anything rather than lose face. He is egocentric. He behaves as if anything concerning him is of utmost importance, yet he has no interest in other people's lives. He may be generous but only when such a show will earn him the momentary respect of others. He strains to “keep up with the Jones's,” since outside appearances mean so much to him. Things are either good or bad depending on whether they enhance the writer's self-image or detract from it. Whatever strengthens his position becomes desirable and important. On the other hand, what diminishes or detracts from it is undesirable, bad, and to be avoided.

The writer does not do things in his own real interest. His goals are not for his own enjoyment and growth, but rather serve to enhance or magnify his image. Above all, he must maintain his picture of himself as a superior human being.

He has the tendency is to overlook anything “small.” This includes personal relationships as well as vocational challenges. He loses many opportunities to advance himself by belittling the worth of the task, or the people who offer him the job.

Exaggerated pride prevents the writer from asking for help or admitting failure. He hates to admit that he could be wrong and it takes a lot of conflict to humble him enough to seek advice from someone else.

With self-confidence very low, there is conflict. The writer wants to be out in front but is afraid. (This is one reason why some people turn to alcohol, they hope to be able to let themselves go.)

With manipulative or antisocial high, the writer expects to get away with things other people would get caught for.
narasi.medium:
The writer has periodic, short-lived feelings of inadequacy and inferiority. They are normally triggered when he becomes involved in something unfamiliar. This increases tension temporarily and is alleviated once the situation becomes familiarized or he successfully completes or avoids it.

He wants recognition, but for what he has done, not just for what he is. He relies on past accomplishments to speak for him. Well aware of past failures and mistakes, he tends to base future plans on what has worked before. He lacks showmanship and does not push himself into the forefront to gain rightful recognition. He hides his light under the proverbial bushel. He does not care what kind of showing he makes, so long as he does his job.

The writer tends to be more considerate of others. He has a feeling for their needs and is more conscious of their interests.

The writer’s drawback is that he fails to take advantage of opportunities. He tends to stay with fields he is familiar with. He usually has far more capabilities for development than he gives himself credit for.
narasi.low:
With self-confidence high, the writer is accomplished but modest. He does not want attention drawn to himself. He is content to work behind the scenes rather than in the forefront of activity. He does not let pride interfere with must be done.

The writer enjoys approval and recognition, but does not deliberately seek notice. He is willing to give credit to others. He is able to take criticism that is diplomatically given. With self-confidence low, the writer feels unimportant and inadequate. He is afraid of ridicule, humiliation and failure. He is very self-conscious, vulnerable and insecure. He can do an adequate job as long as he is doing what he knows best, or has had successful experience with. He feels most comfortable when he is permitted to work more or less in the background. If he is thrust into a new position, especially one that entails meeting the public, he may not be able to handle the situation. This may cause him to become discouraged with his abilities and thus reinforces his lack of confidence.

The writer feels uneasy and indecisive. He is unable to rely on his own judgment in taking correct action. He is dependent on the aid of others instead of on his own strength and resourcefulness. He is fearful of failure and lacks faith in his abilities. He is too frightened to be able to look at himself realistically. He is afraid to see his limitations and shortcomings. He is prejudiced against himself and finds it difficult to accept his good qualities. He is quick to see his faults but not his good points. Instead of building on his strength, he is concerned with his weaknesses. He tends to run himself down and depreciates his own worth. He feels that he is no good and that others are disappointed in him. He places more importance on their judgment of him than on his own. He needs a large amount of sincere encouragement, approval and recognition from others. No matter what he does, he needs to be accepted unconditionally. His self-esteem will go up when others treat him kindly and courteously and indicate that he is a worthwhile person in his own right.

In dealing with others, he frequently fails to assert himself because he is fearful to voice his own thoughts and opinions.

The writer has few inner resources and has a hard time coping with the problems of life. He is easily manipulated by people and circumstances. He is subject to easy discouragement. Worry and tension limit his personal growth. Under pressure, he is inclined to act stubborn, intolerant and inflexible. He is using these defenses to function at least somewhat effectively. (The writer would be a prime candidate for alcohol and/or drugs that temporarily reduce tension and give him a temporary euphoric feeling of adequacy or well-being.)

narasi.high:
The writer is a well-balanced individual who is not easily ruffled or disturbed. His behavior is healthy, adjustive and effective. He is resilient and highly functional and his personality is smooth and quite predictable. He is emotionally stable and seldom subject to moods. He is neither unreasonably elated by success nor crushed by failure. He has a healthy measure of self-respect and good inner resources.

The writer feels people are worthwhile and valuable, including himself. He treats himself with dignity and does not belittle or degrade himself. He is mature and growth oriented. He moves steadily toward self-actualization and the higher development of his capacities. He is productive and creative. He does not scatter his energies in the pursuit of prestige or to impress others. He does not allow himself to be diverted from his real goals. His main emphasis is on the development of his own talents and skills.

Confident in his own ability, the writer has well-developed inner resources. He can adjust quickly and smoothly as the circumstances require. He can deal with stress, even that which is directed against his ego. He does not constantly have to seek approval from others to prove that he is worthwhile. He respects his assets and liabilities and is proud of his efforts.

The writer is basically courageous. He does not let himself be pushed around. Without being hostile, he is assertive and defends himself and what is important to him. He seeks new experiences and is open and curious. He can tolerate risks and uncertainty. Above all, he is not afraid to try. If he fails, he usually has learned something from the experience which helps him to do better the next time. He is not devastated by failure. He worries mostly about real problems, not possibilities. He respects dangers but he does not magnify them.

The writer is a realist. He sees things accurately and there is little wishful thinking in his makeup. He respects the limitations of time, energy and resources. Because he knows he cannot do everything, he concentrates on what is important to him.

The writer has developed a set of values that are appropriate for him. He accepts conventional standards when they are suitable. He rejects or modifies them when it is better for him to do so. He neither timidly accepts everything that is being imposed upon him, nor does he reject established standards to prove his independence. What he accepts are now his values and he can live with them and accept responsibility for them.

The writer has self-discipline. It shows in the ability to postpone gratification. He does not have to satisfy all impulses and needs immediately. He has good judgment. He does not make problems complicated, he simplifies them. He can get down to the essentials, to the heart of the matter. He does not get lost in unimportant details and trivial issues. Nor does he expect perfect solutions. He looks for alternatives and picks out a reasonable course of action.

His ability to learn and reason is markedly influenced by the frame of reference he has developed. His assumptions about himself and about the world are fairly consistent with reality; he can adjust his behavior accordingly to meet new demands. He is able to reinterpret situations realistically and see new factors and relationships in it.

The writer is in good contact with his feelings and can express them openly. He does not panic easily. He does not fear losing control of his emotions and can express them in an appropriate manner. He can respond simply and directly to what is going on in the present, whether it be with anger or love. He is very much involved with life. He is natural and spontaneous. He can be himself. He does not have to impress people, submit to them or fight with them. His relations with other people are good. He is compassionate without being sentimental. He is generous and helpful to others.
narasi.medium:
The writer is generally stable and can handle an average amount of stress. He has sufficient inner resources to rebound from some stress directed against his ego. He is emotionally affected by both successes and failures but is able to put them into perspective. When stress is severe, it overtaxes his resources to cope and inhibits integrated functioning. He may try to maintain composure through a long series of irritations or frustrations only to explode in the face of the final straw.

Sustained stress or encountering a number of stresses at the same time can make a difference, too. The resulting reaction will be more severe than if these events occurred separately. Under severe stress, there will be an exaggeration of the ego defenses that the writer customarily relies upon. The writer becomes more rigid. It is harder for him to adjust effectively to new or changed conditions.
narasi.low:
The writer's pattern of living and his values and goals are creating more stress than his powers of adaptation can cope with. Consequently, he has an exaggerated need for security. He is afraid to jeopardize what he has or to take the risks involved in achieving his full potential. The slightest frustration or pressure places him under severe stress. He is especially susceptible to threat that is directed against his ego and constantly experiences apprehension. Situations which threaten his adequacy, loss of social status, failure in his chosen occupation, or desires which he considers incompatible with his self concept, all involve a strong element of dread. Such situations place a great deal of stress upon him. They evoke feelings of inadequacy, isolation, and insecurity and seriously impair integrated functioning. Emergencies, disappointments, and other life problems that other people can take in stride may cripple his functioning ability altogether. He feels easily threatened in situations which place demands on him that he perceives as important but beyond his power to meet.

The writer typically has little insight into the causes of his difficulties or the inadequacy of his reactions. His lack of insight makes it impossible to choose more effective ways of coping. His reasoning is further impaired by the emotional processes that typically accompany severe stress. He is rigid and inflexible and approaches problems in a stereotyped way. The more severe the stress, the more reasoning, problem solving and adaptive efficiency decrease. As a consequence of his over-reaction to the stress situation, he either experiences disorganizing anxiety or keeps relying on defenses. In either case, his behavior is maladaptive.

narasi.high:
The writer follows sound moral principles. He is honest and sincere and conducts himself in a trustworthy and upright manner. He is open, honest and he tells the truth, regardless of consequences to himself. He does not talk around the point. He speaks facts and he is responsible.

The writer is very concerned with accountability and values. He has worked out a set of guidelines that are appropriate for him and he is firmly committed to his own code of ethics. If he does anything less, he feels uneasy and ashamed. He places high value on truth and honesty. He repays loyalty with loyalty. He finds unfair tactics and unethical behavior offensive.
narasi.medium: The writer is trustworthy under most circumstances, except in situations where his ego defenses become aroused. Mostly, he wants to avoid being pressured, either from within or without. If he promises something and he forgets, he is likely to practice a little involuntary deceit the next time he meets the person to whom he made the promise. He wants to avoid appearing in a bad light.
narasi.low:
The writer's integrity is dependent upon his emotional feelings about a situation or person and how much is at stake as far as his self-esteem is concerned. One of his greatest worries is the fear of exposure. Exposure may lead to embarrassment, shame, ridicule, and feeling inferior. He fears being confronted with the realization that he is not what he is supposed to be. He fears exposure of alleged limitations and defects.

In situations where he feels threatened, he may be putting on a mask to protect himself from being found out to be weak, or inadequate to either the person with whom he must deal or the task which he must perform. He may deliberately try to disguise his uneasiness by misleading others and obscuring his real feelings and intents from those with whom he deals. In either case, the result is that he cannot be trusted. He is misrepresenting something and aims to deceive. There is a real risk in dealing with him. He cannot be counted on to be acting in good faith. The result will be that those who have to deal with him will feel uneasy and distrust him.

narasi.high:
The writer exercises control over himself, his emotions, desires and deeds. He considers consequences before he goes into action and rarely responds before he has the occasion to think. He does and says what is most effective and efficient in most situations. He is neither prone to hasty judgments nor impetuous acts. His responses are the result of a conscious thought process.

The writer has trained himself to approach situations logically. This has become a habit, and now he functions rationally, working from the head, not the heart. Professionally, this can be an advantage. He appears more objective and self-possessed and his restraint helps him to keep his composure in difficult circumstances. This spares him emotional involvement and allows quicker handling of problem situations. If someone is showing a greater response than he is comfortable with, he may increase his impersonal demeanor and thus signal to others that he does not appreciate what they are trying to accomplish.

The writer's appearance of reserve in emotional circumstances may make him less approachable, as far as other people are concerned. Since his feelings are less likely to show, they are significant when they do surface. Under extreme pressure, he could respond impulsively; however, such action is not his normal response. When it happens, it means that the emotions within him have exploded past his normal control.
narasi.medium: The writer uses self-control in most areas of his life. He attempts to approach situations objectively and to keep his emotions, desires and actions under control. He usually thinks before acting, except in situations that are very personal or highly emotionally charged.
narasi.low:
The writer is impulsive and inclined to act before thinking or to act without thought. He responds to the emotion of the moment. His automatic response comes from his feelings, not from his thinking. He lets action get ahead of thought. He responds automatically to the way other people and situations affect him. Whatever he feels pours out before he has time to think it through. His emotional reactions surface without restraint. He is aware of what he is doing, but only after the fact, not before. At the time he is rashly expressing feelings or an idea he is not thinking of consequences.

In situations where it is important to express an immediate reaction, he works to advantage. But where a considered response is required, he is a liability. He is not likely to take time for second thought and often finds himself committed to something he does not really want to do. It is hard to predict what he will say or do next.

The writer is likely to be a poor listener. He often changes the subject or interrupts. He cannot hear what others are saying because he is talking himself, or just waiting until he can say what he wants to say. Quite often, his impetuousness will cause damage that will take longer to repair than it did to destroy. He is often sorry, but even experience does not change this kind of conduct.

narasi.high:
The writer is able to change without difficulty so as to conform to new and altered circumstances. He is accommodating and yielding to the desires of others. He adapts to his surroundings by changing his behavior according to the requirements of the situation. He looks at the alternatives, and from those available, picks out a reasonable course of action.

The writer is receptive to outside opinions. He is willing to try the unfamiliar and he will compromise, if that seems the wiser thing to do. He has the ability to revise his attitude in keeping with changing situations in his life. He is easier to live with than a more rigid person. He is slower to become irritated or upset by little things.

The writer would function to advantage in areas where self-directive ability is not an essential requirement for success, such as mail carrying, bakery work, production line work or some jobs in the creative field.

With adaptability very high, the writer is too easily influenced. He is subjective and suffers frequent changes of mood. He takes things at surface value and is uncommitted. His native tendency is to act on feelings rather than facts.

The writer lacks self-directive ability. He tends to pursue various interests and most likely, will let others set his goals for him. He wants to feel that he is part of every new development, every new event or relationship. Others, however, may feel that he is too changeable and cannot be relied upon. They think he is irresponsible when he moves from one kind of experience to another, from one opinion to another. He compromises himself by his lack of mental commitment.
narasi.medium: The writer has the ability to adjust to change in situations and with others, if necessary. This is especially true in areas where he already knows what he can expect or in situations where he feels fully competent. Defensiveness and insecurities will interfere with his flexibility in situations that are unfamiliar and therefore threatening, or when dealing with people who are superior or unfamiliar to him.
narasi.low:
The writer is adverse to change. Once his mind is made up and his attitude is fixed, it is hard for anyone else to convert him. Foremost, he wants security and certainty. He keeps to his chosen course and is unwilling to compromise, even when evidence exists as to the advantageous results of the compromise. He will not change his mind and has little “give” under pressure.

The writer is afraid to try the new or let anyone else try it. He finds it difficult, if not impossible, to adjust to any kind of deviation he, himself, has not initiated. His rigidity is often instrumental in keeping others from trying out new approaches if he feels that they are threatening to him. His natural tendency is to cling to the familiar and to the security it affords. He recreates, and repeats what he has been doing before. He regulates his life strictly according to established rules. Moreover, he tries to force his routine on the people around him.

The writer is more liable to labor steadfastly to make a relationship work, “for better or for worse.” Vocationally, he would function best where unyieldingness is needed as part of the job, such as accounting, auditing, law enforcement, or criminal correction.

narasi.high:
The writer is very sociable, expressive and demonstrative. He is able to communicate his thoughts and feelings openly without the need to resort to indirect forms of intercourse. He takes more time to cover a subject and may even ramble on with words.

The writer is more personal in what he talks about and he can talk freely of even the most personal aspects of his life. He can express openly and directly what goes on in his life in the present, whether it is anger or love. If he feels hurt, he verbalizes his anger right away; he does not get an unexplained headache a day later. He knows he is angry and expresses it appropriately. He does not have to store it up unconsciously until he explodes over a trivial incident. Once his anger is expressed, he is released from the inner pressures that would upset him further.

The writer is not afraid to speak his mind. He is able to accept criticism or different opinions that others may offer. He contributes his own ideas to make his work more efficient and productive. He often interlaces what he has to say with personal examples that enhance his communication. He is easily puzzled and upset with others who are more close-mouthed and reticent.

The writer is willing to stand up for his views and he will clear up misunderstandings, even though the result might be detrimental to him. He believes that a healthy degree of friction between people leads to better communication, better understanding, and mutual respect.

The writer is well qualified as public speaker, teacher, entertainer, or sales person.
narasi.medium:
The writer is willing to communicate openly in situations where he feels sure of himself. He stands up for his opinions as long as his self-esteem is not threatened.

In situations where he feels insecure, he is more taciturn. He appreciates when others take the lead in the conversation. He glows when others give him a compliment or talk about things that make him look good. He welcomes talking to someone who is interested in him as a person rather than just talking about himself.

When the writer feels uneasy, he is more likely to communicate through obscure methods, or not at all.
narasi.low:
The writer is self-conscious and secretive. In personal relationships, he appears hesitant and fearful. He is reticent and uncommunicative, most of the time. He needs much encouragement and coaxing to speak of matters of personal concern. He feels threatened by overt communication and often keeps his thoughts and feelings within.

The writer’s communication with others is composed mostly of agreements or silence. He is more inclined to listen to what other people are saying than to speak himself. When he talks, he has a strong need for assurance that he has said, done and concluded the right things.

When the writer is most upset, he is least inclined to talk it out. He holds back his emotional distress and personal dilemmas. But they weigh on him.

The writer is unable to clear misunderstandings when they occur. It is difficult for him to start talking and he rarely comes right to the point. Instead, he starts by talking around what he really wants to say. He is more likely to write down his most personal thoughts than speak about them.

The writer cannot disagree or argue because he is afraid of losing friends. As a result, something unspoken frequently stands between him and the people close to him.

The writer refuses to tell others how he feels and thereby denies others the support they may be glad to give, if they knew how. On the other hand, he often feels people should be doing things for him without direct request and he feels slighted when they don’t perceive his needs.

The writer would function to advantage in positions requiring discretion. He fits well into banking, investments, insurance, property management or corporation law, for example.

narasi.high:
The writer has a strong need for constantly being surrounded by people. He has the urge to form friendships with the people he likes. He actively seeks the company of others. He is informal and easy to meet. No one seems a stranger to him. People stimulate him to think and feel. He enjoys social gatherings and derives a sense of security from group support. Given the choice, he will be with people every time. Working with inanimate objects or information may be a problem.

The writer likes people who are warm and quick to show their feelings. He is uncomfortable with individuals who are cold and detached, as they do not meet his need for closeness and affinity. His family and his friends mean a lot to him. He needs to be near them geographically, at least part of the time. He may get involved on impulse and his emotional needs are such that he may intrude even where he is not wanted.

The writer is unable to work or perform well without others with him or at least being near. He is lonesome and despondent when denied the company of others of like mind. His need to associate may be especially intense when feeling anxious or upset. He expects support from others and finds it difficult to stand alone. He is a more sympathetic appearing person, and he is moved by the troubles of others, just as he is by his own.

The writer shows little discrimination in relationships. He reacts immediately to another person. He is readily accessible and less formal in style. He is familiar in tone, language and attitude. He becomes acquainted so easily and with so many people that he classifies everyone he meets as his friend. In the office or on the job, he might spend a great deal of time visiting and talking to other employees rather than doing his work.

With this writer, others can almost always count on the conversation taking a personal trend.

His attitude would be valuable in professions such as nursing, reception work, teaching, the healing arts, service organizations, and anywhere where he must deal with the public in a service related way.
narasi.medium:
The writer enjoys being involved with people on an interpersonal level; however, after a period of closeness, he needs periods where he can be by himself. If the writer works in close association with other people most of the time, his need for interpersonal relationships may be filled on the job. On the other hand, if he is forced to work by himself most of the time, he may seek “social” time to balance this.

The writer is especially interested in people with whom he shares a common interest or who represent purposeful accomplishment to him. He is irritated by the uselessness of social activity for its own sake.

The writer respects the personal sphere of other people. He anticipates to be treated in the same way. He would resent personal questions that, in his opinion, are too intimate.
narasi.low:
Outlets in the intellectual or productive area stimulate the writer’s mind. His response to people is limited. He is discriminating and seems to know instinctively whether he does or does not want to be associated with a certain individual. He manifests a restraint that automatically places a barrier between himself and his acquaintances. He selects few friends and he is close to few people. He withdraws from personal contacts that he, himself, has not desired.

He likes to be treated with formality and respect. Unless he is well acquainted with someone, he expects them to call him by his title and last name.

The writer distrusts relationships that are too emotional or too intimate too soon. He is strong on being properly introduced. He resents any apparent invasion of his privacy or the taking of acquaintanceship for granted. He is uncomfortable in the pressure of large crowds and uneasy in the ordinary give-and-take of daily living. He likes his privacy and prefers to be left to himself and his own introspective thinking.

The writer focuses on how he, himself, is feeling rather than on the people surrounding him. He has difficulties with people who make demands or cling to him. His personal life is private, with few people allowed to share his personal sphere. He does not burden others with his personal problems. Even if he longs for support, it is difficult for him to reach out and communicate his need.

The writer’s interest is focused on his own goals and problems instead of on others’ interests or dreams. He can be with a group of people and yet not hear much of what is going on, for he has a highly developed mechanism of “tuning inward.”

The writer may have difficulty demanding proper recognition for his work or asking for a raise. He may rationalize that it is not important when the truth is that he hates to get involved. He functions best with co-workers or partners who will take care of the public duties that he finds uncomfortable to do himself.

If the writer is intelligent and creative, his basic personality may work. Otherwise, he may perform well below efficiency. Work that is well within his capacity may be avoided because it involves too much close contact with others.

narasi.high:
The writer has a warm and friendly personality that attracts others. In his relations, he is outgoing and sympathetic. He is thoughtful and compassionate. People warm to him quickly and are pleased to be in his company. He shows his friendly feelings in his eyes and with the expression of his face. He is kind from the heart and uses his smile a lot. He has a special skill for putting others at ease. Spreading kindness is what he enjoys most in life. He takes delight in seeing others happy and willingly adjusts to their needs. Others are attracted by his warmth and cannot help but like him.

The writer communicates genuinely and in a kindly manner. It is important to him that others should know his feelings as well as his intent. He is especially amiable with those people close too him. He is never too busy to share himself with them and listen to their problems. He may call them just to ask how they are.

The writer is particularly kind when another's situation is similar to an experience he, himself, has endured in the past. In relationships with others, he is steady and dependable. He feels genuine loyalty to those he gives his friendship to.
narasi.medium:
Most of the time, the writer is friendly and consistent in his emotional reaction to people. On the job, he is pleasant but matter-of-fact. He shows that he has manners and good taste. He is friendly without being personal. And he expects others to be businesslike, too. He gets along best with people who think equally purposefully.

The writer may have self-protective feelings in some areas that may cause him to pull back under certain circumstances.
narasi.low:
The writer is emotionally immature. He is subjective in his relationships with others. He tends to focus on how he, himself, is feeling at all times. He has trouble getting sentiment into a conversation. He may be moody and unpredictable.

When the writer is friendly, it is an act of conscious choice because he believes it is to his own advantage to act in a friendly way. In reality, he is hardly considering others' sensibilities.

The writer responds more selfishly and appraises other people's reaction on how he, himself, would think and behave under similar circumstances. When the writer puts himself out for someone, he usually makes sure that he gets credit for what he has done.

aspek.keterangan_umum: This trait is a major indicator of how an individual is responding to life, either in terms of human (spiritual) or material values.

narasi.high:
The writer is able to identify with others. He has an intellectual and intuitive awareness of another person's state of mind. He is truly empathetic. He can share another's sorrow as if it were his own. He knows how the other person feels and has the ability to communicate this understanding to him. He has a desire to reach out and help those who are less fortunate than he is, himself. He often places the welfare and happiness of others above his own.

The writer has experienced many ups and down in life. He knows how it felt, and he has empathy with those experiencing similar situations. He feels involved with the people around him and appreciates others' wins and losses.

The writer is charitable and performs tasks for other people without expecting a monetary return. He responds to the needs of others automatically and performs the service himself, personally. He is full of human warmth, caring about the needs of others. His desire is to be of service and it is the personal touch he loves to give. He is concerned with healing, helping and making others comfortable and happy. Material things, for him, are less important than human relationships.
