The writer often believes in a sort of barter system of labor, commodities, friendship, or any medium other than dollars and cents.

Helpful and service oriented, the writer would like to be in a position that gives him the opportunity to comfort and protect others. He is easily moved by people in plight. This desire to help could lead into a career concerned with the welfare of others. He gravitates toward nursing, teaching, or service kind of jobs.
narasi.medium: When the writer's defense system does not interfere, he is empathetic. He can feel with others and put himself into their place. Sometimes, he is too taken up with his own affairs to be able to sense how others are reacting. He believes in paying for what he receives. He also believes in just monetary return for whatever services he renders.
narasi.low:
The writer finds it difficult to share feelings and experiences other than his own. His focus is on “me” rather than “we.”

The writer lacks spontaneous helpfulness. He often has to be told what others need instead of having the ability to sense it. When he responds, he may secure the service, but he will seldom perform it himself, personally.

The writer is concerned with value for money, securing the best service at a bargain. Those close to him may see him as caring more for material things than relationships. He seems to be putting a price tag on everything and trying to “buy” his way. The writer is a good administrator. He has an appreciation for money and its use. He can keep accounts effectively or stay within a budget. He always knows what his service is worth.

The writer works best where impersonal relations are the rule, where there is organizing to do, where value for money comes first, or business as such is to be conducted. Whatever field he enters, he tends toward the administrative rather than the service end. He fits well into accounting, hard sell operations, administration, efficiency and time study work, work involving money directly, such as banking, investment and loans, appraising, commercial teaching, or credit management.

aspek.keterangan_umum: Endurance is an important trait. It indicates the natural positive or negative tendency of the writer to express himself in continued real, observable accomplishment. The function of most other characteristics is affected by the intensity of this trait.

narasi.high:
The writer is result oriented. Once he decides on a goal, he follows through and keeps moving until he attains it. He stays with what he is trying to accomplish. He even thrives in adverse surroundings. He makes a commitment and perseveres despite temporary doubts or personal limitations. He has the ability to let go of something that paralyzes so many people – insistence on the guarantee of the desired outcome. He proceeds instead with the conviction that he will grow with the demands and will be “big enough” to meet the challenge.

The writer does not have to be prodded. He moves forward because of an inner desire to get the job done. He stays away from mental considerations that bring him into defeat. Only positive pictures are allowed to stay in his mind. He keeps moving regardless of how he feels in the moment. When he is faced with an obstacle, he takes it as an opportunity and tries to find alternative means to finish what he has set out to do.

Vocationally, the writer's attitude is an asset. It enables him to succeed in whatever field he has chosen. He finds it painful to do superficial work. He is likewise distressed when others do not finish the job according to his measure of completion.

To others, his sense of commitment may appear ruthless. He seems to be thinking only of his goals and often creates opportunities at the expense of others. He uses others’ services to further his own interests. To him, the end justifies the means.

Vocationally, the writer serves well in the healing arts, in emergency situations, in the military, or in political and financial enterprises. Other suitable occupations are engineering, law, architecture, and most types of investigative work.

With self-confidence low, determination enables the writer to move forward no matter how inadequate he may feel inside. Others may be amazed to learn that his confidence is low because of the accomplishments he has achieved. He may continue to have doubts about himself, but he still keeps his focus forward on his goals.
narasi.medium:
The writer is a moderately determined individual (but without the friction in personal relations that characterizes the high score on this trait). Once he is familiar with a project or task, he will complete it, even with some setbacks. He takes advantage of opportunities; however, he will not use others to get ahead.

The writer is not leaning too far either way; he can continue to move reasonably in a forward direction, or make a sideways shift, if that seems to be the reasonable thing to do. If he feels blocked, he is willing to try another way of achieving a goal or will move forward by maneuvering. The writer may need to be motivated by someone else to undertake unfamiliar projects (unless the score in motivation is high). He requires specific instructions to handle unaccustomed jobs.

(High scores in the Defenses Syndrome will lessen the determination to finish a job.)
narasi.low:
The writer lets go under pressure before it is necessary or right. He needs supervision to complete what he initiates. He usually starts out fine but gradually loses interest. He gets bogged down while thinking about problems and gives in to obstacles too easily. He builds up negative pictures in his mind and takes setbacks as a personal affront. He is indecisive when opportunities present themselves.

The writer needs much outside encouragement with difficult or long-lasting jobs. In order that he complete a task, someone else needs to outline the procedure in advance. While working, the writer will do exactly the parts assigned to him. If a detail is left out, the job will either stop at that point or will be done incorrectly. If the writer occasionally has to alter the procedure, he will not succeed.

However, once he learns how to do a certain task, he will be a reliable worker in that field. He can be depended upon to do a routine job just as he was taught to do it.

(The writer is likely to be an under-achiever unless he has many compensating high scores.)

Important! The score may be low due to old age or poor health. This should be ruled out before drawing a conclusion. The writer lets go under pressure before it is necessary or right. He needs supervision to complete what he initiates. He usually starts out fine but gradually loses interest. He gets bogged down while thinking about problems and gives in to obstacles too easily. He builds up negative pictures in his mind and takes setbacks as a personal affront. He is indecisive when opportunities present themselves.

The writer needs much outside encouragement with difficult or long-lasting jobs. In order that he complete a task, someone else needs to outline the procedure in advance. While working, the writer will do exactly the parts assigned to him. If a detail is left out, the job will either stop at that point or will be done incorrectly. If the writer occasionally has to alter the procedure, he will not succeed.

However, once he learns how to do a certain task, he will be a reliable worker in that field. He can be depended upon to do a routine job just as he was taught to do it.

(The writer is likely to be an under-achiever unless he has many compensating high scores.)

Important! The score may be low due to old age or poor health. This should be ruled out before drawing a conclusion. With self esteem low, he is more inclined to sulk instead of speaking up. With low determination and high authoritarian, the writer exerts pressure for awhile but finally gives up in frustration because all his fortitude did not bring results.

Important! Compatibility between people with greatly differing scores is difficult. The low score writer is a constant source of frustration for the other. He can destroy the relationship with his ever-present doubt and the calamitous tendency to give up.

aspek.keterangan_umum: Physical energy is not a major trait, generally speaking. However, it is significant in discerning the basic reaction a person will have. It reveals whether the individual will react predominantly on the mental or physical level.

narasi.high:
The writer has a great deal of physical energy. He has the strength to sustain long hours of work and maintain high performance, even under stress. During prolonged or arduous tasks, he remains relatively calm and competent. He may set a fast pace for others because he, himself, has so much stamina. He is naturally active. To others it may appear that his physical nature governs his whole personality. He is quickly aroused and involved physically. He enjoys doing physical things. His initial response to anything is usually on the bodily level and he will take action to work something out.

The writer is a matter-of-fact individual. He is concerned with the realistic areas of life. With this pragmatic bent of mind he is good at taking knowledge and turning it into useful application. He has the energy and the drive to put his ideas into action. Usually, he simplifies complicated information to deal with it more effectively.

The writer is built for continuing physical action. He needs active manual labor to use up his strength. If unreleased, the pent-up energy turns into restlessness. He functions to advantage where physical action is the key to success. His body is ordinarily in better shape to take the demands he places on it. He is usually interested in sports, endurance contests, tests of stamina or hard manual labor. Jobs such as lumbering, mining, carrying mail by foot, excavating, construction work, road building and handling of freight would be ideal.
narasi.medium: The writer starts at a satisfactory balance between mental and physical energy. He has sufficient stamina for average needs. He would function well in a position that requires a more even output of mental and physical energies. Nursing, geology, anthropology, or civil service jobs would be satisfying.
narasi.low:
The writer does poorly where vigorous physical activity is involved. He has little stamina and fatigues easily. This, in turn, affects other traits such as optimism and enthusiasm. Through motivation, the writer may counteract part of this.) He will prefer to work with his mind, rather than his hands, most often. He usually does well in desk or office work. With motivation, he will stay with mental work until it is completed. He should be permitted to engage in mental rather than little physical labor. Since he does not like bodily activity, he is inclined to disregard the physical side of life. He fails to keep his body in shape and usually has less recuperative strength.

The writer functions best where thinking and planning, not physical follow-through, are required. He is more naturally suited for office vocations, white collar or mental-emphasis fields.

narasi.high:
The writer favors progress and seeks continuing improvement. He moves forward and onward toward desirable results. His focus is outward on the new. He is courageous and thinks ahead rather than back to the past. He adapts to new people, locations and situations painlessly.

The writer is the kind of individual who builds from the ground up and gets wrapped up in his career and projects. If he has a choice of jobs, he will often deliberately take the one that offers a risk. He prefers to be engaged in work where he can employ his flair for devising novel methods and inventing and not just maintaining or conserving. He is ingenious and likes to put forward new options. He is a natural innovator and not afraid to risk his reputation for the implementation of progressive concepts.

The writer has a strong desire for self development and attainment of personal goals. His conviction is that he is going to make the future what he wants it to be. He focuses his energy on the plans and actions required to exceed himself. He is willing to evolve and grow in order to be “better than he ever was.” Inwardly, he feels secure. He may be faced with frustration or conflicts, but he has the power to go ahead anyway. He is able to achieve innovative and satisfying results, not just once or twice but repeatedly. He gives himself a chance of achieving at peak performance and maintaining this level once he gets there.

The writer is innovative and creative and possesses a special ability for devising more efficient ways of handling the work load. He will deliberately try a different way of doing something rather than use a tried and trusted process. He is not prepared to be a slave to outmoded ideas, nor does he adhere to tradition for the sake of custom. He has to see a good reason for continuing to use established procedures. He prefers to work with new concepts and preferably new materials. He thinks in terms of building the new rather than conserving the old. He dislikes working with leftovers and reusing materials, as a general rule. He may show little concern with time, cost, or where the money is coming from.

The writer will not be content without some expansion, however minor. There may be no dramatic sweeping changes, and progress may be made one step at a time. He may build gradually, without flash or fanfare, but he will develop and build. His greatest satisfaction comes from improving what went before and this is what he aims to do in his work and his life. Once he has planted himself in a position where he can build higher, he moves forward with confidence.

The writer is willing to contemplate the viewpoints of other people while retaining the ability to generate his own. He sees himself, and people in general, as the basic natural resource and acts with confidence that human beings are capable of much more than defending the status quo.

If he encounters obstacles, the writer is unlikely to give in to anger or despair. He responds with purposeful activity and focuses on transforming the stumbling blocks into stepping-stones. No matter how rough it gets, he always feels that he can do something about it. He is able to use a lesson learned from failure constructively in seeking future success. He takes setbacks as signs that it is time to correct course. He is willing to make the necessary changes in his habits of mind and work, so that more satisfying results will be produced the next time. He sees the ability to correct course as a necessity in fulfilling his goals. He anticipates and adapts to major change while maintaining momentum within the overall plan.

The writer can take constructive criticism. He accepts it when it is justified and ignores it when it is not.

He sees himself differently from other people. He is setting new norms. He focuses carefully on what he needs in order to excel. He does this by thinking carefully about what he wants, how and in the future, choosing the most important goals, ruling out those that are for him too easy or too risky. He determines what he truly cares about and then devotes himself to that pursuit.

The writer is bound by no preconceived limitations. He has the ability to reach for what could be, and to rise above his fears. He knows how to act decisively when opportunity presents itself. He has the ability to start many things on his own and he has the drive to put his ideas into action.

The writer has a deep commitment to his goals. He feels that what he is doing is the result of his own free choice. He is doing it because he wants to do it, and the consequences of his activities will be valuable to him.

He is inclined to get wrapped up in his career and projects. He is the doer and less the enjoyer. He is likely to miss meals and does not consistently take care of his own health. (He is probably a poor housekeeper.)

The writer functions best in situations that challenge his mind to unfold. He is unhappy with dull, mundane detail work. He would be happier as an efficiency expert in charge of trouble shooting than being forced into the confining mold of a nine-to-five position, no matter how fancy the title. If there is a bottleneck somewhere in the production line, he can be depended on to come up with a workable solution. “Anything can be improved on.” is his motto and he will be happiest in a job where he can experiment and test his ideas in different and dynamic ways. An employer will not find him edgy or peeking at the clock around five o'clock. He will willingly put in extra hours if necessary, or if there is an exciting project under way. And with his progressive schemes and original plans, he may double the companies profit and lower its overhead.

Progressiveness is desirable for work as an engineer, draftsman, architect, builder of all kinds, shop foreman, mechanic, designer or artist.

With progressiveness very high, the writer may be extravagant in his demands for new materials. He prefers to work with the new when what is at hand would serve as well. In this sense he is wasteful. He is so interested in producing something innovative that he overlooks the cost of production, the demand, and the profit margin. He focuses so much on the new that he fails to appreciate older, worthwhile concepts and ideas.

With physical energy high, the writer is a lover of action and motion. He likes activity for himself and is interested in anything that moves, such as automobiles, railways, printing presses, steam shovels and airplanes. He is interested in agriculture, and in such activities as exploring, building and aviation. With physical energy low, the writer usually will start more than he can finish. In his complete involvement with the project, he may overlook his own creature comforts and allow himself to become run down.
narasi.medium:
The writer is an adapter. He is at his best when he is improving, not changing, what he already knows how to do. Average levels of performance are acceptable to him. He feels more comfortable with established procedures and prefers to keep doing things “the way they were always done around here.”

He likes to blend the old with the new. He has trouble adjusting himself to progress he, has not initiated. When asked to support innovative concepts, it is very difficult for him to be enthusiastic, especially if renouncing “something that has worked just as well” is involved. Once he is familiar with an idea, it is difficult for him to readjust his thinking. He likes to preserve traditional ideas just as he likes to conserve material things.

With self-confidence or motivation high, the writer may be in a developmental or transitional stage where his inner security is growing. In that case, he would be willing to slightly upgrade his skills, take some chances, or adapt somewhat to changing conditions.
narasi.low:
The writer is conforming and conventional. He is distrustful of new ideas, new approaches and new materials. He is bound to the familiar. He feels most comfortable with established procedures and prefers to keep doing things “the way they were always done around here.” He may use persistence, stubbornness or a domineering demeanor to help him preserve the status quo.

The writer relies on past successes as a guide to what he undertakes or is willing to try. He is traditional in the sense of wanting to do only what has already been proven satisfactory by others and therefore seems safe and secure to do. He is stuck in an excessive need for security. He wants to remain inside a comfort zone where things are familiar, unchallenging and, unfortunately, less productive.

(Such writers often “pack-rat” away items that they may never have use for, but just cannot throw away. They usually love food and will relish being asked to dinner or to other congenial occasions. They are distressed by seeing anything thrown out or going to waste. They often over-eat to prevent waste of food. They are prone to buy “bargain materials” that are of inferior quality simply because they make a temporary saving by doing so.

These writers are generally great at entertaining and at creature comforts. They have a knack making the most of food and shelter and set up housekeeping wherever they go. At the ball game, they may be organized with blankets and refreshments they have brought along. They like to make use of leftovers. They are known to combine errands, to save extra expenditure of time and gasoline.)

The writer looks for direction every time he has to make a move. With his fearful attitude, he is a hindrance to his organization (employer) and to himself.

What the writer is doing has been imposed on him by others, he is doing it because he is forced to, and the consequences of his activities will not be a source of pride for him. Since he feels that external factors determine his fate, he does not consider carefully his goals in life, nor does he concern himself about what he himself can do to further his cause.

The writer has an aversion to risk taking and innovation. Fear of failure, real or imagined, thwarts result-oriented activity. He considers short-range objectives as ends in themselves, forgetting where they were originally intended to take him. Being busy often passes for being productive. He engages in random activity which is quite different from motion with purpose and clear direction.

If the writer encounters stumbling blocks he responds with vexation and helplessness. He acts not on insight but on memory and on old information (which may not have been accurate in the first place) that there is nothing more he can do.

Vocationally, the writer is most satisfied in a “conserving” kind of job, such as museum keeper, repair mechanic, antique dealer, dentist and all kinds of maintenance work.

narasi.high:
"The writer is able to deal promptly and effectively with difficulties. He has the ability for effective brainstorming and the potential for finding options and alternatives in the absence of normal resources. He envisions innovative solutions to problems and makes useful contributions to his line of work. He can find ways to improve almost anything.

The writer is a good associative thinker. He deals easily with various kinds of situations. If there is a solution to the problem, he can be counted on to find it and he is capable of offering answers that will be quite original.

The writer is adept in the art of mental replay and has a built-in ability to deal with emergencies. He can meet a crisis swiftly. He mentally reviews what worked in the past and then applies the solution to present problems.

The writer uses his imagination in a practical way to improve upon tangible things. He may streamline existing work methods for more efficiency or find a new use for existing things. He may envision how to change the form and shape of products, how to package them more attractively, or how to market more seductively. He is an excellent person to have on the payroll because he can find many ways to keep costs down. If there is a suggestion box around, he will drop in many unique, workable ideas.

There are few situations that the writer cannot deal with. He is flexible and adaptable when working things out. He appreciates the usefulness of others' creative ideas and will probably throw in a few promotional schemes of his own.

The writer would be well suited for work as a designer, advertiser, architect, sales person, efficiency expert or trouble shooter."
narasi.medium: The writer has some ability to be resourceful. However, he does not use this skill consistently. He applies his ingenuity mostly in areas with which he is already familiar. When he sees tangible results for his effort, this encourages him to be resourceful in similar situations.
narasi.low:
The writer has a one-track mind. He lacks innovativeness, especially under pressure. He needs to be shown how to do a job. He needs prior experience in order to apply knowledge to a new situation.

The writer takes risks carefully. He prefers traditional methods in doing a job. He is bound to the familiar and distrustful of new procedures. He clings to known methods and “safe” routines. He is unable to develop alternative procedures if one method does not work out. His approach seldom varies since it has been proven effective in the past. He may apply force instead of reason.

The writer needs to adhere to a fixed program or routine. He can be depended upon to follow guidelines in areas which he already knows. He is dependable in applying instructions but will be overwhelmed when faced with challenges larger than he is accustomed to.

The writer would be competent working as an accountant, auditor, banker, pattern maker, adjustor or ticket broker. He fits into more routine activities such as production line assembly worker, machine operator, bookkeeper or file clerk.

narasi.high:
The writer is well organized and excels in planning strategy. He has a flair for organization, for handling numbers of people and projects. Time, materials and place are all important to him. He is never more satisfied than when they all form a harmonious whole of which he is the center. Efficiency and order have tremendous appeal to him.

Once he has made plans, he carries them out methodically. He budgets his hours so well that he gets much done in a relatively short period of time. He knows exactly how much time should be allotted to different tasks. When he makes a commitment to be somewhere at a certain hour, he is there. If he says he will have a task completed by a certain date, others can rely on him.

The writer derives satisfaction from systematic accomplishment and he plans efficiently and effortlessly. His greatest satisfaction is to put everything neatly in its place, and he tries to accomplish this in every department of his life. He makes and stays with schedules and may list in writing at the start of the day what he wants to accomplish. He assembles his materials for a given task before he actually commences work. The extra time spent in planning saves him many hours in preventing hit-or-miss starts and retracing his steps later on.

He has a keen feeling for the organization of situations and projects. He has a strong sense of order and a feeling for the natural progression of events. He comprehends projects in their entirety and knows the significance of each component part. He has the ability to make segments work in consonance with each other and integrates them into one efficient whole. He feels where each part goes to build the complete project.

The writer has little patience with schedules that are wasteful or procedures that lack efficiency. He will rearrange office or business systems to make sure that the organization runs with sensible proficiency.

His sense of time and involvement with organizational detail is applied to the management of people as well. However, as soon as the human element enters the picture, the task becomes more difficult. People are not satisfied to be assigned a slot like pieces of machinery. He must bring into play considerable management ability. He must plan time and space for them with careful observance of personal considerations.

If the writer has spare time, he uses it productively and he expects others to imitate him.

The writer enjoys activities that require intricate planning. With his ability to handle and organize people, equipment and materials, he would fit well into a position where he constructs a whole organization. He would be excellent in planning within a large corporation. Whatever he does, he would function best in directing active, growing projects.
narasi.medium:
The writer plans his activities but he does not spend more time with scheduling than is necessary. Particulars are not his forte. He neither programs every detail nor does he try to foresee every contingency. He takes a chance that he can handle some unexpected changes and make decisions as he goes along.

He likes to know what is coming up ahead of time, but he does not like to be so tightly organized that he cannot make last-minute changes in his schedule or plans.

While he may have the capacity to plan ahead, it is often difficult for him to stay with his original schedule once the project is underway.
narasi.low:
The writer has difficulty managing time and resources efficiently. He handles things as they are happening and makes arrangements as he goes along. His “moment to moment” approach suggests poor foresight and diminished planning skills. Most of the time, he lives an unscheduled life. He takes life as it comes and trusts in his ability to make random choices that will bring him to his desired goals.

With his loose organizational style, the writer would work better in a structured environment that dictates how much will be done in any given day.

aspek.keterangan_umum:
Psychiatrists have long had difficulty in classifying the antisocial personality. In 1835, J. C. Pritchard offered the first systematic description. He coined the phrase “moral insanity,” applying it to individuals in whom the moral and active principles of the mind are strongly perverted and depraved,” making them “incapable of conducting themselves with decency and propriety in the business of life.”¹ The term “moral imbecile” was widely used in the nineteenth century to indicate that these individuals were intellectually sound but ethically defective.

Many investigators used the term “psychopathic personality” but this phrase was criticized as implying mental illness. The term was dropped in the 1968 revision of DSM-II (Diagnostic and Statistic Manual of Mental Disorders); instead, antisocial personalities were classified as individuals suffering from “personality trait disturbances.”² Many authorities believed that the disturbance is due to a hereditary neurological disorder, but others have submitted contradictory reports. Some investigators have found abnormal EEG patterns in 50 to 80% of the cases, but this finding has also been challenged. Others have attributed to impairment of higher control centers in the nervous system. Eysenck believes that the individual does not develop an adequate conscience because he does not acquire the conditioned reactions that lead to normal social behavior.

Others have attempted to search out psychological and environmental factors that might give rise to this particular life style. Undoubtedly community influences play a role in some cases: crowded conditions, deprivation, gangs. But these do not appear to be key factors for two reasons: antisocial tendencies frequently make their appearance early in life, before neighborhood influences could have much effect; and antisocial individuals are by no means concentrated at lower socio-economic levels. In fact, a high percentage come from middle- and upper-class families. Evidence has shown that in a large proportion of the cases the mother was easygoing and overindulgent. The father was usually distant, stern, hard-driving and very successful. The child therefore failed to develop a deep attachment to either parent, although he usually found it easier to adopt the easygoing attitudes of the mother than to live up to the father's expectations. Such families put on a good facade in order to conceal their inner conflicts from the world, and this contributes to the shallowness of the child's emotions and his feeling that he must put on an act to win social approval. It is not far cry from such an attitude to the superficial charm and tendency to manipulate other people that characterize the antisocial personality. Nor is it hard to understand that a boy who has been rejected by his father may become hostile and resentful toward all authority as he grows up.

Successful treatment of the antisocial personality is largely a hope of the future. The behavior patterns are so firmly established and there is so little self-understanding and genuine desire to change, that the individual is extremely resistant to therapy of any kind. As a group, they include a varied assortment of unscrupulous business people, politicians, prostitutes, and impostors. They are rarely committed to mental hospitals but sometimes serve jail or prison sentences for their offenses. Most of them, however, manage to keep out of the hands of the law and talk their way out of conviction. The two characteristics considered most typical for the antisocial personality are “lovelessness” (the inability to feel any empathy for, or loyalty to, another person) and “guiltlessness” (the inability to feel any remorse for his own actions, no matter how reprehensible).

narasi.high:
The writer is impulsive and unable to abide by the customs and laws of society. He lacks anxiety or guilt regarding his behavior. The specific symptoms include (1) defective conscience; (2) good intelligence; (3) absence of anxiety; (4) putting up a good front; (5) inability to form attachments; (6) disregard for truth; (7) self-defeating behavior: the writer frustrates his own apparent aims by actions that bring on failure and disaster even at the height of success; (8) rejection of authority and discipline; (9) lack of foresight: lives for the pleasures of the moment; (10) extreme irresponsibility; (11) failure to learn from experience.

Lying, stealing, truancy, vandalism, initiating fights, running away from home, are typical childhood signs. This pattern then continues into adulthood. It may include failure to honor financial obligations, to function as a responsible parent, and an inability to sustain consistent work behavior. The writer fails to conform to social norms and tends to be in continuous social and legal trouble. He repeatedly performs acts that are grounds for arrest, such as harassing others, destroying property, or having an illegal occupation. When his anger is aroused, he can become violent, even cruel. After the incident, he is annoyed if others are upset. He cannot understand why they dwell on the damage he does. He shows no remorse and benefits little from punishment. He feels justified in injuring or mistreating others and has great facility in lying. He is a show-off who presumes he has a lot of power and revels in the pain he inflicts on others. His capacity seems limitless. He is easily bored and has a constant need for thrills. He fails to respond normally to the threats of danger that deter most people from antisocial acts. (The writer may be driving while intoxicated or frequently be getting speeding tickets.)

The writer is often attractive, intelligent and charming but maintains no deep loyalties to any persons or groups. He seems to be unable to sustain lasting, close, warm and responsible relationships with friends, family or sexual partners. He often manipulates others for his benefit. (He is the typical “con artist.”) His sex life tends to be impersonal and trivial. He lacks self directive ability. He is highly impulsive and unable to follow any life plan. He gives up goals and success for reasons that others cannot understand. His facade of competence and sincerity often wins him promising job opportunities, but he has little staying power. His restlessness and impulsiveness soon lead him into escapades that reveal his true nature. He may accumulate debts, commit crimes, or desert his family. When caught, the writer's declarations of repentance are so dramatic that he often escapes punishment and is given another chance. But he seldom lives up to these expectations; what he says has little relation to what he does. He can be very dramatic or he may display an uninviting behavior, with drink or sometimes without.

Important! The antisocial personality rarely carries out suicide threats.
narasi.medium: The tendency toward antisocial behavior exists in this person but it will show in behavior only under extreme stress. If circumstances in the writer's life produce only manageable amounts of stress, no antisocial behavior will occur. The type of antisocial reaction will also be far less intense and may go unnoticed by outsiders.
narasi.low:
With other scores in the “Vulnerability To Stress” syndrome low, the writer has good coping ability and is able to remain functional and effective under stress.

With other scores in the “Vulnerability To Stress” syndrome high, the writer still will not display criminal, dishonest or illegal behavior under stress. He will use other defenses to cope with the strain.

narasi.high:
The writer is emotionally immature and has poor self-discipline. He is at the mercy of his moods and subject to abrupt changes of feeling. When emotionally high, he is extremely optimistic, hopeful and apparently outgoing. When the wind changes, he does not just go down, he plummets into depression and fear. He presents a different face to the world just about every day. He cannot be depended upon from one moment to the next.

The writer's behavior is erratic. He is unable to control his reactions and attitudes. Others do not know what to expect from him from one minute to the next. He is “for this” today and “for that” tomorrow. He is especially unpredictable in situations where he feels powerless and he seldom realizes his own inconsistencies.

The writer's personality is a liability to those who have to depend on him, and his company is fatiguing. His friends learn to be cautious of him, knowing he is likely to be pleasant and obliging one moment and bitterly resentful the next. He has a tendency to make those around him suffer because he, himself, is dissatisfied. Sometimes they may feel he is merely out to make trouble for them. Not surprisingly, he encounters considerable discord with the people who must work and live with him.

The writer is unable to admit the truth about himself. Although he is very astute about criticizing others, he loathes having his faults pointed out. He tends to overlook his own shortcomings. He refuses to acknowledge that he may be wrong and prefers to blame the outside world for his imperfections.

The writer's assumptions about himself and others are subjective. Regardless of the facts at hand, he is unwilling to look at an issue from anything but a personal perspective. New experiences which are incompatible with his viewpoint are rejected or given a distorted meaning. Thus he avoids disturbing his structure of spurious assumptions.

The writer's loyalty is subjective and may be short-lived. He may be stubbornly loyal to avoid losing face by backing down. But if being true to a person or cause turns into a threat for him, he quickly changes.

The writer is unpredictable in expressing anger. He has not learned what to do with it. He is capable of suddenly blowing up and (with physicalness high) becoming physically violent. At other times, he may be mild-mannered even though the situation is similar. He is inclined to express anger in indirect ways, such as sulking, being sarcastic or disappearing into this shell and staying there without a spark of communication.

The writer is unpredictable in his work habits, too, and his working capacity is random. He is absent-minded, easily distracted and incalculable in his reactions. His instability may be either mental, or physical, or both. He either overrates his abilities and tackles more than he can realistically accomplish or he shies away from a difficult task because he underestimates what he can do. What the writer starts in one mood, he is prone to let go in an alternate frame of mind. He may give up or destroy what has taken him weeks or months to create. The effect in his everyday life is increased nervous irritability.The writer reacts without forethought to unfamiliar conditions. He is liable to make wrong responses, resulting in inconsistency and carelessness.
narasi.medium: The writer feels fairly confident in his ability to control and direct his own behavior. Unless he is under severe stress, he can be relied upon for loyalty and stability. Occasionally, he may act impulsively, but he is able to restrain impetuous and aggressive urges when necessary.
narasi.low:
The writer is predictable and stable. He is emotionally mature and has a fair sense of duty. He is persevering and uses his abilities, whether meager or ample, in productive activities. He uses good judgment. He looks at the facts and accepts reality as it is. He believes that problems can be worked out logically.

The writer thinks and acts in conformity with standards that are acceptable to him and to the society in which he lives. He finds many things set up to his advantage in the way of standard arrangements, procedures and routines.

The writer is loyal and dependable. He is careful and reliable in all areas of his life. He examines carefully the circumstances that may affect a decision or behavior. He chooses a judicious course of action and so avoids failure and disaster. Usually, he delays decisions until he has examined all possible ramifications of a project or relationship.

The writer may or may not be subjective. If he is, it will not affect his performance. Subjectivity would be more related to interpersonal relationships.

Important! Other traits in the stress syndrome may modify the findings in this trait.

aspek.keterangan_umum: The manipulative character is conditioned early in life. A child who has been badly hurt in relating to a parent may later take pride in never asking the “tyrant” for anything. By extension, he will ask nothing from life anymore. Instead, he will take and seize what he can, through craft. He will rather do without than request, or depend upon the kindness of others. He will seek to manipulate others into being forced to yield whatever he wants. He would rather fail to obtain the desired object, than achieve it through appealing to love and cooperation.

narasi.high:
The writer is egotistical and likes to manipulate people and situations for his benefit. He tries to control others artfully or by shrewd use of influence, often in an unfair or fraudulent way. He juggles or falsifies facts for his own purpose or profit.

He is a skillful manipulator and everything he does is well thought out to bring him the maximum advantage. He is so concerned with protecting his own security that he has become extremely self-centered. He regards himself as the only person who is important. He considers other people's welfare and reactions merely in order to gain his personal ends. He tries to get what he wants with a minimum of giving in return. Friendships are often made only after he considers how he can profit from them. He lives his own life so preoccupied by his own necessities that he either forgets about the needs of others or considers them invalid when they don't fit into his own scheme of things. Others find it painful to be around him because while he may seek affection he never seems to be able to reciprocate.

Even in close relationships, the writer always calculates his options. He tries to anticipate every one of his partner's moves. The entire relationship seems more like a game that he is determined to win. He is distrustful, superficial, oblivious to others' needs, evasive and defensive. A superficial friendliness enables him to get on well with people in order to obtain what he wants with a minimum of conflict and effort. The writer enjoys the cat-and-mouse game, carefully baiting his unsuspecting opponent and skillfully maneuvering him or her into a vulnerable position.

The writer may have a realistic perception of how to get what he wants but lacks internalized ethical principles. He has no conscience. Superficially, he conforms to social standards to gain personal advantages. That such outward compliance is a sham is proven by the fact that he is inconsistent in living up to moral standards. He behaves in ways considered proper only so long as it is advantageous for him. If he can gain more by being dishonest, particularly without being caught, he does so. His ego and inner resources are weak and he often fails to foresee the effect of his behavior. Under pressure, he will do whatever comes into his mind to get himself out of an unpleasant situation. At the moment of acting, he is not thinking of consequences or remembering past experiences. The only consideration he has is so lessen the tension that he feels. He will take every available action that fits that immediate need. This may include blaming other people for his own worst faults, lying, stubbornness, resentment, manipulation and aggressiveness.

With insincerity, the writer is likely to live off others by stirring their sympathies with lies about his misfortunes.
narasi.medium: The writer seldom resorts to manipulative behavior. Under stress, he uses other defenses to relieve the tension. (Scores in other syndromes and traits areas are important here.)
narasi.low:
The writer has the ability to meet the demands of life effectively without resorting to manipulative behavior.

He is realistic in appraising his reactions and abilities and in interpreting what is going on in the world around him. He does not wrongly perceive what others say and do. He evaluates his capabilities in a realistic manner without hiding important feelings and motives from himself. He conforms or fails to conform to social norms, but the decision is a voluntary one rather than the result of uncontrollable impulses.

The writer has the ability to establish constructive associations. He is comfortable with other people and able to react spontaneously during social interchange. At the same time, he does not feel obligated to subjugate his opinions to the group.

He is able to form close and satisfying personal relationships and can love someone other than himself. He is sensitive to others' needs and does not make excessive demands for the gratification of his own desires.

He is able to handle everyday situations, including his own emotional upsets, without excessive stress and without resorting to inappropriate behavior. He can work regularly, think clearly, manage his emotions, and keep on relatively good terms with most people, including himself.

narasi.high:
The writer displays a pattern of frequent emotional outbursts, self-centered behavior and dependence upon others. His relations with others are never fully satisfying; but in the process of interacting with them he derives secondary satisfaction from setting up dramatic situations and/or outwitting them. His behavior is more or less consciously adopted to attract attention or get his way. His emotions are shallow, and he is unaware or unconcerned about the ways in which others are affected by his behavior. He seeks attention through irresponsible or unreasonable conduct, he tends to over-react to circumstances that appear threatening to him. Stress may trigger an emotional eruption or, with physicalness high, a pugnacious response.

When frustrated in his dramatization or confronted with his ploys, the writer may respond with an illogical outburst of verbal abuse or (if the physical area is well developed) uncontrolled physical action. What induces such behavior on the writer's part is the momentary belief that he cannot cope. And what makes him usually feel he cannot cope is the feeling that he is in an alien world that is indifferent to his needs. Another reaction (if withdrawal is high) is physical flight.

With communication low, the writer may mentally freeze under stress. He is unable to think and has to rely upon past experiences to know what to do or say. Stress limits his options. He is unable to think fast enough or innovatively enough to respond with alternative behaviors. He may be confused or disoriented. In this state, it is difficult for him to do anything other than duplicate past behavior patterns.

The writer's relationships are permeated by an atmosphere of tension, although he usually lacks an awareness of his effect on others.

With withdrawal high, the writer may resort to physical flight. He is not only fleeing from himself but also from any kind of responsibility.
narasi.medium: Extreme stress may cause the writer to respond in a hysterical but socially acceptable manner. He reacts with a behavior that has been conditioned over a long period of time. Headaches, excessive need for sleep, writer's cramp, extreme fatigue or abnormal forgetfulness, are all hysterical reaction with acceptable social overtones.
narasi.low: The writer remains calm in the face of emergencies or under stress. He is able to think clearly and behaves logically. He is able to weigh alternatives and choose the most appropriate response. (Other scores are important; stress may bring out another entirely different illogical response.)

aspek.keterangan_umum:
Tension is not a static condition but a motivating force. Unlike anxiety, it is a conscious quality. It is a result of frustration and will be decreased when the cause has been removed.

The person who lives under tension has a restless urge to “do something – anything.” Many accidents are caused by the urgent need for tension reduction, and a good deal of delinquency is due to the “acting out” behavior of young people who lead tense, frustrated lives. Persistent feelings of tension may also produce certain specific symptoms, such as tension headache, nail-biting, etc. They are frequently a major factor in alcoholism and drug addiction.

narasi.high:
The writer has difficulty dealing with the stresses and strains of daily life. He suffers from a feeling of physical and psychological tension accompanied by discomfort, uneasiness and apprehension. He has long been under strain; he is constantly driven and feels under pressure all of the time. He experiences tension most acutely in situations which evoke feelings of frustration, inadequacy and insecurity. He finds delay or being thwarted hard to take and either increases his tension still further.

While in a state of tension, the writer is prone to overreact to minor annoyances which the normal person would take in stride. He feels himself having to fight every step of the way to do even the simple things expected of him. He may maintain composure through a series of minor irritations only to explode in the face of the “final straw.” Continued strain also leads to an increase in general body tension which in itself is unpleasant and disturbing. Under acute stress, most bodily systems are activated to meet the emergency. The writer's muscles are taut, the fingers tremulous, the facial expression is fixed and the heart quickens its pace. He may be fatigued at the end of the day due to the physiological effect on his nervous system. (He may be a prime candidate for ulcers, high blood pressure, circulatory problems, digestive problems, heart attack or arterial disease.)

Under tension, the writer's reasoning and problem solving ability diminishes rendering his thinking less effective. It becomes increasingly difficult for him to reinterpret a situation or see new factors and relationships. He is not doing any directive thinking. Instead, he is allowing the external circumstances to determine what he does. He approaches problems in a stereotyped way. He stays with unproductive behavior patterns, even though more efficient alternatives are available. He tries to maintain existing procedures because (a) they provide a basic source of security in dealing with the world; (b) it requires less effort to follow established patterns than it does to modify them or adopt new ones.

While he can go ahead working at familiar tasks, and still do them quite well because habit is helping him, he will find it very hard to concentrate on any new or unfamiliar job, person or idea. His thoughts scatter, he has difficulty focusing on new things.

While the writer is under strain, it is useless to reason with him. He cannot be convinced of anything, except what is wrong. Arguments literally solve nothing. For with the upset that comes from an argument, the writer becomes more tense, and as he does, his ability to think decreases even further. Quarrels, debates, any situation in which the writer feels himself being pressured or put on the spot, or in which he feels he is being shown in a bad light, or lacking in integrity, will bring the tension zooming up.

Another effect of tension is hostility toward the object or person viewed as the source of frustration. These feelings of hostility demand discharge, yet our civilized society permits few direct outlets. Consequently, they are often discharged in other indirect but “safe” ways which, in effect, are detrimental to the writer himself. One of the most common “safe” ways is a tension headache produced by unreleased strain. It is usually accompanied by insomnia and general irritability. The pain is due to prolonged contraction of the neck muscles resulting from pent-up emotion.
narasi.medium:
The writer can withstand a certain amount of stress before his functioning is noticeably impaired.

He has sufficient tension to motivate himself to work, but once he has accomplished something the tension is relieved temporarily until he gets involved in something else.
narasi.low:
The writer's disposition is normally calm and pleasant. He is not easily ruffled or disturbed. He can handle a good deal of stress without his functioning ability becoming impaired. He is able to handle everyday demands and situations without excessive strain. The higher the troubles pile up, the more strength he finds to bear them. Emergencies don't throw him off balance. He handles them with calm efficiency and a crisis brings out the best in him. He is dependable under pressure and can help others to overcome their panic and hysteria. Even when situations reach the crisis point, he manages to keep his cool and carries on efficiently as though nothing unusual were happening.

The writer has a sense of well-being and functions effectively in life. He takes things and situations as they come. He seldom gets uptight over anything. He is relaxed and adaptable. He looks at the facts and accepts reality as it is. He believes that most problems can be worked out logically. The writer respects the limitations of time, energy and resources without becoming uptight. Because he knows he cannot do everything, he concentrates on what is important to him. He does not get lost in unimportant details nor does he expect perfect solutions. He looks for alternatives and picks out a reasonable course of action. The writer is in good contact with his own feelings and can express them openly. He knows when he is angry and reacts appropriately. He can respond simply and directly to what is going on at the present, whether it be with anger or with love. He is very much involved with life. He is natural and spontaneous and can be himself. His relations with other people are good. (With low scores in motivation or self-control, the writer may be too lax to pay attention to deadlines and commitments.)

narasi.high:
The writer has a deep, hidden desire to be taken care of by someone stronger than he feels himself to be. He is timid, helpless and totally lacking in self-confidence. He takes no action, remains passive and lets things happen. He has the tendency to constantly manipulate relationships with others so that he will be taken care of or given emotional support. If he cannot be liked, at least he wants others to feel sorry for him. He has developed a “poor me” attitude and may even escape into being sick. This keeps others benevolently disposed toward him and gains him the attention he seeks. Suffering ostentatiously or looking pitiful may be such a security operation. By appearing awkward or ill, the writer forestalls what he senses to be imminent attacks by others.

The writer is unable to make everyday decisions without an excessive amount of advice and reassurance from others. He may even allow others to make most of the important decisions for him. His excessive dependence on others leads to difficulty in initiating projects or doing things on his own. He feels uncomfortable and helpless when alone. He will go to great lengths to avoid being unaccompanied. His social relations are limited to the few people on whom he is dependent. Once he finds such individuals, he is often inclined to let his every move revolve around them. He is devastated when close relationships end, and tends to be preoccupied with fears of being abandoned. Basically, he has allowed himself to be placed at the mercy of others. He is easily hurt by criticism and disapproval. Fearing rejection, he constantly worries about what is being said about him. He fears that others will only see his alleged faults. His outlook is negative. He is easily influenced by his environment and needs constant reassurance that he is acceptable and good. When support is not forthcoming, he is prone to spells of the blues. He tends to subordinate himself to others. He has great trouble saying “no” and goes to great lengths to please. He is reluctant to refuse a favor outright. He is more likely to say “yes” to a request and then make an excuse to get out of it later.

For fear of being rejected the writer agrees with people, even when he believes them to be wrong. He will volunteer to do things that are unpleasant or demeaning in order to get others to like him. He wants to please and can be devastated when his efforts are rejected. So great is his need to be liked that he may bend the truth. He is inclined to tell others what he thinks they want to hear. He fears confrontations of any kind. He keeps the peace by being accommodating. He does not allow himself to get angry and rarely carries a grudge. When someone is unkind to him, he quickly excuses the snub. He may, for instance, tell himself that the person did not mean it, after all. He strains to live up to others’ expectations in every way. He is so self-effacing that people often forget he is around.

The writer's vocational functioning may be impaired if the job requires independence. He finds it difficult to make demands or give orders. He becomes frightened when he is in charge. Unconsciously, he provokes others to take advantage of him. He is quickly recognized as an individual who will not fight. Considered an easy pushover, he is often victimized. He becomes the target because his demeanor reveals how weak he basically is. His behavior has serious flaws. Since he wants so much to be liked and accepted by others, he must see them as good and kind, not as they really are. And since he is living for approval from others, he is not living his own life. He has to do what will please others and ignore his own feelings and goals. His energies and resources are not used to develop his own potential and he does not give himself a chance to grow into a self-actualized individual. Furthermore, when the dependent writer encounters rejection, he has nothing to fall back on and can be crushed. When he seems rebuffed, he feels inferior and worthless. Since so much of his life is lived in the fear of rejection he tends to feel chronically apprehensive and depressed.
narasi.medium: The writer dislikes friction and argument. He can compromise but only after exploring the reasons for it. Unless the situation is emotionally charged, he will try to take action to resolve problems.
narasi.low:
The writer is an individual with a firm identity. He sees himself accurately and is accepting of himself. He takes responsibility for his own life and for the fulfillment of his needs. He knows where he is and where he is going. He sets his own course and continues to expand and grow as an individual. He is competent in handling his life and his environment. He makes up his own mind. He is independent rather than leaning and dependent.

The writer will stand up for his own rights if necessary. Freedom to do things his own way is one of his goals in life. He appreciates people who share his belief in the importance of each person doing his or her thing. He avoids the tendency to complain as a way of getting attention and sympathy. He talks about things which inspire others and lets them know how he enjoys life. He gets actively engaged in projects and tasks. He does not expect others to solve his difficulties. He deals purposefully with problems. He distinguishes between that which can be changed and that which must be endured. He maintains a sense of personal worth, even in defeat.

aspek.keterangan_umum:
Withdrawal is a defense trait. Many people become accustomed to withdrawing when they are quite young. They may, for example, seek relief from constant demands from people around them. They may feel uncomfortable with others and try to avoid the feeling by keeping to themselves.

While the circumstances surrounding their early decisions may have been long forgotten, the implications can be seen in their behavior in adult life. Whenever they make the decision to withdraw, they are acting out an old childhood pattern of refusing to deal with people. They decide to reject the world before it can upset them.

Unfortunately, when they made the early decision they were far too young to assess decisions adequately or to investigate things for themselves and make up their own mind about them. However, over the years, their automatic response to situations has become so ingrained, so much part of them, that they never think to question it. They probably consider it “their nature” to act the way they do.

The withdrawal response is notoriously difficult to extinguish. If a person keeps withdrawing from what he considers anxiety-producing circumstances, he may never give himself a chance to find out that the situation is in reality no longer painful.

narasi.high:
The writer has an exaggerated need for solitude. He withdraws physically or mentally from other people and situations that arouse a sense of threat. He closes himself off and erects a barrier that others find difficult to penetrate. He is cold and unresponsive, even though he may not want to be that way. Circumstances, particularly in childhood, probably exposed him to harsh treatment and he has unconsciously steeled himself against being hurt again.

In every area of his life, the writer needs an inordinate amount of space to surround him to feel secure. He makes as few social contacts as possible and probably has no friends to speak of. He consciously controls the number and the extent of personal relationships he gets involved in, depending on how they will affect him and his emotional security.

The writer is insecure in the give-and-take of everyday relationships. While his need for contact may be strong, his fears are more intense. He feels uneasy in any situation that requires close contact with another person. To reduce anxiety he uses, as a matter of course, unconscious techniques to keep others away. He protects himself by putting distance between himself and others. He retreats into a world of his own making, which nobody can penetrate. He focuses on the sensations within him and is more concerned with his own reactions than he is interested in life around him. He becomes withdrawn, self-protective and uncommunicative.

The writer much prefers working in isolation, locked up in his office, away from the co-workers' camaraderie. He may choose to work out of his home, and may actually accept a smaller income to do this, if the opportunity comes along.

Even when interacting, the writer has difficulty spontaneously initiating, or planning with other people. He is unable to mingle freely and communication is an effort. He cannot share his experiences and even in a group appears to work independently rather than cooperatively. Since he withdraws from personal contacts he, himself, has not desired, he is close to few people, and may be far more lonely than others. He may rationalize his behavior by saying that he has not much in common with others, or that they don't understand him anyway. This may be accompanied by such phrases as, “Leave me alone,” or “I just want to be by myself.”

The writer recoils from involvement and is fearful of relationships that become too intimate. He has difficulty with people who make demands or cling to him. He is much more comfortable with people who respect his privacy. He is afraid of being vulnerable if he exposes too much of himself. He feels that by staying detached from people they can neither disappoint nor hurt him. He disappears into his shell and stays there without any spark of communication.

Protecting himself by keeping apart does not necessarily mean that the writer removes himself physically. It means being independent of others regarding his internal and external needs. He has made the conscious or unconscious determination not to get emotionally involved in any way, whether in love, fight, cooperation or competition.

The writer discovered early in life that natural responsiveness left him vulnerable, and that it was safer to hide his emotions whenever he could. He began to mask his feelings and put on a facade. In later life, that mask became his face. He even learned to think of his lack of response as an accomplishment. He felt he was “more in control” if he did not allow himself to “feel.”

The writer spent a lot of time and energy suppressing emotions until control finally became an end in itself. He may even have stopped using the language of emotions. He may say “I think” instead of “I feel.”

The fallacy is that withdrawal did not stop the hurt and fear inside but, unfortunately, he can no longer reach out to anyone, nor can they reach out to him. Withdrawal means lack of communication, isolation and a sense of real separation. Since his protective attitude has become a pervasive part of the writer's lifestyle, he finds himself deprived of the opportunity to have positive emotional experiences or form healthy attachments to other people. A loving relationship with another person might be foregone because it makes the writer vulnerable to being hurt.

Unfortunately, by withdrawing, the writer also hurts the feelings of others who believe he does not need or want relationships or their support. And since they assess him only from what they can see, they may be judging him incorrectly or miss his true feelings entirely.

Withdrawal is carried out at considerable expense to the writer himself. Every time it is used, he is bound to become more fearful and less likely to cope with a similar situation in the future. In addition, he may fall prey to feelings of guilt for having retreated, or he may suffer hostilities toward those people whom he falsely considers to be the cause of his frustrations.

Withdrawal affects every area of the writer's life, particularly the sexual sphere. He exercises the same defenses in his sex life that he exhibits in other areas of his personality. While sexual relationships could mean much as a bridge to others, he is only able to enjoy them if they do not interfere with control over his feelings. He wants sex confined to the compartment he has set aside for this part of his life and he would rather withdraw than surrender his controls. Sex can only be enjoyed with persons toward whom the writer has no tender feelings or, toward whom he has contemptuous feelings, or none at all.

A permanent relationship would be an especially threatening to the writer because of the intimacy involved. Any close and lasting association could jeopardize his need for privacy, unless the partner had an equally strong need and each partner would respect the other's need for distance.
narasi.medium: The writer maintains the proper perspective in interpersonal relationships. He is comfortable working with and around others. He is relaxed alone or in groups. He needs, however, a certain amount of solitude before involving himself. He wants to consider the possible consequences of his actions.
narasi.low:
The writer is emotionally secure and is willing to try unfamiliar things. He loves to explore new areas and exciting relationships. He actively seeks the company of others. He is informal and makes others feel at ease, too. He enjoys being familiar with others and is accessible to friendly overtures.

The writer is more communicative. He talks with greater freedom about personal things. He does not look upon other people's personal questions as an intrusion into his private affairs. Their interest in him gives him a sense of being involved.

The writer's attitude would be valuable in professions such as nursing, reception work, teaching, the healing arts, service organizations, domestic help, and in any area where he must deal with the public in a service related way.

aspek.keterangan_umum:
The fundamental source of suspicion is a lack of trust. The writer suffers from unconscious feelings of inferiority growing out of failure to meet the goals set by the parents.

Suspicious individuals usually grow up in families where the parents are overbearing, critical and ambitious. As children, they are made to feel that they will not be accepted or loved unless they prove themselves superior. As a result, they become sullen, resentful and stubborn and fail to develop warm relationships. Attitudes of intolerance and arrogance, taken over from their parents, further interfere with their social relationships.

These individuals are often not accepted by their peers and, instead of trying to become more congenial and friendly, they become aloof, hostile, suspicious, and sensitive to unintentional slights. As they grow older, they become even more distrustful, suspecting and domineering, constantly finding fault with others and demanding recognition for themselves.

narasi.high:
The writer habitually distrusts and doubts. He believes in others' motives being bad, wrong or harmful with little or no supporting evidence. He automatically doubts what others accept. His first reaction is to be skeptical. It is almost impossible for him to accept anything at face value.

The writer is skeptical of new ideas. He tends to dismiss what he is not familiar with. He is exaggeratedly concerned with sources, authority and corroboration. He is unwilling to accept what is seen, and much less so what is heard. Unfortunately, most of the time his skepticism is based on feeling, not on facts.

The writer tends to create an atmosphere of suspicion and doubt. His skepticism is instrumental in keeping others from trying out new approaches, if he can help it. By doing this he may help to hold back much progress.

The writer is emotionally unstable, irritable, resentful of criticism and very arrogant. His outward air of superiority is actually a cover for inward feelings of inadequacy. He has so frequently failed to live up to expectations, he has been so severely criticized in his early life, he has antagonized so many people, and he has experienced so many rebuffs that he is haunted by a sense of failure.

The writer usually exhibits a pattern of chronically unsatisfactory interpersonal relationships. He is very critical of the people around him and distrustful of their intentions and motives. He suspects them of unjustified ill will, jealousy and hostility against him.

The writer tends to make remarks like, “others don't like me, they are evil.” He may accuse others of being unfair competitors or of being dishonest. Although there may be an occasional attempt at interpersonal relationships, the writer gains satisfaction only when he retains control and does not see himself as being manipulated by the other person.

The writer's skepticism causes many misunderstandings. He is unaware of how his suspicious attitude is affecting others and tends to misinterpret their negative reaction to him. Instead of looking inward to find the source of his difficulties, the writer protects himself by blaming others for everything that happens. The more he does so, the more problems he generates. As his problems multiply, so do his defensive reactions. The writer isolates himself because he feels that there is no one he can trust. He begins to feel that others are talking about him behind his back. He searches for hidden meanings in glances and gestures. He has the idea that others are actively working against him.

The writer reconstructs “facts” to fit his own biased conceptions, and then seeks additional data to support his own conclusions. He is manipulative in his relationships to prevent the other person from “gaining the advantage.” Such people frequently become a nuisance through perennial complaints and lawsuits against other persons.

The suspicious person fits well where doubt is needed as part of the job, such as accounting, auditing, law enforcement, and criminal correction. Suspicion augments the effect of low empathy and low friendliness. With high scores in antisocial or manipulative, the writer seems cold, antagonistic and inaccessible.
narasi.medium: The writer is cautious in relationships and undertakings. He remains skeptical and doubtful until he can prove something to his satisfaction. He believes others only if there is a good reason for his trust. He will never be taken in a second time by a person who has disappointed him before.
narasi.low:
The writer is inclined to trust others automatically. He is too easily taken in because he assumes that what is being said by a person in authority is true. Even with years of experience of being embarrassed for having believed someone foolishly, the writer is still vulnerable. He keeps believing people who have won his confidence. His problem is that he does not know when and when not to trust.

The writer automatically has faith in what looks right to him. He accepts the new with less reservation and is willing to give it at least a try. Such credulity augments the effect of high empathy, involvement and impulsiveness. It makes it harder for the writer to direct these traits.

The writer fits well into fields where “taking things for granted” is acceptable, such as production line work, mail carrying, bakery work, and some creative and artistic fields.

aspek.keterangan_umum: The negative writer is under strain and has been for an extended length of time. (This strain may arise from either mental or physical origins.) He has become more and more aware of, and unable to deal with a problematic situation. It is weighing upon his mind. His negative attitude affects him mentally and physically. He may experience low self-esteem, poor concentration or decision-making ability. He may show no appetite or a tendency toward overeating, he may suffer from insomnia, low energy or fatigue. Most of the time, he suffers from chronic feelings of hopelessness.

narasi.high:
The writer is in a dejected mood, most of the time. He expects misfortune or the worst outcome in any situation. He tends to look on the dark side of things. His general disposition is discouraged and melancholic. More than the usual strain has been placed on him. He suffers from a lack of mental energy and finds it hard to think effectively. His initiative is lost and it is difficult for him to make decisions. He can work at familiar tasks, and still do them quite well (because habit is helping him) but he finds it hard to concentrate on new or unfamiliar subjects, people, or ideas. His thoughts scatter and he has difficulty focusing on things. Instinct and habit are his prime motivators instead of considered choice and awareness of consequences.

Pessimism prevents him from developing a flexible attitude. He overestimates obstacles to such an extent that he finds it difficult to follow a line of action or get wholeheartedly involved in a relationship. He is discouraged before he starts.

The writer finds conversation difficult and may become absorbed in melancholic ruminations. He talks more and more about what is wrong in his life. He may complain to others that he feels unwanted, unloved and unappreciated. With his ever-present doubt, he easily becomes a source of depression to others, too, and they find it difficult to have him around. Because pessimism develops gradually, the writer may still think of himself, in many cases, as being positive. He may not be fully aware of how pessimistic he looks, sounds, and really is. He may not realize just how much he has been taken over by his own negative feelings. His negative conduct depresses people. His obvious despair and his refusal to try to improve his condition make it difficult for them to stay around for any length of time.
narasi.medium: The writer has basically a realistic attitude and a matter-of-fact approach to the practical problems of life. He is positive about people and circumstances much of the time. Occasional feelings of lessened enthusiasm are usually tied to a tangible cause. If he becomes temporarily dissatisfied with the way things are, he is usually able to overcome these negative moods.
narasi.low:
The writer is optimistic. He usually feels good about people and circumstances. Part of his strength comes from inborn cheerfulness. His positive attitude is reflected in his expression. Others will seek him out because he is an inspiration and they can depend upon him to cheer them up. He will do less complaining about unexpected impediments. He generally looks on the brighter side of things and expects them to work out in the end.

The writer has initiative and feels optimistic about life in general. He is more progressive and happy about himself, his work and what he is accomplishing. He focuses on the goals ahead, not on how he feels along the way. He is aware of positive possibilities in other people, in himself, and in the circumstances around him.

aspek.keterangan_umum:
The writer with fears may be afraid of ridicule, loneliness, criticism, rejection, etc. These fears are often caused by emotional insecurity and by emotional deprivation of one kind or another.

Fears can be activated in many situations and under many conditions.
A writer's particular fears and what effect they have on him will be explored in this section.

For trait descriptions: Go to the individual indicators and look them up alphabetically.

narasi.high:
The writer is physically restless. He likes to be active and rushes from one place to another. He wants to be where things are happening and needs to be constantly “on the go.” Restlessness makes it impossible for him to settle down.

The writer scatters his energies, both mental and physical. He is constantly busy at many things and few people can keep up with him. He has too many irons in the fire and is usually behind in finishing what he has begun.

To gain the feeling that he is alive, the writer needs change and variety. Anything new or different holds appeal. He probably loves travel and doing things on the spur of the moment. He craves the unexpected and adores novelty. Without change, he feels stagnated, any kind of routine makes him feel caged in. He resents drudgery and monotony almost fiercely. He becomes bored, irritable and restless when his work or relationships are unvaried and dull. Nothing is worse for him than being in a rut. To sleep in the same bed every night, eat at the same restaurant, follow the same path to work, and do the same thing every day leaves him frustrated and depressed. His restless nature demands constant excitement and change or he becomes dejected and morose.

It is unlikely that the writer will own a house because it would be too permanent. He probably changes his residence more often than his job, and he is always on the move in one way or another toward a new horizon.
