His conversation will be full of phrases like “Let’s give it a spin,” and “I’ll try anything once.” And he will too. Try anything once, that is. Twice it out. He is bored by then.

There will always be slight whirl of confusion about him and constant activity. Keeping up with him will be tiring and knowing where to look for him may take a little forethought. He could be in one place this minute and somewhere else the next. He will dart off in a different direction almost before you can say hello.

The more staid people in his environment may think him irresponsible when he moves from one experience to another without fully experiencing any of them. His restlessness may be interpreted as lack of responsibility and fickleness.

The writer is unable to sit still or stay quietly in one place. He tends to get restless and needs frequent breaks. He will wear a hole in the carpet pacing up and down if he is caged up in an office too long. He feels confined when he cannot be up and moving around. He will have to change his position frequently to drain off some nervous energy. He may walk about, even while holding a serious conversation that has his entire attention. His movements serve to relax the physical body. They have nothing to do with mental inattention, in such circumstances. Unfortunately, his seemingly pointless fidgeting, wriggling, and moving about may irritate those with whom he deals. He wastes time and annoys others with his aimless wandering.

It is difficult for the writer to stay with any kind of mental activity for a longer period of time. He may have the habit of falling asleep while other people are talking or socializing. They may be offended by this alleged slight, especially when the writer snaps back as soon as something of interest to him enters the conversation.

The writer lives an unscheduled life. His pattern of working is by fits and starts with many interruptions, both created and allowed. His attention shifts from one thing to another and he becomes impulsively involved in projects and relationships, regardless of whether he has the time or means to sustain such ties. He responds automatically as soon as his interest is aroused.

Over-involvement affects his organization and planning ability. He often takes on more than he can accomplish in a given period of time. He frequently finds himself committed to something he did not want or cannot really afford to do. He tries to participate in so many things that he is unable to finish any of them. He may complete a project partially and then is so eager to get on to the next task that he has trouble finishing the final parts of the job. Or he may already get involved in the next project while still, usually reluctantly, completing the final portion of the job he was involved with.

The writer gets impulsively involved in other people’s lives. He is often tactless and inconsiderate; he invades the space and rights of others, whether he is wanted or not. Like in all other areas of his life, he detests routine in sex. Whatever can be predicted, is anathema to him. If his home is not stimulating, or if his partner seems dull, he will get just as bored as with routine on the job. He is apt to lose interest in someone he knows too well. He may seek a new partner (this may be contradicted by other traits in the writing, such as loyalty, etc.), new friends, new work, new recreations, just for the sake of change.

Vocationally, the writer rarely remains long enough in one job to get him anywhere. Restlessness makes it impossible for him to settle down. He is likely to be a wanderer, moving from job to job and place to place. You will never know for sure where he is going to be.

He needs a schedule that is varied enough to hold his interest. He works best where he encounters some change on a daily basis. It would be difficult for him to stay retired from active life or from something that interests him. Whatever he does, his work should involve diversity and travel, if possible. If bored, he may be tempted to change jobs for the sake of change rather than advancement. He needs companions like himself and diversion during his recreational time. When he has these plans in mind, it will be easier for him to endure the monotony of daily life. When boredom threatens to overcome him, he can focus on the excitement lying ahead.

The writer functions best in fields that are active and vigorous on the physical level. Transportation or construction worker, wood cutter, telephone line man, are desirable kinds of jobs. He would make a fine traveling sales representative, itinerant lecturer, or space explorer. He will do well in any kind of occupation where his natural urges can be expressed, any other job will seem like drudgery.

With restlessness very high, the writer is nervous and agitated without reason. He is restless and it irritates him to be inactive. Often his movements are random, they lack purpose and direction. He walks, just for the sake of walking. He may be finger-drumming and/or foot-tapping.

He has trouble concentrating, he bores easily and needs an energy release mechanism such as constant talking. He does not relax enough and wears himself out physically. He should be encouraged to engage in directed physical activity to work off nervous energy. Activity will wear him out so he can sleep.

With anxiety high, the writer is irritable and tense. He is likely to overreact to situations other people take in stride. He may be subject to high blood pressure, circulatory diseases and kidney ailments. He may have difficulty getting a normal night’s sleep. Mental distraction, forgetfulness, and inattention are results of high nervousness. The writer may develop an “accident habit” and show a history of minor mishaps before a major accident is incurred.

Important! Nervousness and a constant need for activity may be a cover-up to conceal inhibition and/or a poor self-concept.
narasi.medium: The writer feels the need to be active. Without directed activity or something that he wants to accomplish, he feels restless because of excess energy going to waste. He is sometimes unable to relax but his nervousness is usually due to specific circumstances. It subsides once the situation is resolved.
narasi.low:
The writer is calm and inwardly controlled. He is able to take most situations in stride and has a good amount of patience. A frightening or tension-arousing situation has no or little negative effect on him. He is able to stay relaxed and remains functioning. His physical and mental energy is usually good.

The writer is less excited by change. He will not take risks because he feels easily overwhelmed. He prefers to deal with familiar things and conventional methods. He can live and work contentedly without excitement and diversity. He stays closer to home and clings to his lifestyle. He is satisfied with routine activities. The writer is most comfortable using proven methods. He is not likely to experiment with unfamiliar ways of doing things.

The writer would perform best where excitement and change are not part of the daily routine. He would work reliably as a bookkeeper, bank teller, claim examiner, loan counselor, housekeeper or machine operator.

aspek.keterangan_umum:
Inhibitions are a form of defense. They reveal that the writer is unable to recognize or give full expression to his instinctual impulses. He does not know them and he does not want to know them. Either he does not feel them at all or he feels only a small part of them, or he experiences them in a distorted way. Anxiety is always the promoting factor. The inhibited function has unconsciously an instinctual sexual or hostile significance against which the defense is really directed.

It is not clear what determines the kind of inhibitions being developed. They depend partly upon the person's history and character.

Inhibitions in the sexual area are most frequent. They may cover the whole area of sexuality or only certain aspects of it, such as sensuality, or tenderness, or only certain types of partners. Perhaps sex can only be enjoyed with persons toward whom the writer has no tender feelings or even, toward whom he has contemptuous feelings, or none at all.

The writer structures his life to avoid what gives him pain. By inhibiting certain areas of his personality, he either does not deal with these problems or he submerges them under logical sounding excuses.

narasi.high:
Inhibitions are a form of defense. They reveal that the writer is unable to recognize or give full expression to his instinctual impulses. He does not know them and he does not want to know them. Either he does not feel them at all or he feels only a small part of them, or he experiences them in a distorted way. Anxiety is always the promoting factor. The inhibited function has unconsciously an instinctual sexual or hostile significance against which the defense is really directed.

It is not clear what determines the kind of inhibitions being developed. They depend partly upon the person's history and character.

Inhibitions in the sexual area are most frequent. They may cover the whole area of sexuality or only certain aspects of it, such as sensuality, or tenderness, or only certain types of partners. Perhaps sex can only be enjoyed with persons toward whom the writer has no tender feelings or even, toward whom he has contemptuous feelings, or none at all.

The writer structures his life to avoid what gives him pain. By inhibiting certain areas of his personality, he either does not deal with these problems or he submerges them under logical sounding excuses. for one reason or another, gravitate toward work he despises, or which utilizes his talents only minimally.

If the writer, in his opinion, has certain personal defects, they may provide an impetus for some over-compensation. The writer will not be able to admit the true reason behind his inner drive, even to himself.

In the emotional area, the writer is generally unresponsive. While a “normal” person is able to remember how he felt as a child, he has “forgotten” childhood memories and more or less tries to avoids emotions altogether. He may rationalize that he is more efficient depending upon logic rather than feelings. He deals with others dispassionately. He may be well acquainted with people in his immediate environment, but rarely knows anything about their personalities. He does not even really know his friends.

Outwardly, he may appear as an easygoing, calm, unhurried individual. To most people he will present a picture of unruffled poise. Many people will look upon him with admiration and remark that nothing seems to bother him. He may have learned to act extroverted when it seems the expedient thing to do. He may behave as if he had real feelings and contact with people. However, such behavior is spurious and calculated. (Depending on other scores, he may use an ingratiating personality to get along well with others.) The inward personality remains inhibited and self-protective at all times.

The existence of inhibitions is revealed through an unexplained general weakness. The writer lacks vitality and initiative. Energies that are needed for the defensive struggles are deflected from other functions. He may seem to live less intensely than others. He may be conspicuous for his apathy.
narasi.medium: The writer is more aware of what he is experiencing and how is responding to his feelings. He can endure instinctual impulses as long as certain reassuring conditions are present. For instance, he usually tolerates emotions until a certain height of excitement has been reached. He is frightened it this intensity is surpassed. Emotions must be neither too intense nor too serious.
narasi.low: The writer is able to function independently. He has a realistic view of himself. He faces life's situations squarely, without avoidance or much realization. He establishes constructive relationships with other people. He is able to release his inner resources and potentialities without indulging in compensating behavior. He is free of disabling symptoms such as severe tension or anxiety, and he is unhampered by serious inner conflicts.

aspek.keterangan_umum:
A conflict within the personality is a distinct inner struggle, caused by the operation of opposing drives, impulses, wishes or external or internal demands. The person with conflicts suffers from contradictory attitudes toward others or self, from opposing characteristics, or from a controversial set of values.

Some people gradually outgrow their conflicts. In time, their healthy capacity becomes strengthened. They learn from their experiences in living. They use their abilities and talents to do useful work. Gradually, they obtain a good measure of satisfaction and self esteem.

Many, however, are not so fortunate. Conflicts continue to grow and have a greater and greater influence on their lives. In some people, conflicts exist on the conscious level. They can be treated constructively through direct confrontation of the underlying causes.

A continuing state of unresolved conflicts is far more critical. It may lead to the person repressing the conflict altogether in order to create a condition of artificial harmony. The result is anxiety which, in turn, creates feelings of helplessness, impotence and inactivity and drastically increases the seriousness of the original conflict.

narasi.high:
The writer suffers from the simultaneous presence of opposing or mutually exclusive impulses, desires, or tendencies. He has a similar like or dislike for an object or person, or the conflict is caused by an incentive that is at once positive and negative. He is very frustrated and dissatisfied in the areas of his life where he encounters conflicts. He is troubled himself and makes others around him uncomfortable, too. He is moody, subjective and unreliable with friends and family. He is difficult to live with because of his unpredictability.

The writer is unable to work productively. He may be forgetful and confused. Because of his lack of concentration, he may be accident prone. He feels very negative and may become apathetic as a result of stress.
narasi.medium:
The writer is able to deal with most of the conflicts in his life by analyzing the situations and trying to adjust. He may suffer temporary periods of discouragement and moodiness. At times, as a result of temporary stress, he may become unpredictable or do the unexpected. (Problem areas scoring high on the Trait Inventory will indicate which part of the personality is subject to breakdown under stress.)

Under pressure, the writer experiences some disorganization and inefficiency; however, he is conscious of it and takes steps to counteract errors that might occur because of temporary strain. He may have trouble concentrating on a task until he finally gets immersed in it and closes his mind to outer distractions.
narasi.low:
The writer handles life with composure and inward calm. He has few frustrating desires or impulses that are opposing each other. The conflicts he feels he is able to deal with directly, thereby eliminating the cause.

The writer is well organized. He works carefully and efficiently. He functions reliably under pressure. He is orderly and stable. He feels at ease with himself and comfortable with other people. He is content with his goals and with the direction in which his life is going.

aspek.keterangan_umum:
Anxiety versus fear

Fear and anxiety are both emotional reactions to danger. The symptoms are similar: a pounding heart, rapid breathing, sweating, feeling of faintness, trembling, jitteriness, diarrhea, etc. The difference is that fear requires a definite object of which one is afraid, whereas anxiety is not associated with such a consciously perceived stimulus.

Anxiety, like fear, is an emotional reaction to danger, but the danger is an internal one. The person's pattern of living, his values and goals are creating more stress than he can cope with. This is a most unpleasant emotional state because the individual who is anxious does not know what he is afraid of. His reaction is not logical. He cannot understand it, nor can he control it, and therefore he feels helpless. People like to feel that they are in control of their lives, but the anxious person realizes that he is not. There is no limit to the number of situations which may trigger anxiety. Patterns of anxiety vary as widely as people's personalities. Anxiety may be added on to a realistic fear and, for a long time, go undetected. However, in time, it will become clear that the person's fear is out of all proportion to the actual risk involved.

Anxiety is not a localized illness like a foreign body or a tumor which can be removed surgically. Nor is it the memory of a singular painful event in childhood that has been repressed and only needs to be recalled into consciousness to produce a dramatic cure. There are few quick restoratives. A period of anxiety may be relieved by reassurances from an authority or from someone the anxious person trusts. It may be alleviated by drugs, alcohol, vacations, hobbies, etc. It may also be relieved by employing various defense strategies. But none of these factors will effect a cure. Only when the individual can express his emotional needs appropriately, when he has achieved a good understanding of his real self and sees the world realistically, do anxieties stop.

narasi.high:
The writer suffers from a feeling of mingled dread and apprehension about the future without a specific cause for fear. He essentially goes through life frightened. He feels lonely and helpless toward a basically hostile world. He is afraid of the risks, uncertainties, and dangers in his environment. He feels anxious in situations that most other people handle without difficulty. He suffers apprehension and uneasiness whose cause he does not know. Still, he is so uncomfortable that he will go to any length to avoid the sensation or to bring about its reduction. His apprehension is chronic and illogical, although he may be quite logical otherwise. He suffers continuously from an undefined inner dread that he is unable to explain satisfactorily. He cannot understand his fear nor can he control his responses to it.

The writer is unable to attribute his reaction to anything in particular or to any cause that can be removed to reduce the anxiety. He does not consciously know what he is afraid of and he is too frightened to look at the danger accurately and realistically. He distorts the real nature of his problems and is unrealistic in his problem solving ability. He feels distressed, distracted and sometimes confused. He is in the grip of worry and distress and has a painful feeling of being powerless to do anything about it. His outlook is negative, optimism and enthusiasm are both low. He feels inadequate to deal with many everyday problems and may overreact to ordinary situations. He has trouble sleeping and relaxing. He is forgetful and finds it difficult to make decisions.

The writer's physical stamina may be poor. He may suffer from breathing problems, sweating, etc. (He may be inclined to take drugs or medication for his “problems.”) When anxiety persists, he tends to use many defense strategies to obtain relief. The fallacy is that in time, they turn into consistent needs. In the long run, they create more anxiety than they alleviate. His conflicts disturb his relations with others and himself. He is so preoccupied with his problems that he cannot genuinely be interested in the concerns of others.

Defensive strategies interfere with the growth of talents and skills on which his real security rests. When wasting time on trivia, the writer functions relatively smooth; however, when he tries to do something essential, apprehension arises within. He becomes tense when he attempts to work constructively. He suffers depression when he seeks to achieve. In order to escape anxiety, the writer gives up the opportunity to grow and realize himself. He wastes time on trivia. The major drive in life becomes to escape from anxiety.
narasi.medium: The writer's anxiety is closer to the surface but still affects all areas of his life. The writer worries over problems that he is unable to work out. He feels distracted without being aware of what he is really apprehensive about. He may be forgetful and prone to making errors. The fear of committing blunders increases his anxiety and results in increased tension.
narasi.low:
The writer is basically courageous and deals with circumstances as they arise. He may not like a certain situation but he accepts it as it is, and in so doing, he has control over what to do and how to respond.

The writer accepts occasional failure as part of the growing process. He tries to understand what went wrong so that he can learn from the experience. Most importantly, he gives himself credit for trying.

The writer feels deeply, whether it is sadness or joy, love, anger, frustration, hunger or fatigue. He is not usually in doubt how he feels and he is not afraid to express his feelings openly.

The writer is able to face his problems directly. He admits to doubts and fears that make him uneasy. He sees danger in the proper perspective without exaggerating it. He solves conflicts by actively dealing with the cause and the anxiety associated with it. He realizes that everyone is subject to fear now and then and that it is better to share his apprehension with others rather than keep it to himself. His relations with other people are good. He is capable of loving and giving love in full measure.

narasi.high:
The writer has a disorderly mind. He fails to distinguish between important and unimportant ideas and things. He cannot organize himself and has little self-directive ability or self-control. He is disorganized with regard to what goes on around him. He plans poorly and tries to crowd too many projects into his working day. He takes on more than he can handle or has too many interests. He lacks perspective in viewing situations realistically. His mind is not easily directed toward one activity for a longer period of time. He suffers from scattered thinking and his concentration is poor.

The writer is emotionally immature. He speaks and acts impulsively and fails to consider the consequences of his acts. He talks too much without ever coming to the point but seldom hears what other people reply. He is tactless and inconsiderate. He invades the personal sphere of others without giving it a second thought.

The writer spends much time worrying about what he should do. He thinks when he should be doing. He wastes mental energies and is absent-minded and error-prone. He frequently feels tense (due to a specific cause) and anxious (a temporary disturbing feeling), or both.
narasi.medium:
The writer suffers from temporary tension which is due to specific causes. He has too much on his mind and becomes prone to errors due to overwork. Usually, he tries to compensate through special care and attention.

With motivation high, the writer will constantly drive himself (which may be one of the causes for his problems). He may suffer from insomnia, headaches and irritability. He has trouble forcing himself to concentrate on tasks that require mental energy.
narasi.low: The writer is well organized. He is a logical and objective thinker who plans his life and his activities efficiently. What he expresses is the result of conscious thought. His ideas flow systematically and he has the ability to concentrate. He has self-directive ability and can apply himself fully to his tasks.

indikator.keterangan: The writer is self-disciplined and a disciplinarian. He will not shirk difficulties and will try to conquer opposition and impediments. He lacks the willingness and/or ability to adapt. Instead, he expects that others should conform to him. In most matters, he has definite views and looks on everything as black or white. He is intolerant and may be unreasonable when attempting to prove a point. He tends to be judgmental in keeping with his prejudices. Much of the time, he suffers tension related to "work fanaticism."

indikator.nama: Final strokes downward in triangular lower zone loops
indikator.keterangan:
These writers appear to have a dual personality with their true self seldom revealed to the world. In public, they place their best foot forward, appearing kindly, outgoing, and benevolent.

In reality, they are frustrated due to repressed sexual desires. While they hide these feelings from the outside world, they vent their anger on the family. At home, they are dictatorial and bossy and torment their families with constant criticism and demands. (Old graphology called them “house tyrants.”) They “lay down the law” and expect everyone to do their adjusting to them. They want things done their way, or else. They are overbearing and make important decisions without consulting the family. They dictate how things should be handled and will not tolerate dissent. They want to be asked for their opinion in everything and react with anger to being ignored. They are quick to jump into a conversation, even when they are not asked, but they adamantly refuse to listen to the viewpoint of family members when it differs from their own. They immediately take offense when they are criticized for meddling. These writers’ acrimony is a constant strain on all. (Preyer noticed that they have a tendency to trip those who interfere with their plans.)

While their bossiness is most aggravating to family members, it is seldom noticeable to outsiders. On the contrary, others usually consider the writers charming and congenial and may tell family members how lucky they are to have them around.

This implies abruptness and lack of generosity.

The writer lacks skill in handling people. He does not know when to be tactful even if he would like to be. In speaking and in writing, he is blunt and to the point. He withholds his own time and also denies others the opportunity to express themselves. He will interrupt, cut off, or silence them altogether.
These writers insist on having the last word in conversations. In extreme cases, they are inconsiderate. Heams explains that “communication is emphasized at the last moment with extraordinary force.”

indikator.nama: Final strokes from middle zone end in lower zone
indikator.keterangan:
Final strokes on letters-or-words should fall into the middle zone. They should not end in the upper or lower zone. If they extend into the upper or lower zones, then this indicates that the writer feels some insecurity in the interpersonal (middle) zone.

The writer is very tense. He insists on having his own way and the last word in conversations and arguments. He enjoys lecturing others. Muller-Enskat speaks of “a drive to rape other people’s souls.”

With increasing pressure, say Muller-Enskat, the writer is putting others down, he is literally pushing them down and brutally standing on their shoulders.

The writer glories in hard work, will-power and success. He applies extra effort toward future plans and goals. He is very ambitious and determined to succeed. He is proud of his ability to work hard. Driven by his desire for achievement and acclaim, he desires to take over and to be in control.

With extremely heavy strokes, the writer is self-righteous and obstinate. He tries to demonstrate willpower he does not really possess.

In negative writing, heavy horizontal strokes expose antisocial aggression.

indikator.nama: Initial downstroke from upper zone very high
indikator.keterangan: The writer has exalted ego demands and demonstrates unjustified pride, arrogance and superiority feelings. He believes in unquestioning obedience to authority. He is power oriented in his relationships and sees the world divided into the weak and strong. He gives orders instead of asking and usually makes immediate requests on others’ time and resources and always puts his own concerns first.

These writers are disgruntled individuals. They harbor an unconscious desire for power and display domineering tendencies to compensate for hidden feelings of dissatisfaction. An unsatisfactory sex life is often the reason for the discontent. They often seem to find their partner sexually unsuitable or unsatisfactory. Because the sex life is inadequate, the writer becomes irritable, sour and aggressive.

indikator.nama: Pressure displaced in the middle zone
indikator.keterangan:
The writer pours all his energies into an exaggerated drive for achievement and assertion. Displaced pressure is characteristic for people who as children felt neglected or overpowered by a dominant mother and lacked recognition from the father or a father figure. They never really felt secure. Foremost, they want the security sequence of successes, they achieve to gain recognition that was withheld before. In most cases, the writers are intelligent and talented and often achieve impressive results. Often, they are looked up to and admired. Many of the world’s outstanding leaders in politics and business belong to this group. In their personal life, however, they are not likely to enjoy things. Too driven to be able to relax, they are unable to be spontaneous and to enjoy things.

The writer may not know that he is sublimating libidinous energy, but handwriting analysis can tell. The reversed pressure pattern shows that he expends energy in strokes moving away from himself and his instinctual drives and concerns into the social sphere.

One characteristic of energy displacement is that it is never completely successful. Once the writer relaxes his controls, the suppressed emotions come to the forefront and the forced neglect of the emotional side of his nature makes him unhappy and dissatisfied. He tries to overcome such periods of frustration by striving even harder to attain his goals.

It is difficult for the writer to get along cooperatively. He forces issues and people because he conceives opposition where it does not normally exist. His dominating tendencies have a pronounced effect on his relationships. His blind effort to get the job done, he pushes people, ignoring personal needs and destroying their willingness to cooperate. He is too forceful and too demanding, much of the time.

In company, he may be accused of being aggressive, or too loud, and of speaking only of himself. While he can respect the accomplishments of others, he does not simply and naturally like people.

The writer feels that only his own needs are important and to be respected; however he is quick to disregard the feelings and wishes of other individuals. He thinks only in terms of how people can be used in his pursuit of success. He can be benevolent and helpful when it furthers his own interests, but only to those who do not challenge his influence or success.

The writer is unwilling to take orders and resists pressure of any kind. When his wishes are disregarded, or when someone achieves something he does not, great anxiety is stirred up.

The writer wants to overcompensate for deep-seated inferiority feelings. He believes that it would be to his advantage to appear more important and more assured than he really is.

With the signature strongly exaggerated, the writer may attempt to build himself up with claims that are not based on reality. He may use extravagant mannerisms or brag. Rather than being supportive of others, he will be concerned primarily with his own advancement and concerns

The writer is frustrated at being unable to direct others effectively. Consequently, he tries to control them and the situation through bossiness. He does not know how to be considerate and tactful, even when he would like to be.

His get-someone-else-to-do-it approach always involves a mixture of aggressiveness and hostility. If this method fails, he may nag, whimper or whine until others do his bidding. He may domineer with a “poor me” attitude.

The writer fails to realize that the effect on other people is that they become exasperated. While the domineering approach may produce outward conformity, it also gives rise to rankling resentment. It makes others all the more eager to get away from the domineering individual.

The writer exercises control over others by the force of his will. He is skilled at influencing them and getting them to do things his way.

He is much happier giving orders than taking them. He wants to be in charge and have the final say. He can be quite bossy and expects to have his way. He is more demanding than accommodating and it is difficult for him to cooperate.

The writer is mentally restless and irritable. He is temporarily under strain, either due to mental or physical causes. The stress may be long-lasting or immediate. Quite often, irritability is the result of not having enough rest to keep alert. Tiredness, exhaustion, the busy pace, strained relations, increased output demands, excessive noise, all contribute to restlessness. He is bothered by minor annoyances and has to make a special effort to remain in control of himself. Every little thing that irritates him adds fuel to the fire until he feels that everything is wrong. Arguments during this period are useless. Disputes, any situation in which the writer feels himself being pressured or put on the spot, will bring the irritability rising up.

In the authoritarian or antisocial personality, jabbed i-dots have an additional meaning. They make the person even more irascible.

indikator.nama: Final strokes end in upper zone
indikator.keterangan:
Final strokes on letters or words should fall into the middle zone. They should not be in the upper or lower zone. If they extend into the upper or lower zones, then this indicates that the writer feels some insecurity in the interpersonal (middle) zone.

The writer is seeking notice, prestige or is particularly ambitious. If finals angle sharply upwards, he uses forcefulness to compensate for emotional insecurity.

Elaborated strokes have a breaking effect upon the writing and contribute to slowness and left tendency.

The writer works uneconomically. The invested energy is disproportionate to the result. To make himself look better in the eyes of others and to attract favorable attention, he flaunts himself; he boasts and exaggerates his achievements. After even the smallest performance, he will stop to applaud himself. Such writers are unpleasant people to have around because they will attempt to tyrannize any group in which they find themselves.

The writer needs much space in which to operate, both mentally and physically. He needs freedom from restrictions. He is determined to take up all the space in his life that he feels he is entitled to.

indikator.nama: Initial and final garlands on the same word
indikator.keterangan: The writer can be unduly influenced by other people. He exerts himself for others in order to secure their recognition and support.

With initial letters much larger in size, the writer wants to impress others with his importance. (With no additional signs of vanity, he may simply be trying to create the best possible impression, such as in sales, etc.)

These writers often have a poor sense of value. They tend to spend imprudently and fail save enough of their earnings for emergencies. They don’t know how to make money work for them, and few of them are cautious with cash. They spend it on what they are interested in at the moment and lack the ability to stay within a budget.

With initial letters elaborated, the writer is vain, ostentatious and shows an exorbitant need for recognition. He is trying to impress others with the importance of what he going to say or do. In reality, he spends much time reflecting and making elaborate preparations with little follow-through. He may waste time and energy without actually starting to work.

The writer is arrogant only with subordinates or with people he feels are of lesser importance. Toward superiors, he is servile and obsequious. He tries to remain inconspicuous and demonstrates feigned modesty. He lacks a resolute attitude and the ability to resist. Most often, he maneuvers covertly to achieve his egotistical aims.

With narrow writing in the text and broad initials in the signature, the writer is trying to hide his insecurity behind a facade of exaggerated assurance. Since this confidence does not come naturally, it often manifests itself as pomposity or arrogance.

To compensate for strong insecurities, the writer puts up a front of arrogance and vanity. In relationships, he is often rude and impertinent. The writer is extremely vulnerable to criticism. To keep himself from losing face, he may resort to subterfuge, misrepresentation, and deceit.

The writer has a strong material orientation and cherishes possessions which provide a measure of status or prestige. He has visions about sexual conquests, money, or material things.

With loops returning to the baseline, the writer is innovative in the material area. He can perceive better working methods, envision changes in quality, or alternatives in problem solving in order to obtain the most positive result.

The writer is restless and constantly needs new experiences and relationships. He is imaginative in interpersonal and sexual encounters. He craves the unexpected and enjoys the changes which bring new physical sensations to him. He tends to become bored when relationships and projects are unvaried and monotonous. He likes to share his interests with many people. Since he is fascinated by so many different things, he likes people who get equally involved.

With loops not returning to the baseline, the writer fails to use his ideas to best advantage. He tends to contemplate rather than act. His initiative fades out and he fails to drive his ideas through to completion.

indikator.nama: Middle zone letters displaced into the upper zone
indikator.keterangan: The writer is beset by the desire for greatness and accomplishments he has so far failed to achieve. This is usually associated by guilt feelings and regret. Deep down he feels that according to his abilities this should be his normal level of accomplishment. (This can contribute to motivation.)

The writer has large ego demands and a strong need for recognition. He will work hard for reinforcement of his self-esteem. His rewards come from being noticed and recognized by people important to him.

The writer is primarily concerned with the present; what is going on right now is of prime importance. He enjoys working with people and before the public, and compliments and praise enhance his performance. If others demonstrate to him that they have noticed he is doing well and that they approve of him, he will try especially hard to do a fine job. He does whatever enhances his ego. For instance, he may be generous in situations where generosity can be used to enhance his self-esteem.

The writer shifts projects and subjects easily to accommodate what he feels is important in the moment. In fact, it is normal for him to do more than one job at the same time. He may be impatient and he has a shorter attention span. To others, he may appear inconsiderate when he interrupts them or expects them to refocus to meet his immediate needs. His pattern of working and learning is by fits and starts with many interruptions, both created and allowed.

With middle zone width equal to middle zone height, the writer is very confident and capable. He presumes his own authority and is threatened only by very large responsibilities. He is progressive. He has bigger concepts and thinks in bigger terms. He is particularly competitive in situations where the reward is applause or prestige.

The writer is able to enjoy sexual activities (if confirmed by lower zone indicators). They enhance human relationships. He is sure of himself in such encounters and not afraid to reach out to the other person.

The writer works to advantage in situations that call for leadership. He feels stimulated by challenges. This does not mean that he does not know fear. In fact, when an immense hurdle blocks his way he may be very much afraid. And since he has seldom felt alarm before, it is difficult for him to handle it. He feels temporarily confused and completely frustrated. In other words, when the “large” writer feels fear, it is an unfamiliar experience and he perceives it more intensely than anyone else.

The writer has feelings of self-importance that are egocentric in nature. He is generally unconcerned about details and has a tendency to overlook anything small. He feels he does not have to deal with trivia. This includes personal relationships as well as vocational openings. He loses many opportunities to advance himself by belittling the worth of an assignment or the people who offer him the job. He thinks he can handle anything better than they can. Most of the time, he gets off to a good start; however, this does not always result in a good finish.

With middle zone width narrower than height, the writer suffers an undefinable sense of anxiety. He requires constant reassurance of his real or imagined abilities. He repeatedly needs the proverbial pat on the back. To hide his insecurities he tends to brag about his alleged capabilities. Regrettably, his boasting keeps him so busy that he does not have the time to do a good enough job to back up his bragging. This, in turn, increases his uneasiness.

The writer appears very positive and confident. He has a natural sense of assurance when it comes to tackling new experiences. He moves right in and assumes authority. What others consider risky or frightening does not even give him pause. He thinks he can handle anything and is satisfied only with large responsibilities.

The writer is self-sufficient and has a low fear threshold. He knows he can deal with pressures coming from the outside. He is less likely to be intimidated by people he does not know or who are superior to him. He is not afraid to speak his mind or to defend his own opinions. Because he feels more adequate to everything, he welcomes responsibility. He works well under pressure and often spearheads activities. Others tend to look to him for leadership. It takes a very large setback or problem to make him feel threatened or afraid.

The writer feels it is his right to lead. He may overpower others with his commanding personality. His real challenge is to stop assuming that he is in charge and learn to support those more qualified to be in command. He has little patience with less confident people who, in his opinion, lack the courage to be spontaneous and progressive.

Important! Just because he appears strong and assured does not necessarily mean that he actually possesses these qualities. If they are not confirmed by strong supporting traits, the writer is putting up a facade to hide inner insecurities.

The writer has an exaggerated pride about himself, his plans and his accomplishments. He wants to attract notice, be admired and draw attention to himself. He is self-centered and egotistical. He builds up anxiety how he is being received by others and how their reactions will affect him. If others demonstrate that they have noticed him and approve of him, he feels assured. If he is criticized, especially in front of others, he is devastated. He is afraid of being laughed at or of making a mistake. Comparisons are particularly offensive to him. He always wants to be given more recognition than others. He wants to rank above others in preferment or his pride is hurt.

To keep his self esteem intact, the writer puts up a facade. He will go to great pains to avoid losing face and may greatly exaggerate what he has achieved. More often than not, he is unable to back up his claims with true success. He is afraid to see his limitations and shortcomings. By creating in his imagination a picture of himself that is superior to everyone, he can ignore the reality of what he is. The idealized self-image, however, has far reaching consequences. It leads to distortions in his attitude not only toward himself but toward others, too. He is unable to establish meaningful relationships. He isolates himself to avoid all danger of exposing the real picture of himself.

He is unable to do things in his own interest. Above all, he must maintain the glorified picture of himself. His goals are not for his own enjoyment and growth but rather for what enhances or diminishes his image.

Basically, the writer is egocentric. He ignores others' feelings but expects them to defer to him and his needs. He is willing to be considerate of others as long as it does not

draw attention away from him. He will use such good behavior to earn momentary applause but he begrudges others their turn in the spotlight. He constantly tries to “keep up with the Jones's” because outward appearances mean so much to him.

The writer has an exaggerated need for exaltation. More than anything, he wants to be considered exceptional. Often, this is coupled with the inability to realize even modest goals.

With very narrow capitals, the writer displays a modest facade. While he longs fervently for recognition, he will not push himself forward to gain rightful respect. His demeanor tends to be humble and shy. On the inside, however, he nurtures an inflated self image which is ultra-sensitive and easily bruised. He has an “elephant's memory” and it is hard for him to forgive even the slightest affront.
The writer is placing more importance on his public than on his private life. He wants to work in the public eye. He wants to represent, be noticed and receive recognition.

The writer seeks and enjoys the importance and recognition of public life. He is conscious of rank, title and position. He appreciates social formalities. He wants to overshadow other people and impress the public with his significance.
The writer constantly seeks public acclaim. He hides his insecurity behind a facade of exaggerated assurance. Since this does not come naturally, it often surfaces as arrogance and impudence.

indikator.nama: Signature middle zone height larger than middle zone height mode
indikator.keterangan: The writer seeks recognition in public life and tries to appear more important than he inwardly feels. He is conscious of rank, title and position. He wants to overshadow other people and impress the public with his significance. In reality, his confidence depends upon the approval of others and he can lose self-possession quickly with direct criticism or a put-down.

The writer is insecure and puts up a front of confidence he does not have. Foremost, he wishes to impress. He is very conscious of the impression he makes as a person. He may put undue emphasis on external accouterments such as dress, hair, etc. He is self-centered and projects an exaggerated appearance of importance; he strives to enhance his image as much as possible. The writer tries to build himself up with claims which are not based on reality. He uses extravagant manners or boasts to hide the fact that he is insecure.

Basically unreliable, the writer conceals through manipulation and uses alibis trying to obscure his real intentions from those with whom he deals. He frequently over-reacts or responds inappropriately because in reality he is scared.

Since he, himself, is so unreliable, he tends to be distrustful toward others, too.

The writer has a poor sense for essentials. He may miss out on some opportunities because he tends to belittle the worth of an assignment or job.

indikator.nama: Final strokes garlanded above middle zone apex
indikator.keterangan:
The writer has an excessive need for attention. To compensate for feelings of insecurity, he wants to attract notice at any cost. He is unable to recognize and appreciate himself as a worthy and adequate individual. He wants to be shown by others that his is “O.K.” and that they approve of him. But regardless of the attention he gets, the painful feeling of deprivation persists and he is unable to get rid of it.

Every time he is not the center of attention, he feels unworthy and insignificant. Deep-seated feelings of inadequacy drive him to seek extra acknowledgment all of the time, and more when he is under stress. His need for attention makes him an easy target for manipulative flatterers who use his weakness to their advantage.

The writer seeks friendly, congenial relations with other people. He is good natured and adaptable. The more the garland leans toward the right the more he needs contact with the you. He is dependent and has, as Pophal uncharitably states, “a herd instinct.”

The writer tries to avoid conflict because he lacks the energy or courage to deal with difficulties. He is more willing to compromise than to resist. In order to keep harmony, he often simply agrees. He wants to keep situations comfortable with the least amount of strain.

The writer is often credulous in responding to emotional pleas. Because he automatically tends to believe what is being said, he is more easily taken in. Even if he has been burnt he remains vulnerable.

With extremely regular writing, the writer assumes an ethical demeanor while in reality he is weak. This may lead to self-deceit and even intentional deceit. He may employ a helpless attitude to camouflage selfish schemes.

The writer is basically timid with an exaggerated need for demonstrated approval. To gain the coveted acceptance, he may behave with calculated friendliness. He tends to approach others in an obsequious and servile manner while in reality, he cares about nobody but himself. He is too absorbed with his own concerns. He may prattle, or chatter away, or he may be a busybody who meddles in other people’s affairs simply to involve himself in other people’s lives.

Many of these individuals are preoccupied with reminiscences and have an overwhelming yearning for the past.

The writer has the desire to acquire, to possess and gain. Acquisitiveness may pertain to material assets, to people, knowledge or property. He does not merely want to use a thing; he yearns to possess what he admires. He derives satisfaction simply from accumulating money or objects as opposed to putting them to use. He bases his security upon what he can save or own. (What he is likely to desire depends upon other personality traits. Literary interest = book collector; need for recognition = trophies, symbols of status and achievement.)

The writer enjoys collecting things. He accumulates items that he may never use but simply cannot throw away. When his possessions are taken away, he responds with intense anger. He hates waste in anything. He may, for instance, overeat to prevent the waste of food. Building security is his foremost concern. With one eye always on the future, he can become a miser who hoards for tomorrow and neglects living today. He wants to hold on to his assets; he parts with what he has only to trade for the better. Usually, he is unwilling to loan anything and other people’s carelessness with possessions is very distressing to him. To him, success becomes directly associated with material gains and he drives a hard bargain, as a rule. Nothing is too trivial, if the bottom line means profit for him. If his drive for gain goes unchecked, greed may be the result.

He is as possessive of his family and friends as he is of material things. His attitude toward people is to own rather than to love them. He wants to manipulate their lives in order to have more control over them.

The craving for possessions is often a defense against anxiety. The need for affection is repressed to such a degree that it no longer appears on the surface while the fear of rebuff is so great that it prevents the writer from letting others know that he aches for some kind of acceptance. The longing for material things then momentarily or permanently takes its place. To compensate for his lack of self-worth, the writer clings to material things which provide a measure of security.

The writer’s basic reaction to any situation is on the feeling level and he tends to react to emotional stimuli.

The writer is anxious in interpersonal relationships and finds it hard to interact naturally and spontaneously. He is impulsive in his emotional reactions and becomes involved indiscriminately in relationships. To those who are less emotional, he appears over-responsive or even insincere.

He lacks definite standards and seems too permissive regarding others’ behavior. He wants other people’s acceptance so much that he will agree with everything they say or do while in their company. With another person, he shifts his allegiance so that he agrees with the second individual.

The writer is poorly organized and lacks method and orderliness. Reacting strictly on impulse, he is unreliable where goals and deadlines are to be met.
Angular forms would indicate harshness, resistance, intolerance, and unwillingness to compromise. Lack of angles shows absence of these characteristics.

indikator.nama: Lower zone looped and loops return to baseline
indikator.keterangan:
The writer is able to apply his imagination in a resourceful manner. He retains the memory of past experiences and he can apply what he has learned beneficially in the present situation.

With proportionate pressure and well-formed loops, the writer is people oriented. He seeks contact on the interpersonal level and shows normal interest in sex.

indikator.nama: Lower zone and middle zone downslant are both toward the right
indikator.keterangan: The writer wants both emotional and physical contact with others.

The writer responds immediately on the emotional level. He is excitable and demonstrative. Responsiveness is demonstrated in every aspect of his behavior. He has a strong need to be with people because he needs others to respond to him. People stimulate him to think and feel. He can be easily influenced through his feelings and he can reach others through an emotional appeal.

The people close to him are always on his mind. He likes to be asked about the well-being of his loved ones, people as well as pets. In all relationships, personal and business, he wants to be shown that people are compassionate and care. A hug, an arm around the shoulder, remembrances on special occasions, notes of appreciation, they all mean a lot. He wants to express what is going on inside of him. He dislikes people who try to interrupt or stop his emotional display.

The writer becomes emotionally involved with anything that attracts his interest. It is difficult for him to stay with long term projects that require emotional stability. Once he becomes excited about something new, he loses the determination to finish a task that is already under way.

The writer’s subjective attitude affects his estimation of other people. This, in turn, affects his relationships with them. He prefers associates with whom he can be exactly what he is feeling. He is easily hurt by coldness or disinterest, not to mention slights or hostility. On the other hand, he is liable to buy from a salesman regardless of price, simply because he has come to regard him as a friend.

The writer’s automatic responses are on the emotional level. He finds it impossible to check his impulsive reactions and it is easy for others to tell what he is feeling just by looking at him.

The writer needs people to fulfill his emotional needs. Once he becomes involved, either in love or hate, he gets carried away. He is very much subject to the influence from others. He indulges in self-pity for slights, real or imagined, especially when he reaches out affectionately and is rejected or rebuffed. His overly emotional behavior may easily become an irritant to others who are less emotional. They may treat him like a child and dismiss his displays of feelings as a sign of immaturity. Professionally and personally, this makes for real problems in communication.

He responds with his feelings, not with his mind. Instead of acting on considered thought, he pours out emotions without considering the effect. Emotion is the driving force in most situations and relationships. Since he acts on impulse alone, he often finds himself committed to something he does not want to do or he gets involved in situations he regrets. He is emotionally unpredictable and goes from high to low moods within short periods of time. Emotionally speaking, he is either “all joy” or “all pain.” He cries easily or shows sentiment. And he is just as likely to become part of other people’s negative moods as he will share their positive frame of mind. He judges according to the present mood rather than facts and he tends to have a strongly biased point of view. He sometimes manipulates others by instilling guilt.

The writer is unwilling to forego gratification in the moment for future gains; therefore, he needs immediate or short-term goals. He seeks self-satisfaction at the moment and often cares about no one but himself.

The writer is not in charge of his own expression. Within him, the emotional side is too dominant. He permits himself to wallow in his feelings. He is irritating to others and a liability to himself. He pours out his feelings, positive and negative, indiscriminately and without conscious control.

Basically, the writer is anxious much of the time. He feels inwardly inadequate with the result that he has an exaggerated need to “fit in” with other people. He over-responds or reacts inappropriately. He deals in quantity rather than quality when getting involved in relationships. He may be obtrusive to fulfill his emotional needs. He feels coerced by people he views as superior to him and feels the pressure of those in authority all of the time. He believes that they are trying to drive him continually, whether this is accurate or not.

The writer lacks control to such a degree that his emotions carry him away. He wallows in his feelings and is unpredictable and moody. He easily loses his grip on himself. He is unable to regulate and restrain his feelings toward others. He tends to exaggerate and thus makes an unrealistic assessment of situations and people. His view of others and of circumstances is subjective. He sees things from his own particular perspective and as a result, distorts reality. The writer has more than average amounts of defensiveness. Basically, he feels inadequate and suffers anxiety all of the time. He tries to lessen the strain through excessive agreeableness, superficial friendliness, self-deception, alibis, submissiveness, or projecting blame on other people.

The writer is insecure and needs people to fill his emotional needs. He feels apprehensive by himself and needs companions to keep anxiety at bay. Because his needs are so strong he is often intrusive in trying to establish such bonds. As far as others are concerned, he becomes too familiar too soon and offends accordingly. He gets acquainted with too many people and wastes time with unimportant relationships. To the writer, possessions represent security. Since he is so fearful, he is unable to be generous.

The writer has an inordinate need for people. Being alone creates intense anxiety. He gets involved on impulse alone and his emotional needs are such that he intrudes even where he is not wanted. With him, one can almost always count on the conversation taking a personal trend. He talks freely about personal matters, even to strangers.

The writer finds it very difficult to think logically. Thinking tends to run on one track without consideration of anything else. Organizational ability is usually poor. He gets lost in details and is unable to see the overall project. And while he craves to work with the public, he is neither orderly nor efficient.

The writer shows ambition and a desire for greatness. He is envious of the rank or status enjoyed by those he considers above him. He strives to attain for himself a position that is higher up, more lofty or elevated. He may be subservient to people of higher standing or status and is susceptible to their praise and criticism. Pulver speaks fittingly of “the writer’s frog perspective.”

The writer plans to surpass the level at which he presently is. His aims are expansive. He seeks betterment, particularly self-improvement. He desires to achieve something that will bring him prestige or proves him to be outstanding in some way.

The writer’s aims are very high. He has an ardent desire to surpass the level at which he presently is. He sets objectives which may be impractical for others but which seem realistic for him.

Very light i-dots could mean fanciful illusions.
See 03-4 on page 16.

The writer is interested in the physical aspects of life and in material things. He desires tangible evidence of success.

With loops returning to the baseline, the writer is flexible and consciously tries new ways of doing things. He is open to new and varied kinds of relationships. He has a well developed memory for past experiences and applies what he has learned in the present situation. He will not make the same mistakes over and over again. He has many good ideas to improve the efficiency and quality of his work. In the sexual area, he is imaginative, too.

The writer functions best when he is not bound to old conventions, materials and working methods. He is most satisfied applying new techniques rather than adapting himself. He dislikes making do with left-overs or re-using materials, as a rule. He takes things as they come and is able to change his schedule at the last minute without becoming upset. With loops not returning to the baseline, the writer spends too much time thinking without using his ideas to best advantage. He has too many unresolved designs and plans and is inclined to contemplate rather than act. His initiative fades out and he fails to drive his ideas through to completion.
See 02-6 on page 10.
See 02-8a on page 10.
See 02-8b on page 11.
The writer applies his energies unevenly. He neglects the emotional and instinctual areas of his life in favor of the rational or mental sphere.

indikator.nama: Pressure displaced into upper zone upstrokes
indikator.keterangan:
Displaced pressure reveals that the writer’s ego is replacing an offensive original impulse with one that is less offensive and compatible with the ego. This is more positive than repression because the ego forms a “channel” and not a dam for the instinctual drive.

Displaced pressure is characteristic for people who as children felt neglected or overpowered by a dominant mother and lacked recognition from the father or a father figure. They never really felt secure. To compensate, they pour all their energies into an exaggerated drive for achievement and self assertion. Foremost, they want the security they never had. They seek material things that equal security. Through a continuing sequence of successes they endeavor to gain the recognition that was withheld before. In most cases, the writers are intelligent and often achieve impressive results. Many of the world's outstanding leaders in politics and business belong to this group. In their personal life, however, they are not likely to be so successful. Too driven to be able to relax, they are unable to be spontaneous and enjoy things.

The writer may not know that he is sublimating libidinous energy, but handwriting analysis can tell. The reversed pressure pattern shows that he expends energy in strokes moving away from himself and his instinctual drives and centers it in the rational sphere.

One characteristic of energy displacement is that it is never completely successful. Once the writer relaxes his controls, the suppressed emotions surge to the forefront and the forced neglect of the emotional side of his nature makes him unhappy and dissatisfied. He tries to overcome such periods of frustration by striving even harder to attain his goals.

The writer wants to attain something, regardless of available strength and abilities. He re-directs his energies from the interpersonal area into the mental sphere. He tries to compensate for unsatisfactory relationships through intellectual or artistic accomplishments. He is often gifted in both areas. He is excited about theories, mathematics, philosophy, anything that permits him to achieve mentally. He puts priority on time alone to process intellectual subjects that interest him, or work on projects of concern. He becomes most involved when he sees a purpose for whatever mental energy he is expending.

The writer has limited interest in interpersonal relationships. This has a diminishing effect on empathy, friendliness, and extroversion. It makes him less of a social person. A side effect is that he causes unintentional arguments. In reality, he is not trying to convince or change another person’s mind, he is simply reaffirming his own point of view. However, his reaffirmation is impersonal and cold; it lacks the warmth of human communication. The writer states what he believes and refuses to discuss the matter further. Other people are upset by this attitude because it leaves them out and makes them feel that the writer is quarreling with them.
See listing 01-5 on page 4.
See listing 01-9 on page 5.

The writer’s aspirations are expansive and he sets high standards for self-improvement. He is progressive in setting his goals and willing to challenge himself to surpass the level where he presently is. He wants to achieve something that will bring him prestige or prove him to be outstanding in some way. He is alert to opportunities to advance himself and willing to sacrifice present gratification for the sake of future aims. He thinks in terms of what he is planning for the moment will relate to the fulfillment of his ambitions for the future.
The writer sets his sights high; he is internally driven, and his emphasis is on reaching his goals. With strong willpower he will allow nothing to stand in the way of accomplishing his aims.

The writer’s aspirations are toward intellectual pursuits. He seeks a position where mental activity dominates. He wants to explore new areas and increase his store of knowledge. His general orientation is toward intellectual work and understanding theory is a driving motivation. He needs constant mental challenges and is unable to turn off his mind. He deals effectively with complex situations. When mentally bored by an “inferior” subject, he may tune out and in his mind occupy himself with more stimulating ideas. Intellectual companionship is stimulating to him, both at work and during recreation.

The writer sets high standards for himself and has feelings of obligations toward others.

With displaced pressure, there may be sublimation of drives into the intellectual sphere.

Important! Upper zone height is no guarantee for mental accomplishment. It does not mean that the writer is automatically an intellectual. It merely shows that he has an intellectual inclination and that the mental realm is his area of interest.

The degree of connectedness shows how the writer associates with the surrounding world and how capable his mind is of seeing how things are connected.

The writer desires participation and involvement with other people. He wants to include them in his life. In his social behavior, he follows conventional ways. He thinks logically and solves problems in a methodical step-by-step manner. In his interactions with others, he desires clear communication. If he feels he is not understood, he attempts further clarification because others' comprehension is important to him.

The writer has accepted a fundamental set of values. He lives by these principles and will do nothing to belittle himself. He derives a sense of self worth from knowing that he conforms to rules which he considers valuable and which he expects others to respect. Living according to this code gives him stability as well as inner security. It also makes him predictable. Since he does not seek rewards for good behavior from others, he does not feel threatened by possible criticism. He enjoys a sincere compliment when it is given but he is not susceptible to empty flattery.

The writer can deal more easily with other people because he does not take their words or behavior personally.

The writer tries to live according to an intrinsic set of ideals. Knowing that what he believes is acceptable to those whose opinions he values gives him a feeling of security. He is somewhat sensitive when others censure the standards by which he lives. However, he is able to deal with the criticism so as not to let it influence his functioning ability.

Empathy enables the writer to identify with and understand another's situation, feelings and motives.

The writer has accepted an fundamental set of values. He lives by these principles and derives a sense of self worth from knowing that he conforms to rules which he considers valuable and which he expects others to respect. Living according to his code gives him stability as well as an inner feeling of security.

The writer is motivated by a sense of good taste and dignity. His speech and behavior are refined. This includes dressing suitably for each occasion. His taste in clothing will probably lean toward the conservative.

The writer is somewhat sensitive to criticism but not enough to deter him from doing what he wishes to do. He will not immediately change his behavior when someone does not approve of him. He would first consider whether or not such demands are reasonable.

The writer is able to recognize the feelings that are being experienced by another person. He sensitive to, and can vicariously experience these thoughts and feelings himself.

The writer has a conforming nature. He accepts the standards society has set up as a protection and moves smoothly within the limits imposed upon him. He adapts to the views and standards of the more conventional people.

The writer's taste leans toward the conservative. He follows a conventional code of behavior and adheres to laws of conduct that are traditional and generally approved. He abhors flashiness and has a eye for subtle quality. He is less likely to upset his friends or get in trouble with the law. He finds many things set up to his advantage in the way of standard arrangements, laws, procedures and routines. He can live his life staying with what is traditional and well approved by everyone who fits in the same category.

The writer is not one to blaze trails and forge ahead by himself. Foremost, he is concerned being approved by people in his group and by those in authority. He is a reliable follower and in his work habits and performance he is conforming. He prefers traditional methods of getting ahead. Vocationally, he fits well into a position where exact standards are to be held and maintained, such as being an insurance underwriter or a member of an accreditation team.

The writer adapts himself to the surrounding world and behaves according to customary habits and rules. He desires open communication and wants to be understood by others. He is self-disciplined, dependable and predictable; he has a good capacity for purposeful work. Most likely, he will be punctual and orderly.

With copybook writing, the writer is concerned with other people's opinion about him. He tries to obtain their approval and acceptance through conventional attitudes and behavior. He conforms because of the feelings of security he derives from doing so. He is somewhat uneasy with people he does not know and in situations that are unfamiliar.

The writer is conservative in his emotional expression. He lacks spontaneity due to insecurity. The emotions he feels inside will be expressed when it seems appropriate and acceptable to do so. He is concerned about doing things right. Since society puts a premium on emotional control, he attempts to fit in with the standards of the group. He is just as likely to regulate the display of affection as the expression of negative feelings. He is uneasy when someone is showing more feeling to him than he is comfortable in showing back.

With people he knows well and in familiar circumstances, the writer is friendly, caring, and kind. He is less inhibited and it is easier for him to accept their ideas and working methods. He also responds more readily to their emotional needs.

The writer's behavior in his day-to-day relationships is approval seeking. He conforms to the standards of most of the people in his group. While behaving conventionally and associating with people who behave in familiar ways, he feels safe and at ease. He feels comfortable living relatively close to them and enjoys being included in their activities. He likes to communicate with them and talks freely about personal matters. Questions about his private affairs give him a sense of being included. In response, he spontaneously asks questions of others himself. The more involved he is, the more spontaneously he displays. He might, for instance, impulsively hold out his hand, or he may touch others while talking to them.

The writer makes decisions subjectively. His conclusions are based upon feelings more than upon considered judgment.

The writer is conforming and his work habits are conventional. He adapts to traditional procedures, to proven methods, and to work habits of the group. He invests a great deal of time and energy so that no cause for criticism exists. Because of the tension he feels in unfamiliar areas, he limits himself to fields in which he has had prior successes. He is a better follower than leader and lacks the essentials for leadership.

In his sexual behavior the writer is conventional. He conforms to what he has been brought up to do and what he has been exposed to within his peer group. He adapts to the expectations of the group of which he feels a part. He suffers guilt when he departs from conventional standards. He feels uncomfortable and inadequate, too.

The writer consciously controls his behavior and the degree to which he becomes involved in projects and relationships. He is careful and seldom acts without due consideration. He plans his undertakings with feasibility and security in mind. He likes to act on precedent, on what has been proven by experience, either his own, or some recognized authority's. It is difficult for him to move beyond what is familiar and to adjust to progress he, himself, has not initiated. Before planning too far, he stops to consider whether his actions will threaten his security. He believes in taking precautions and usually holds back until he is certain that a realistic chance of a successful outcome exists.

The writer voluntarily adheres to certain rules or principles, he regulates his mental output and his impulses by the will. He has a unique attitude toward what he considers his duty and he will not deviate from his goals. He is steady and reliable and purposes are hard for him to make do or compromise where his purposes are concerned.

The writer conforms to accepted customs and traditions. He derives a sense of self worth from knowing that he adheres to principles which he considers valuable and which others respect. He moves smoothly within limits accepted by his superiors and peers.

The writer will satisfy his interpersonal needs in conventional ways. He is home oriented and his socializing tends to center around people he knows. He stays with what is considered traditional and well-accepted behavior by society. He has a natural sense of what can threaten his security and responds to new people and situations with caution.

He is more self-protective with people he does not know or knows only slightly and it takes a long time before he feels fully at ease in a group. With people he knows well, he is cooperative and considerate. He is courteous and kind and takes delight in being accepted and recognized. He expects support from the group and finds it difficult to stand alone. He does not look upon personal questions as an intrusion into his private affairs. To him, they are signs of acceptance and he freely offers advice or asks questions himself.

The writer moves comfortably within a moderate amount of space without feeling crowded. He feels at ease living close to people he knows and expects to be included in their activities. Without close relationships, he tends to get lonely and depressed.

Basically, the writer is not a generous person. His native tendency is to hold back. Giving comes only as the result of a conscious decision and after considering the results. It does not happen automatically. Most importantly, the writer knows the value of his gift.

In his sexual behavior, he is conventional. He conforms to what he has been brought up to do and what he has been exposed to in his peer group. He adapts to the expectations of the group of which he feels a part.

The writer is concerned about doing things “right.” Since society seems to put a premium on emotional control, he attempts to fit in by exercising restraint. The emotions he feels inside will be expressed when it seems appropriate and acceptable to do so. He regulates the display of affection and the expression of negative feelings. He is uneasy if someone shows more feeling than he is comfortable in showing back. With people he knows well and in familiar circumstances, he is less inhibited and reserved.

The writer submits to conventional ways of thinking because he is afraid to set himself apart. He is unoriginal in most of his opinions and thoughts and follows the concepts established by family, teachers, and most importantly, his reference group. He finds that being conforming is safer than following his own independent beliefs. Being basically a follower, he takes directions more easily. He understands the cause and consequence rule and relates to it. He follows the customs of his peer group due to fear of being thought of as unconventional and he seeks approval for what he does and for complying with others' expectations.

The writer is dependent and predictable. He is uneasy when he violates standards of behavior and becomes upset when others disregard established rules. Contradictory behavior in others is hard for him to accept. He becomes indignant, even intolerant, when he sees violations of the rules he, himself, obeys.

The writer is undemanding and content to stay with current opportunities. Usually, he limits himself to projects he had success with before. He takes risks carefully and prefers traditional methods of getting ahead. He is bound to the familiar and distrustful of new ideas. He clings to known methods and “safe” procedures and works best where no independent thinking is required. His approach seldom varies since it has been proven effective in the past. He prefers to deal with small areas rather than large regarding responsibility and authority. Foremost, he wants security and certainty. He starts one thing at a time and only what he knows he can finish with a reasonable assurance of success. He avoids extending himself to the point where he might be challenged. He wants approval and encouragement. For that reason, supportive roles come more natural to him than leadership positions.

He works best in support of stronger personalities because he finds it difficult to be relaxed with people over whom he has authority. He can be depended upon to follow instructions in areas which he already knows but he is easily overwhelmed when faced with challenges larger than he is accustomed to. At all times, he takes pride in jobs assigned to him and he invests a great deal of time and energy so that no cause for criticism exists.

He is most comfortable when he can “ease” into a new situation.
