If he should get involved in unfamiliar activities, either by being chosen, or through circumstances beyond his control, he feels extremely threatened and moves ahead by will alone. In the end, he usually succeeds, although the tension leaves him exhausted. The success experience then increases his willingness to become involved in a similar activity again. What he has learned to do well adds to his sense of security.

Vocationally, he is most satisfied in a conserving kind of job, such as the healing arts, museum keeper, repair mechanic, antique dealer, dentist, domestic help, and all kinds of maintenance jobs.

The writer holds to traditional views and his value system is conventional. He accepts the standards society has set up and moves within the limits established for him.

He has feelings of obligations toward others. He feels at a loss in the face of radical ideas; inconsistent views by others are hard for him to accept.

Such people are at a disadvantage in the creative field because they tend to re-create rather than create. Their thoughts are geared toward preserving that which they are already familiar with. When presented with new concepts, it is very difficult for them to be enthusiastic, especially if it means discarding a notion or belief that seems to have worked well in the past.

With defenses strong, conventionality and conservatism may be self-protective maneuvers stemming from insecurity and fear of change. The writer conforms because he is afraid to do otherwise. In fact, he not only wants to meet society's standards, he wants to surpass them.

The writer's views and opinions, his mental attitudes and his value system are conventional. He is concerned with preserving that for the future which he has used in the past. He wants to perpetuate what is familiar and approved and holds to moral and spiritual values which are approved. When asked to support unfamiliar ideas, it is very difficult for him to be enthusiastic, especially when it means relinquishing something that seems to have worked well in the past. In most instances, he will try to adjust the new to fit in with the familiar. Conforming to the expectations of people he wants to please provides him with inner security. He feels guilty for transgressing from conventional thoughts. He fits best into positions where existing standards are to be observed and maintained. Bookkeeping, banking, maintenance, etc. would be ideal.

indikator.nama: Angles at the top of middle zone letters m and n
indikator.keterangan:
The writer wants to investigate matters for himself. He wants to learn as much as he can. He not only wants to satisfy his curiosity, but he wants to probe into things, to explore.

Eager for continued learning and growth, he has a strong need to find his own answers. He does not want to be told second-hand. He wants to investigate matters for himself rather than just taking someone’s word on it.

He likes to pursue investigations in his own way, and if his interest is challenged, he is capable of probing deeply for information. Once an idea becomes fixed in his mind, he usually sets about gathering large amounts of information to augment it.

With an inquiring mind, he is not an easy person to convince. Constantly questioning and seeking, he is curious about the whys and wherefores of just about everything.

Any new subject excites him and he wants to go on learning new things all his life. He rarely passes up an opportunity to expand his horizon.

He does not like to undertake a venture until he has carefully examined the ground and accumulated the necessary knowledge beforehand.

The writer may be drawn to professions that allow him to indulge in his love for knowledge. Higher education may have a special attraction for him and science may prove a fertile field for his investigative and searching mind. Always trying to broaden and develop his mind, he would be excited to give others the benefit of his knowledge. He would make a capable investigator of insurance frauds, conspiracies, and complex financial swindles.

As an employee, his curiosity goes beyond the immediate task. A strong sense of urgency drives him to learn as much as he can about subjects related to his job. Rarely satisfied with simply getting instructions, he will want to know the why behind the orders and the reason for using certain methods. His desire to improve would be strong enough to overcome the discomfort of learning something new. As a sales person, he may study trade journals or competitive web sites for product specifications, staffing, new product promotions and a host of other information, which he may find helpful.

indikator.nama: Angles at the bottom of middle zone letters m and n
indikator.keterangan:
The writer feels that it is necessary to analyze everything about a situation or problem before he is comfortable enough to act. He has a need to know why, especially in situations that seem unclear or threatening.

He feels compelled to take every “whole” to pieces until he understands the parts and he compares many facts before he is satisfied. But such analysis takes time and, therefore, it takes him a long time to make his decisions.

This works to advantage when he is confronted with new problems or challenges. Accepting little on face value, he examines his data and looks at consequences until everything “jells.” Action will follow the reasoning process. But sometimes even in familiar situations, the person feels compelled to ponder old facts just one more time. This “figure – figure” can be a real trial for co-workers or family. To them, he may seem tedious and wearisome when he wastes time analyzing every little thing.

And the analytical writer expects others to be equally thorough and logical. He wants to know the reasons behind their statements and wants to understand every step of the process by which conclusions are reached.

The analytical thinker enjoys reading, research, or analysis – anything which gives him answers. He likes to figure things out and in diagnostic work, he usually excels.

For most professions, analytical ability is a valuable trait and it is desirable in many trades. Teachers should have some analytical ability. Instructors as well as students benefit by discussions on the why and how of most topics under discussion.

It benefits jobs involving analysis such as science, research, planning, administration, or counseling.

The writer easily expresses himself verbally or in writing. He rapidly connects ideas and smoothly changes from one phase of thought to another. He has a feeling for the way components fit together (ideas, people, things). By softening contrasts he makes the parts work efficiently as a whole.

The writer has a higher than average level of intelligence and a faster than normal speed of thinking. He tends to form his own opinions and is not easily influenced, except by facts.

He possesses an inventive type of creativity and a strong desire for efficiency. Unencumbered by traditional concepts, he is willing to try the unfamiliar and new. He is resourceful in his problem solving. With the ability to think progressively, he seeks to streamline his work in a creative manner.

The writer has the natural ability to express ideas facilely. It affects both his thinking and communication. He not only gets his feelings across better to loved ones, friends and associates, but also enjoys vocational advantages in many fields. He is a better lecturer, teacher, or master of ceremony. He is more effective in sales and on a debating team. He is a more skilled writer and editor. It is rare to find a successful author or public speaker without fluidity in script.

The writer changes smoothly from one phase of thought to another. He has the ability to express himself easily, either in writing or through the spoken word. He has a feeling for the right phrase or verbal presentation. He puts sentences together in logical sequence. His language is usually eloquent and elegant. Important! Effectiveness of this trait may be modified by the writer's level of education. His speaking ability may depend on other traits such as self-assurance and self-confidence.

indikator.nama: Connective forms original from middle to upper zone
indikator.keterangan: The writer has a higher than average level of intelligence. He tends to form his own opinions and is not easily influenced, except by facts. He possesses an inventive type of creativity and a strong desire for efficiency. Unencumbered by traditional concepts, he is willing to try the unfamiliar and new. He is a resourceful problem solver and seeks to streamline his work in a creative manner.

The writer is tolerant of other people's opinions and willing to consider their ideas. He approaches problems with an open mind. Being willing to look at something in a new way, he appreciates the good points in others' suggestions and he can handle progressive concepts without feeling threatened. If others make propositions, he considers them willingly, either accepting them or rejecting them, according to their usefulness. And he is fair enough to admit when he is wrong.

Keeping an open mind is an important trait in leadership. The writer looks beyond the small irritations of the moment and is more open to compromise.

The writer's broader view gives him an advantage vocationally in fields where a tolerant perspective is an asset, such as the entertainment world, art, advertising, recreation, resort operation, etc.

Broadmindedness is an essential trait in many professions. Physicians, attorneys, teachers, or ministers should be tolerant to a degree.

In all occupations in which one deals with the public such as selling or secretarial work, one must be broadminded about the shortcomings of others.

Being more tolerant, the writer suffers less from self-reproach for having “let himself down.” Being less concerned, he usually has fewer health problems, such as ulcers or disturbances of the digestive tract.
See listing 05-10 on page 33.

The writer has imaginative ability. He has a broader outlook and can handle progressive concepts without feeling threatened and without suffering undue stress. He considers new ideas willingly, either accepting them or rejecting them, according to their usefulness. The writer has a more tolerant point of view. He plans more broadly. He looks beyond the small irritations of the moment and is more open to compromise. He is more permissive and does not expect others to behave as he does. He suffers less from self-reproach for having “let himself down.”

The writer has well developed imaginative ability. Most of the time, he likes to think independently.

Eager to learn of new concepts, he is open to subjects that are unfamiliar to him. He accepts new ideas sooner, relating them to his own thinking and accepting or rejecting them according to their usefulness. And, with his imaginative ability, he can see more ways to deal creatively with challenges.

In general, the writer has a tolerant point of view and a broader outlook on life. He sees things more in perspective. Even if he feels deeply about something, he is willing to compromise.

The writer has the ability to see both sides of just about any question. He will consider even those views that are opposed to his own. Overall, he is more easy-going in style and more permissive. He does not expect others to think and behave as he does and he seldom blames himself for “having let himself down.”

The writer has the ability to visualize. He can obtain ideas from his experiences, or from within himself. He can see in his mind’s eye the solutions of problems. For him, half the enjoyment in recreations can be in anticipating, such as in planning a trip. Imagination helps him rehearse in his mind what is coming mentally or physically. He is more easily inspired by the pictures of goals in his mind.

Imagination is a gift in creative occupations such as architecture, writing, advertising, composing or inventing.

Important! To use imaginative ability productively, loops have to return to the baseline.

The writer’s mental processes are aided by intuition. He has a kind of “sixth sense” that works outside the normal reasoning process. These “hunches” often provide him with more insight than he would have if he actually thought about something for some length of time.

Intuition speeds up the comprehending faculties and sharpens the writer’s perception. He instinctively says or does the right thing at the right time without knowing how or why. Often, in a flash of insight, he can get to the heart of the matter, though it may be difficult for him to describe his methodology.

This ability to arrive at a conclusion apparently without reasoning or investigation puts his mental efforts ahead of those of most of his associates, regardless of their intelligence or experience. Hunches are the result of an unconscious trial and error process during which one possibility after another is tested internally until one of them clicks.

“Hunches” may arise from information that does not even appear to be relevant to a problem at hand. Often, they can be stimulated by getting away from a problem or by “sleeping on it.” During this so-called incubation period, the writer’s mind continues to mull over the problem on an unconscious or semi-conscious level and, in some cases at least, a solution rises to the surface and presents itself in the form of a “hunch” or sudden insight. This cuts short the conscious thinking process and reduces the time needed for reaching decisions.

Intuition also warns the writer when something is dangerous. Confronted with some sudden or unusual situation, he will receive a flash-like hunch to do this or that. This serves as a brake rather than an accelerator, so to speak. There are no immediate facts to deliberate upon nor is there exact evidence; still, he instinctively knows or feels that he should get out of a situation or place.

Intuitively, the writer can understand the feelings and reactions of other people. He can usually sense when someone is lying to him or when things “just aren’t right.” His intuition cuts through the poses of personality to see right into the heart of an individual.

Intuition promotes easier adjustment to new conditions. The writer instinctively makes the right move at the right time.

The writer’s instinctive knowledge may be amazing to others but he has probably learned to believe in it. He may know from experience that it is reliable, providing he heeds the small inner voice.

Intuition does not function well if the writer tries to make it work for him. It requires a relaxed state of body and mind. Any forced effort makes for tension in the body and is reflected by a similar state of strain in brain functioning.

indikator.nama: Initial strokes direct in the upper zone
indikator.keterangan:
The writer believes in a simple and straightforward approach, disdaining anything that wastes time and effort. Mentally efficient and direct, he meets problems and challenges head on.

Coming directly to the point, he avoids getting bogged down in trivia. If necessary he can cut across red tape. Concentrating on the essential issues, he quickly discerns what is important from that which is not.

indikator.nama: Initial strokes direct in the middle zone
indikator.keterangan:
The writer is a person who gets things done. He copes with assignments promptly and if possible, will streamline his activities to avoid delays. This facilitates a speedier work flow and the time he saves can be used productively in other areas.

Direct in thought and action, the writer does not squander time in friendly gatherings with others. Viewing “small talk” as wasting time, he likes to say what he has to say, do what he has to do and, other than that, devote himself to the serious issues of his work. He wants to get on with the job rather than waste time in socializing. The writer dislikes wasting time on unimportant issues. Direct in his dealings with others, he wants them to take the same approach with him. His communications are certain to be straightforward and he may be famous for saying what he thinks. He speaks as concisely as possible and makes every word count. Most comfortable with concrete data, he wants facts and information, bare of adjectives and superlatives. He wants people to stop beating around the bush and get to the point. Time is of the essence and he usually interrupts others as soon as he knows what they are going to say. Having to repeat himself to make a point is very irritating. He talks “telegrams” when others expect “letters” and to others, he sometimes appears tactless and unnecessarily blunt.

The writer’s attitude toward sex is uncomplicated and straightforward, too. He does not like games and will be direct in his approach. A more romantic partner may be frustrated by his lack of imagination.
See listing 05-4 on page 29.

indikator.nama: Letters m and n with rounded tops
indikator.keterangan:
The cumulative thinker consciously processes each step of thought. He is more inclined to really think matters through rather than rely on first impressions. He is good where accurate facts are needed. And he retains what he has learned almost indefinitely.

But initially, he has a slower pace of learning – until he grasps all the facts. From then on, he rarely has to repeat that process and moves swiftly. Since he is a rarity among adult thinkers, he is usually under a great deal of pressure to “hurry up” in situations where a premium is put on speed. When such pressure is put on him, his mind tends to go “blank.”

And he is very irritated when he has to deal with people who process their thoughts faster than he. If he does not have the time and repetition he needs to learn the basics of a new subject or skill, he may find it very difficult to move ahead in that field.

This does not mean that he spends all his time thinking slowly. Only when he is faced with a new situation is he likely to take the time to think it through. He is concerned with reasons and with the cause.

Taking time to reach a conclusion is a distinct advantage in many situations. Research and education are natural fields for the cumulative thinker. Any occupation in which planning and fact-finding are involved will give him a sense of satisfaction – as long as he is given enough time for preparation, research and thought. Whatever he does, he functions best where he can work at his own rhythm.

The writer learns best through practical experience. To him, a training session without activity is like a session without learning. As a hands-on type of person, he usually has good manual dexterity. He is deft with his fingers and has good hand/eye coordination. He is particularly suited to work in fields that require special skill with the hands.

The writer’s talent gives him vocational and recreational advantages, should his interest incline him toward creative or manual activity. Wood working, crafts, handling of machinery or office equipment, baking, sewing, and many more activities are enhanced by this ability. It could suggest nuances in vocational selection, such as becoming a surgeon rather than a general practitioner.

With broad-topped “r’s” the writer is mechanically skilled.

indikator.nama: Letters m and n with needle points
indikator.keterangan:
The writer’s thinking seems effortless. He grasps points quickly, applies them to what he already knows, and it does not take him long to move into action. He wants results and he wants them fast.

His thinking processes are so fast that they defy attempts to determine the steps by which the writer arrives at his conclusions. He “thinks on his feet.” He functions to advantage where time is at a premium or where fast decisions are needed.

But the writer’s thought patterns can sometimes cause problems for him. With his fast thinking, he runs the risk of making snap judgments or jumping to conclusions. In his mind, he has thought through all of the issues in a few brief moments and has already come to the final conclusions while others may still be listening to the problem.

With his quick comprehension, he has arrived at the conclusion; however, he may not have all the data necessary to make the “correct” decision. He may think he knows when he doesn’t.

His biggest failing is in not taking the time to think. He is not willing to learn about the cause; he wants to deal with the effect. Reasons, background, in-depth investigation – he is likely to dismiss them in favor of action right now. So when the chips are down he is frequently the person who is wrong because he does not know the full facts of the situation. While he may appear brilliant in the moment, he may show to less advantage in the long run.

And, being a fast learner, he does not necessarily trouble to remember information because it can always be rapidly relearned.

His swift way of thinking may be the cause of misunderstandings. Catching on instantly, he feels others should grasp the meaning of his communications from almost the first word. When they don’t, he second-guesses them, or he becomes impatient, or he “tunes them out.”

Occupations where quick decisions are necessary are ideal for this type of individual. The field of communication would be suitable choice. He could work to advantage where things have to happen fast, such as moving baggage quickly or getting emergency equipment to a disaster scene. Being the engineer of a fast train would offer a natural outlet for his urge to move at greater speeds.

Important! If this is the writer’s only way of thinking he may jump to conclusions which are not always correct. He is unwilling to learn about causes and often dismisses reason and theory. He runs the risk of making snap judgments because he does not take the time to really think important matters through the time to really think important matters through. Dealing with the effects is his only concern. Consequently, he often remembers what he did, but not why he did it.

Rhythmical writing is evidence of the writer’s maturity and inner harmony. He has a balanced output of energy in all three areas of his life; he is well integrated mentally, emotionally, and physically. He adjusts sensibly to his environment or changes it to his requirements. He exercises good rational control and is responsible and reliable.

Rhythmical writers think smoothly and effectively. Their thoughts flow in orderly fashion from one to the other. They are mentally alert and have a productive outlook on life. They are active people who apply their energies systematically. They have inner stability and the energy to live a productive life. With a sense of duty, they apply themselves wholeheartedly to a task. With both vitality and endurance, these writers are enthusiastic and willing to engage themselves. After the job is completed, they are able to relax and enjoy the progress they have made.

These writers are attuned to the rhythm of life around them and have an awareness of the cyclical nature of things. They enjoy the rhythmical beat of music or the steady hum of machinery. They are aware of the finely tuned working of an apparatus and it appeals to them. They usually have good motor coordination, foot and/or hand dexterity. They have a talent for integrating components and for the organization of people and things. Taking the parts of an assignment, they know how to make them work in consonance with other parts.
See listing 05-5b on page 30.

The writer has the ability to be logical and objective, and he methodically processes new information. He views things in perspective; he is concerned with the whole project and with each individual step involved.

In his thinking and actions, he is organized, orderly and proficient. He has a need for clarity and the desire to be understood.

The writer is discerning in interpersonal relationships. He adjusts to his surroundings after careful considerations of all the ramifications involved. He makes conscious selections regarding the people with whom he spends his time and he is more formal in style.

He is less accessible to the friendly overtures by the more affable people. His habitual distance from others may be due to “inner-directedness.” Since he puts priority on time alone to think through matters of interest or concern, being with people is not so much of an incentive.

The writer mentally efficient. Viewing things in context or perspective allows him a degree of objectiveness. He is resourceful in adapting himself to people and situations. He considers the relationship between cause and effect and anticipates the consequences of his acts.

The writer likes order in his life and plans his projects with foresight and efficiency. He is discriminating in interpersonal relationships and consciously selects the people he associates with. He is mainly interested in those who share in purposeful accomplishment.

The writer thinks in an unbiased and discerning manner. He emphasizes objectivity and is comfortable with anything requiring the use of logic, organization, structure and analysis.

The writer works well and purposefully alone. He consciously keeps his distance from the world at large and is very selective in interpersonal relationships. Technology, planning and details are of interest to him.

The writer makes deliberate distinctions. He selects that which aids him and rejects that which hinders him or wastes his time. People often fall into the latter category. With people, he feels out of his element, he is uncomfortable or tense.

The writer is inventive in areas where others see only practicality. He is resourceful and makes creative contributions to his line of work. He envisions original solutions to problems. This ability goes beyond the mere rearrangement of existing resources and materials. His mental pictures are based on past experiences but they are not limited to them.

The writer is independent in his ideas and willing to work with the unfamiliar, either for efficiency or improvement. He is especially qualified for occupations that require creative thinking and originality.

indikator.nama: Connective forms original from middle to the upper zone
indikator.keterangan: See listing 06-2d on page 37.

The writer starts from a harmonious balance between mental drives and the desire for involvement in everyday activities. He has adequate energy with which to accomplish either mental or physical tasks and sufficient stamina to stay with something until it is completed. With normal amounts of sleep he can demand performance from himself without becoming unduly fatigued. He has the strength to be productive and the potential for leadership. He has the capacity to be optimistic and to become involved with people.

The writer is able to place emotional experiences in proper perspective. The memories of emotional happenings may stay with him for a moderate amount of time. While they are active, they may affect his reactions in the present. In due time, however, they will make room for new impressions.

The writer has a balanced output of energy in all three areas of his life: mental, interpersonal and productivity/sex. He is mentally alert with a positive outlook on life. A harmonious distribution of energy helps him to plan his projects and stay with them until they are completed. He is active, resilient and able to relax at will.
See listing 06-9 on page 42.

indikator.nama: Right tendency in the upper zone
indikator.keterangan: The writer’s mind is firmly focused on the future and the goals he wants to achieve. He is thinking ahead and prefers to plan in advance. He strives for intellectual independence and has emancipated himself from crippling memories from the past. Logical thinking ability is pronounced. The writer thinks speedily; he is mentally versatile and self-reliant. He appreciates intellectual contact with others.

The writer is emotionally mature and thinks in a practical and logical manner. With a forthright and efficient approach, he is interested in quick results and disapproves of people who cause delays.

In social and interpersonal relationships he is matter-of-fact. He is direct in style of action and communication. In most situations he “tells it like it is” and acts accordingly.

It is not that he is insensitive. He simply has no time to spend on social niceties. Clarity is his chief concern; ideas and content are more important than style. While his brief, succinct style helps move things along, it may be a problem for those who would appreciate a more considerate approach.

The writer’s mind works in a productively original way. He quickly grasps the fundamentals and eliminates the superfluous. He neither gets lost in unimportant details nor in fancy ideas. As a result, he is mentally productive and efficient.

The writer is mentally mature with a matter-of-fact attitude. He avoids extremes and plans realistically. He has the mental acumen to weigh the soundness of the reasoning of others. He does not get confused if unintelligible or vague ideas are put before him. One of his specialties is to simplify complicated information to deal with it more effectively.

The writer knows exactly how much time should be allotted to each task. He is conscious of the passage of time and can be irritated when delayed. He probably creates many labor-saving devices to achieve the fastest result with the least expenditure of time and energy.

The writer is free from crippling memories from the past and therefore has a more open and unbiased attitude toward the tasks that lie ahead.

The writer is lively and alert and anticipates success. He is enthusiastic and has a healthy amount of energy. He is adaptable to outside conditions and has few unresolved emotional problems or fears.

Speed is part of the writer’s nature. He thrives where briskness is the order of the day. He enjoys rapid transportation. He prefers job opportunities where quick activities are taking place. The person’s mental processes are exceptionally fast. He “thinks on his feet.” Thoughts run smoothly from one to the other and he easily comprehends. He grasps points instantaneously and applies them to what he already knows. He is quick in speech and action. Wherever things must happen fast, he functions to advantage. He is interested in immediate results and loathes delays. He is impatient with slowness or inefficiency. He may be very irritated by people who take longer to process their thoughts and reactions.

The writer’s innate tempo is expressed in the way he thinks, works, and in his sexual encounters. He is active and takes the initiative. (In sex, he may want fast results and may be too rushed to touch and love leisurely.)

Important! Legibility has to maintained throughout the writing.

The writer is self-disciplined and needs control of his life and of situations to be at ease. He likes the structured, reliable and organized. He has a good eye for space, time and distance and a penchant for method and order.

The writer’s thinking processes are well organized. He has a logical, mathematical mind and deals best with facts, mechanics and validity. His main concern is with data and figures which can be examined and analyzed. He uses a methodical way of testing an idea, finding it valid, then going on to the next, using the result of the first.

He is less comfortable when dealing with people who in the majority cannot be as easily systematized.

The writer has a strong desire to communicate on an intellectual level. He is mainly interested in the technical side of life. He is best qualified to work as a mathematician, engineer, technician, machinist or scientist.

Successful blending of cursive and printed writing results in print script. With the letters fused harmoniously, above average intelligence is indicated. If the two styles are not successfully combined, the positive connotation is lost and the writing becomes crude and unrefined.

These writers are mentally independent. Their own ideas carry more weight with them than the opinion of others.

They will not conform to customs or traditions simply because they are established. They need a logical reason for doing so and will acquiesce only if this agrees with their own views. In their speech and character, these people are instinctively refined. They abhor coarseness and vulgarity. They want to be part of an attractive world. When the setting is right, they can be most enthusiastic about their duties while unpleasant surroundings affect their productivity negatively. They want to feel that what they are doing is the result of their own choice. They are doing it because they want to do it, and the consequences of their activities are valuable to them.

These writers get along with others socially, but their basic orientation is toward intellectual pursuits. They prefer to spend less time in person-to-person relationships than in mental activities. Being with people, personally or professionally, is not of much concern, nor is it much of an incentive. As a rule, they prefer the company of people who gravitate toward interests similar to their own. Wherever refinement counts professionally or personally, they function to advantage.
See listing 04-10 on page 25.
See listing 06-3d on page 38.

The writer is levelheaded and has realistic controls over his behavior. He exhibits an evenly balanced mood. He exercises control over his emotions, desires and actions and sees and keeps things in perspective. He is reliable and internally motivated. His performance is steady and he is single-minded in pursuing his goals. He finds achievement rewarding in itself. He is able to mentally schedule ahead and each goal he sets is carefully planned. He works reliably and emphasizes method and order when he is in command. Once he has set up his schedule, it annoys him to have to rework it or make last minute changes. He becomes irritated by interference and delays. To a degree, he is selfish. He utilizes his energies and resources mainly toward his own personal goals.

With fast writing, the individual is diligent, ambitious, and eagerly involved. He takes a hopeful view of matters and expresses himself in a positive way. He focuses on the positive things he wants to happen and expects the best outcome in any circumstance. Cheerful anticipation grows the closer he approaches his goal. He usually feels good about things and optimistic about life in general. He is aware of positive possibilities in himself, in other people and in the situations around him. He concentrates on what he can do about a situation and multiplies what is uplifting. He focuses on the goal ahead, not on how he feels along the way. With that vision he has the courage to move ahead, optimistically. He expects things to work out over a period of time despite temporary setbacks.

With slow writing, the writer is ambitious and diligent; however, these traits seem to be thwarted by some kind of mental or physical impediment.

Important! In slow writing, rising alignment may be due to the paper having been placed diagonally in front of the writer. In this case, ascending lines have no graphological meaning.
The writer is success-oriented, ambitious and positive. He is optimistic in his self-appraisal, most of the time, and focuses on the constructive things he wants to accomplish.
See listing 01-5 on page 4.

With lower zone length proportionate, the writer has good endurance and performs steadily and reliably. Once he decides on a project, he is determined to follow through and he keeps himself moving until he attains it. He stays with what he is trying to accomplish.

With self-confidence low, the writer is still motivated to move forward no matter how inadequate he feels inside. Others may be amazed to learn of his low confidence because of what he has been able to achieve. Even though he may continue to have doubts about himself, he keeps his focus forward and perseveres toward his goal.

indikator.nama: Margin on right narrowing toward bottom of page
indikator.keterangan: The writer is cautious before allowing himself to become involved in a project or relationship. As soon as things are beginning to work out, his skepticism decreases. He grows more enthusiastic and looks forward to achieving his goal or becoming immersed in the relationship.

indikator.nama: Margin on left broadening toward bottom of page
indikator.keterangan: The writer is cautious when starting a project or relationship. The more he becomes involved, the more he overcomes his initial hesitation and his enthusiasm grows. As the project or the relationship continues, he becomes increasingly interested and absorbed. He abandons self-control and reserve for a more spontaneous attitude.
See listing 07-3 on page 46.

The writer performs reliably and in an orderly manner without dissipating his energy. He has a good capacity for emotional experiences and for involvement with his fellow men. He has a materialistic trend and enjoys challenges and accomplishments. This is how he fulfills his ego needs. He is naturally active and has above average endurance for productivity and sex. With lots of stamina to accomplish his goals, he shows perseverance and follows his plans without deviation. He can take more activity without feeling fatigued. His recuperative powers are such that he can do with less rest on a regular basis. Usually, he has strength and determination to spare and his body gives him good support when he places demands on it. He may set a rapid pace for others as he keeps going when they can no longer endure. He functions best in fields that are active and vigorous on the physical level.
See listing 05-8a on page 31.

indikator.nama: Right tendency in the upper zone
indikator.keterangan: See listing 07-5 on page 47.

indikator.nama: Right tendency in the middle zone
indikator.keterangan:
The writer is interested in people and responsive to them. He has at least a degree of assurance and the ability to adapt and get involved.

He is willing to try the unfamiliar in order to succeed. Vocationally, he is oriented toward the future and endeavors which are in the outside world.
See listing 07-6b on page 47.
See listing 07-7 on page 47.

The writer is motivated by pride. It compels him to try hard in every area of his life and sets the standards by which he lives. He wants to be thought of well by others and he wants to think favorably of himself. His self-regard in the vocational area is especially pronounced. It is the measuring stick for what he is and what he wishes to achieve.

Respect and recognition of others are important to him and he will do little to jeopardize his standing in the community. Pride determines with whom he associates. He shapes his ideas and ideals so that others approve. He pays much attention to what they are thinking and saying about him, and his self-esteem rises fast with their acclaim. Likewise, he can lose it quickly with direct censure or criticism. He experiences a sense of failure when he falls short of what he feels is expected of him.

The writer is motivated by a sense of pride. He molds his behavior and mannerisms so that they meet society’s norm. He is conscious of his appearance to those around him, and he is aware of their response to him. He will work hard to be praised. If others demonstrate their approval of him, it adds to his sense of self-respect. If he is criticized, especially in front of others, he is distressed. While he worries about the impression he makes, he has little consideration left to give to others.
See listing 06-2b on page 34.
See listing 06-2a on page 34.

The writer has above-average intelligence. He possesses superior associative skills and logical thinking ability. He is quick-witted and achieves with his mind, rather than toiling physically. He dislikes friction in his work and in interpersonal relationships and as a result, adapts more readily to people and circumstances.

This kind of connection indicates superior intellectual ability. It is found only in the writings of people with exceptional mental ability. The slow, prodding writing never produces this sign.

The writer shows great mental agility and excellent associative ability. Often he becomes engrossed in one particular idea to the exclusion of everything else. He thinks far faster than the majority of people. He can switch from one subject to another with lightning speed. He comprehends quickly and his mental energy is at a peak. Other important characteristics are progressive thinking, resourcefulness and creative ability. A side effect is that the writer becomes impatient or irritable with slower thinkers, or involved explanations, or with slow reacting people in general.

The writer’s thought processes are very fast. Progressive and impatient, his mind is firmly focused on the future. He abhors wasting time by going back in his thoughts to the past. He wants to move ahead and get things done. He also tries to hurry others along. Already he has his mind on the next thing he wants to do and he is pressing forward to that. He is often irritated at things not happening fast enough to suit his mental speed.

With i-dots very high, the writer may be impulsive, careless and unrestrained. With i-dots very low, there exists a conflict between impulsiveness and pedantry. There may exist a tendency toward chicanery.

indikator.nama: Letters m and n with needle points
indikator.keterangan: See listing 06-8 on page 41.
See listing 07-3 on page 46.

The writer has more mental than physical energy. What he accomplishes is the result of thought. What he does represents considered judgment and thought and he has more mental control.

Physical activity is not as easy or natural for him, especially if it is prolonged or exhausting. He is less inclined to become involved manually. Because he tends to neglect the physical side of his being, he is inclined to have poorer health and less recuperative strength. He becomes discouraged more easily and his endurance is less. A normal day’s work leaves him exhausted and sufficient sleep is mandatory for him.

The writer is trying to avoid friction as much as possible and is more likely to adapt and compromise. He cannot use his elbows, so to speak. Meeting others halfway is part of his strategy of getting along. Even when he feels deeply about something he is willing to negotiate. He adapts in order to avoid tension and prevent disputes.

Emotional experiences stay with the writer only for a short duration of time, unless they are steadily reinforced. Important! The slower the speed of writing the less energy the light pressured writer has.
See listing 06-9 on page 42.

indikator.nama: Right tendency in the upper zone
indikator.keterangan: See listing 07-5 on page 47.
See listing 07-6a on page 47.
See listing 07-6b on page 47.
See listing 07-7 on page 47.

The writer is mentally astute. He thinks extremely fast so that few people can match his mental speed. He always searches for the quickest way of doing things. He is concerned mostly with the aim, not how he reaches it. He detests lengthy theoretical explanations and takes care of routine matters without wasting time. He leaps ahead to application as soon as he gets the basic idea. This keeps his attention free for taking care of other matters. He is impatient until the goal is reached.

The writer has an uncanny aptitude to tune into other people’s moods. This gives him the advantage of sensing what other people will say or do. He is very much aware of what happens around him and he reacts speedily to others and the environment.

The writer’s endurance is predominantly mental. It is unlikely that he will engage in physical contests, even where it is necessary.

He has probably a multitude of interests; however, with his facile mind he is natural for politics.

The writer is creative in a practical way. He has a highly developed sense for structure and proportion and a special ability to translate his feelings into concrete finished form or designs.

He is a quick thinker and emotionally mature. In whatever he does, he performs with a sense of purpose. He functions best in designing and directing growing, active projects.

The writer is as concerned about his spiritual existence as he is about his material life. He wants to know where he fits in on every level.

Flourishes in capitals are of positive value only if they are pleasing to the eye and contribute to the legibility of the writing. They reveal inborn creative talent and possible manual dexterity.

The writer has a specially developed sense of form which he wants to express in his work, in recreations or relationships. He has a flair for effect. With a special feeling for representation, he enjoys dramatizing his behavior and appearance. He makes more stimulating presentations because he tends to show the most exciting side of himself. He speaks with more vibrancy and appears to be more emotional. He may appear less restrained than he is because whatever he feels, the outward expression is bound to be more.

The writer relies on his intelligence, instinct and intuition to guide him. He has ambitious plans which he pursues instinctively without much regard for conventional considerations. He fits well into any position where style is important. Fashion, theatrical design or production, entertainment, or sales, are just a few of these.
See listing 06-2b on page 36.

The writer’s ideas are creative and original. He is drawn to artistic and innovative endeavors.

Important! In a style of writing that is not congruent (for instance with copybook style), enriched i-dots would indicate insecurity and conflict which the writer is trying to hide by engaging in some dramatized behavior. In artistic writing, these forms enhance creativity or originality.
The writer possesses creative imagination. He is a spontaneous, outgoing personality in both thinking and behavior.

The writer has literary leanings and cultural interests. By nature, he has good taste and gives close attention to matters of style and form. He loves the harmony of sounds, the rhythm of poetry, and the proper use of words and phrases. He enjoys hearing and reading the well written. He can exercise his vocabulary power and uses language more eloquently. Words are his chief medium and he is usually a delightful conversationalist.

He has a special affection for books and much respect for the printed word. (He may scorn paperbacks, spend much time at the library, or belong to a book club.)

Important! The effectiveness of this trait would be influenced by the writer’s level of formal education.

The writer has literary leanings but they are not usually directed toward the practical area of his life. Most often, this means that he feels incapable of coping with the world around him and escapes in a socially acceptable way into the spiritual realm. Basically, he lacks self-reliance. He is inclined to believe in “destiny” or depends upon a divine power for direction and support. Symbolically, he reaches for “guidance from above.”
See listing 07-1 on page 46.

indikator.nama: Letters m and n with rounded tops
indikator.keterangan: See listing 06-7 on page 40.
See listing 04-4a on page 22.
See listing 07-6b on page 47.

The writer has the ability to individualize his own expression. His mind functions creatively. This ability goes beyond the mere rearrangement of previous experiences; he has the unique skill to create without precedent. He is independent in his thinking with a capacity for abstract thought. Showing high mental maturity, he reaches conclusions that are not the norm. With an original approach to things, he puts his personal stamp on whatever he does. He adds creative thinking to his work. He looks for ingenious solutions to problems and is willing to experiment with the unknown.

The writer may use this trait in many ways. He may create a new product design, an architectural drawing, or a new marketing strategy. He would probably enjoy a career in some artistic field. For recreation, he may derive pleasure from painting, writing poetry or perhaps, music. With his talent, he could create something for practical use. Interior decorating, designing clothes or jewelry, making up faces or styling hair, could hold appeal.

How many of his original ideas the writer expresses depends on how secure he feels in situations and relationships. Originality is often appreciated only until it comes into conflict with expected norms of behavior. Should he be tied down to a routine job, he should be encouraged to keep busy at something creative in his leisure time.

Important! Depending upon other traits, the creative urge may be expressed in destructive ways.

With enriched writing, the writer has good taste and an urge to present things aesthetically. He fits well into any area where style is important. Fashion, theatrical design and production, decoration, and entertainment are just a few examples.

With enriched writing in the upper zone, the writer has artistic and creative ability. He is a builder or designer with a feeling for structure and arrangement. He functions well in positions where he builds up or puts together because he understands where each part goes to build the whole form.
See listing 06-3d on page 38.

indikator.nama: Middle zone width equals middle zone height
indikator.keterangan:
The writer has a healthy personal attitude about who and what he is. He has a sense of personal assurance and feels comfortable with others and himself. His orientation is toward people and he interacts with them spontaneously and naturally without hesitation.

The writer has no trouble satisfying his emotional needs. He can express them openly. He can give and accept ego strokes. Likewise, he readily responds to others’ wants and needs.

With small middle zone height, the writer is comfortable with himself and others; however, he is most satisfied working by himself, according to his own time schedule. His orientation is toward research, study, and things, rather than people. Instead of public acclaim, he seeks goals that offer him personal gratification and increase his self-esteem.

In his dealings with others, the writer's feelings about himself remain constant. He is steady and reliable and predictable in his reactions. He has at least a degree of assurance.

The writer has a unique attitude toward what he considers his “duty.” He has an extraordinary willingness to serve people or causes that are important to him. They become his center of focus, and he gives of himself freely. He dedicates himself to an extent that he may lose sight of other things around him.

The writer sets high standards for himself and others. It is hard for him to make do or compromise where his principles are concerned. His major disadvantage is that he is often unrealistic in what he expects. He becomes bitter when others fail him and his standards. For example, in a relationship, such individuals may expect a partner to whom they can look up to and who, in turn, will protect them from many of the adversities of life. If the partner fails to fulfill these expectations, the writer may become very disappointed and bitter.

The writer will satisfy his need for relationships in conventional ways. He will move smoothly within accepted limits. He is courteous and kind. He stays with what is traditional and well-approved by everyone who belongs to his own group.

The writer submits to the group’s way of thinking, manner of conduct and habits because he is afraid to set himself apart. He is dependent and predictable. He seeks approval for what he does and for conforming to others’ expectations. He follows the customs of his peer group due to fear of being thought of as unconventional. He takes pride in doing well what has been assigned to him. He is uneasy when he violates standards of accepted behavior and tends to become upset when others disregard established rules. Contradictory behavior in others is hard for him to accept.

The writer can concentrate when he must but prefers to be more spontaneous and less involved with details and precision.
See listing 02-8a on page 10.

indikator.nama: Ovals clear (no exceptions, all ovals must be clear)
indikator.keterangan: The writer is assured enough to be honest with himself and others. He says what he means and makes an effort to be understood accurately. Whether well or awkwardly expressed, he tells what he feels and means what he says. He may be less diplomatic at times and may be called tactless by those suffering from his candor, but what he utters is what he truly thinks and believes. Others will know exactly where they stand with him.

The writer has a healthy personal attitude. He feels assured and is comfortable with himself and others. He is able to interact spontaneously and naturally with superiors and peers. He feels all human beings are worthwhile and valuable, including himself.

The writer appreciates recognition when it is deserved; however, he does not constantly seek approval from others to prove his worth. He does not have to impress other people, appease them, or fight with them. Without being vindictive or hostile, he avails himself of the space he feels he needs.

The writer does not let himself be pushed around. He can speak up firmly to defend himself and what is important to him. He feels free to share suggestions and thoughts in order to make his job more effective.

The writer is imaginative in his daily activities and in his relationships. He is receptive to new ideas, untried working methods and novel experiences. He is progressive and willing to take risks in order to work something out. He can communicate, adjust and adapt with a minimum of stress.

Findings in the personal pronoun “I” have to be supported by other findings in the writing.

The writer feels sure of himself and of his own capabilities. He is confident and has a healthy feeling of self worth.

The writer is self-sufficient and has a low fear threshold. He knows that he can deal with pressures coming from the outside. He is less likely to be intimidated by people he does not know or who are superior to him. He is not afraid to speak his mind and to defend his opinions. He encourages others to express themselves, too.

The writer dismisses minor problems as unimportant; he knows he can handle them as he goes along.

He is not afraid of new ideas and can assimilate more before he reaches the point of self-doubt. Because he feels more adequate in everything, he welcomes responsibility. He works well under pressure and against stiff odds. He often spearheads activities and others look to him for leadership. It takes a very large problem or setback to make him feel threatened or afraid.

With narrow middle zone width, the writer is confident of his own abilities; however, he feels doubtful and timid when dealing with co-workers or peers. When forced to work with others, he suffers continuous tension and, perhaps, anxiety.
See listing 02-9a on page 12.

The writer behaves naturally and unpretentiously. His conduct in public and in his personal life is the same. No conflict exists between his private and social life. Both are given the same emphasis, neither is slighted in favor of the other.
See listing 02-9a on page 13.

The writer has a healthy personality integration. His behavior in his private and public life is the same. He behaves naturally and unpretentiously with everyone. To him, his private and public life are of equal importance, neither is sacrificed for the others.

With negative writing, the writer is still functional, regardless of any personality problems he may have.

Underlines beneath the signature emphasize the characteristics in the name. With most of the qualities negative, the underline intensifies the negatives.

With most of the qualities in the signature positive, the effect of the underline is constructive. The writer is self-reliant. He wants to accomplish tasks by himself with as little outside help as possible. He trusts his own judgment and instinctively depends upon himself and his abilities; he is his own authority. He knowns instinctively how a particular task should be done. Presented with something to do or a choice to make, he is competent to handle it relying on his own ability and experience. He will complete the task without returning time and time again for directions on each little step. He takes on a project and finishes it in his own way. Whenever something needs to be taken care of, he relies on his past experience and his instinctive feelings to tell him what to do and how to do it. (He may go into business himself just so he can make his own choices and have things his way.)

Self-reliance is a natural aid to people in the healing arts and in the armed services; it benefits equipment operators, entertainers, or anyone working in hazardous duty positions.

Important! This needs to be supported by positive traits in the writing.

With extra pressure on the underline, the writer has a tendency to become a one-man organization. He finds it hard to accept authority. He automatically takes over because he feels that he is right and does things the correct way and that others “just don’t know.” It is difficult for him to delegate authority and even if he delegates it, he is just as likely to take it back and do the job himself.

With an ostentatious underline, the writer is overbearing, obtrusive and egocentric and uses the underline as window-dressing to impress. The result is that it affects even his positive characteristics in a negative way. His good attributes cannot offset the contradictory effect of the overworked underline.

With the underline connected to the name and moving toward the left, the writer is trying to shield himself against outside forces that make him afraid or anxious. He is trying to conceal alleged unfavorable aspects of his personality and hides what happens “within his four walls,” so to speak.

With the first name only underlined, the writer wants to demonstrate self-reliance as an individual and stresses independence from his family. Most often, however, he is unable to carry the gesture through in reality.

With last name only underlined, the writer relies upon his family, or what it represents in name, ancestry, and social standing.

The writer understands himself and wants to be understood by others. On all levels, he seeks communication without leaving room for misinterpretation. He is sincere and does not think it necessary to conceal certain facts about himself. He is open and straightforward and will not twist or distort reality.

The writer shows consideration for others in his desire to communicate effectively with them. This carries over into his dealings with other people.

The writer has good self-discipline and the capacity for purposeful work.

indikator.nama: Signature and/or ppl without self-protective strokes
indikator.keterangan: Self-protective strokes would show that the writer does not feel good about himself and that he feels the need to cover himself. He would assume that others are criticizing or belittling him. This would affect communication negatively. Lack of this indicator means absence of this trait.

indikator.nama: Signature and/or ppl without encircling strokes
indikator.keterangan: Encircling strokes are self-protective. The writer is very much afraid and covertly defensive. He is symbolically creating a magical circle around himself. He does not know where an alleged “attacker” might hide and therefore tries to protect himself on all sides. This is often a compensation for the writer’s own hostile feelings and dominating attitude. He senses his own malice and meanness and projects it onto others. Such a writer is extremely dangerous because he is very much afraid. He has a host of negative traits and often turns into an aggressor out of fear. Lack of this indicator means absence of this characteristic.

With an elaborated signature, the writer is egocentric and tries to project exaggerated feelings of confidence. Foremost, he wishes to impress. He may try to build himself up with claims which are not based on reality, or he may use extravagant manners, or boast. In any case, he would be unreliable. Lack of this indicator means absence of this characteristic.

The writer places his goals above the level where he presently is. He is desirous of using and developing his innate abilities. His main emphasis is on the development of his own talents and skills. He is willing to evolve and grow. He does this by thinking carefully about what he wants, now and in the future, choosing the most important goals, ruling out that are too easy for him or too risky. He determines what he truly cares about and then devotes himself to the pursuit of his objectives. He is not bound by preconceived limitations. He has the courage to reach for what he could be and to rise above past levels of success.

The writer is courageous and strongly motivated to achieve success. His aspirations are expansive and he sets high standards in his desire for self-improvement. He is progressive in setting his goals and willing to challenge himself to surpass the level where he presently is. He wants to achieve something that will bring him prestige or prove him to be outstanding in some way. He is willing to take chances and undertake the unfamiliar to achieve his aim.

Because he is not afraid, he is more likely to create his opportunities as soon as he knows what he wants. He is programmed toward accomplishment and stays away from mental considerations that suggest defeat. Above all, he is not afraid to try. If he fails, he usually has learned something from the experience which helps him do better next time. He is not devastated by possible failure or embarrassment; he worries mostly about probabilities, not possibilities.

The writer is oriented toward growth and does not allow himself to be diverted from his real goals by the desire for immediate gratification. His main emphasis is on the development of those skills from which he, himself, gains the greatest satisfaction. His single-mindedness may look like aggressiveness to others. They may feel he is cold, selfish and thoughtless in pursuing his aims. In reality, he is completely focused on reaching his purposes and simply is not aware of others at that time.

The writer’s goals are very high. He is progressive and future-minded. He is often dissatisfied in his thinking with his present level of achievement. His main purpose is to advance, to improve himself and fulfill his potential. He not only sees opportunities for advancement, he creates them. He has greater concepts and thinks in bigger terms than most people. He plans at a level that would be difficult for most people to achieve.

Without supporting traits (determination, willpower, persistence) the writer may have trouble focusing his energies long enough to make his goals come true. His goals may remain little more than idle wishes.

With an exaggerated opinion of himself, the writer wants recognition with little real effort on his part. He refuses to consider others’ point of view. He may bluff and promise more than he is able to achieve. Most of the time, he gets off to a promising beginning but his good start does not always end in a satisfactory finish. When he encounters failure, he blames it on somebody else. When he succeeds, he refuses to give others credit for their contribution. Asking for help would be tantamount to admitting that he is less than what he wants others to believe.

The writer will not admit that anything could be of value if he has not heard of it first. If a new subject is mentioned that he is familiar with, he may approve. If he has not heard of it, he may tear it down.

The writer feels he is above the rules of society. He lives according to standards of his own and behaves in ways that are comfortable for him. He tries to avoid people and situations where his alleged superiority could be questioned.

The writer tries to cover up deep-seated feelings of inferiorities by making himself believe that he knows more and is better than anybody else. Exaggerating his own accomplishments, he refuses to admit that often, he does not measure up to his self-made claims. Secretly, he cannot help being worried about living up to them. He has convinced himself that he is almost invincible and is afraid to discover that in reality he is not. With his tremendous ego problems, he needs all the compliments he can get and if they are not forthcoming, he supplies them himself.

Outwardly overbearing and inwardly insecure, the writer hides his uncertainty with an exaggerated sense of pride. He brags to cover up his real inadequacies. Extremely sensitive to criticism, he will do anything rather than lose face. Comparisons are especially offensive to him. He withdraws from situations where he could be shown in a bad light or his superiority could be questioned. His self-respect is based on what he thinks he can do, not on experience. His accomplishments often lag far behind his promises.

The writer believes he is superior to everyone else and can be insulted by the implication that he may be average. This exaggerated opinion of himself makes him hypersensitive and extremely vulnerable to criticism. He tries to protect himself by withdrawing from situations and relationships where his inflated image could be exposed.

In response to criticism, he tends to react with rage, shame or humiliation. He will either mask these feelings with an aura of cool indifference or he may withdraw entirely from the situation or relationship.

indikator.nama: Initial letter in first name very elaborated
indikator.keterangan:
Exaggerated capitals in the signature signify egocentricity, particularly when the initial of the first name is larger than the capital of the family name.

The writer has overly strong feelings of self-importance and desires to enhance his image as much as possible. He may attempt to build himself up with claims which are not based on reality. To him his personal life is so important that it overrules all social rules and considerations. He feels everyone should be interested in him and he may expose the most intimate details about his private life in public situations.

indikator.nama: Initial letters in signature broader than capitals in text
indikator.keterangan:
The writer assumes a role in his personal life which is not a genuine expression of himself. He overcompensates for the lack of true self-reliance. His assurance depends upon being given personal recognition and acclaim. He feels best working in the public eye where he can be individually noticed and recognized.

With initials extra broad at the baseline, the writer is an overbearing, egotistical individual. (This is especially true in a capital “L.”) With the lower loop “dancing” above the baseline, the writer is conceited and elevates himself above others. He misleads others about his competence and once he has successfully duped those around him, starts to believe these fabrications himself. Old graphologists spoke of “dancing letters” or “letters standing on their toes to be seen.” They claimed that they epitomize presumptuousness and impertinence.

With small letter height in the middle zone, the writer is arrogant only toward subordinates. Toward superiors, he is servile and obsequious. He tries to remain inconspicuous and demonstrates feigned modesty. He maneuvers covertly to achieve his egotistical aims. He lacks positiveness and resistance.

With narrow letters in the text, the writer is trying to hide his insecurity behind a facade of exaggerated assurance. Since this confidence does not come naturally, it often manifests itself as pomposity or arrogance.

indikator.nama: Initials in signature higher than capitals in text
indikator.keterangan:
The writer seeks and enjoys the importance and recognition of public life. He is conscious of rank, title and position. He appreciates social formalities. He wants to overshadow other people and impress the public with his significance.

The writer's confirmation of identity comes from the approval of others who see and recognize his performance and comment favorably about him. Likewise, he can lose self-possession quickly with direct criticism or put-downs.

With very high initials, the writer has a need for exaltation. More than anything, he wants to be considered exceptional. (Often, this is coupled with the inability to realize even modest goals. The result is an inharmonious personality suffering from cycles of emotional exaltation and depression.)

With extremely high capitals, the writer is afraid to see himself realistically. As a result, in his mind, he has constructed an unrealistic and glorified picture of himself. He is very afraid to see his limitations and shortcomings. By creating in his imagination a picture of himself that is superior to everyone, he can ignore the reality of what he is. This picture has become more real to him than his actual self, which he has pushed away because he cannot face his limitations. It enables him to feel unique, superior and confident.

The creation of his idealized image has far-reaching consequences in every aspect of his life. The writer must continually perform mental gymnastics to keep convincing himself that he is, indeed, an admirable individual. He must continually distort reality, rationalize, or make excuses when events demonstrate that he is not, in fact, a superior human being.

The writer does not do things in his own real interest; above all, he must maintain the glorified picture of himself. His goals are not for his own enjoyment and growth, but rather what enhances or diminishes his image.

The writer’s self-image leads to distortions in his attitude not only toward himself but toward the world. He is unable to establish good relationships. He isolates himself in order to avoid all danger of exposing the real picture of himself.

With very narrow capitals, the writer displays a modest facade. While he longs fervently for recognition, he will not push himself forward to gain rightful respect. His demeanor tends to be humble and often shy.

On the inside, the writer nurtures an inflated self-image which is ultra-sensitive and easily bruised. He has an “elephant’s memory” and it is hard for him to forgive. He relishes other people getting “what is coming to them.”
See listing 02-8b on page 11.

The writer needs an exorbitant amount of self-praise to fulfill his ego needs. He wants power to compensate for feelings of inadequacy. He dislikes having to do things that are “unworthy” of him.

The writer lacks mental control. It is hard for him to communicate logically or to concentrate for any length of time. He is unable to judge matters realistically and is often confused about facts. His biggest problem is his lack of information. He feels he has nothing to learn because he already knows it all. He refuses advice, even if others make repeated efforts to make him listen. He looks at most people as incompetents and assumes that he can do anything better than they can. He feels free to step in and start arranging their lives and their projects. If he fails, he either blames other people or tries to convince himself and others of the illusion of success.

The writer presumes too much. He thinks himself superior to others and feels he can get away with things other people would get penalized for. He feels alone most of the time because his superior attitude shuts others out.

The writer has an exaggerated pride about himself, his plans and his accomplishments. He wants to attract notice, be admired and draw attention to himself. He is self-centered and egotistical.

The writer builds up anxieties of how he is being received by others and how their reactions will affect him. If others demonstrate that they have noticed him and approve of him, he feels assured. If he is criticized, especially in front of others, he is devastated. He is afraid of being laughed at or of making a mistake. Comparisons are especially offensive to him. He always wants to be given higher recognition than others are. He wants to be above others in preferment or his pride is hurt.

To keep his self esteem intact, he puts up a facade. He will go to great pains to avoid losing face and hates to enter into a new situation unless he is certain of coming out well.

The writer has two behaviors: a gracious, personable one for company, especially if there are new people to impress. He saves his worst conduct for the family. He constantly tries to “keep up with the Jones’s” because outward appearances mean so much to him.

The writer is willing to be considerate of others as long as it does not draw attention away from him. He will use such good behavior to earn momentary applause but he begrudges others their turn in the spotlight.

The writer is self-centered and egotistical. He wants to attract notice, either constructively or destructively. He wants to be admired and draw attention to himself. He goes through life with a superiority complex to cover up deep seated feelings of inferiority. He feels he should be first and unquestionably accepted as the best. He exaggerates his own accomplishments and refuses to admit that often, he does not measure up to his self-imposed demands.

The writer feels that he has to be right at all times, under all conditions and he is unable to back down, admit an error, or give another person credit for something. His exaggerated sense of pride interferes with asking for help, admitting failure, and dictates the kind of work he is willing to do. He is good at bluff and at promising more than he is able to produce.

The writer seeks and enjoys the importance and recognition of public life. He is conscious of rank, title and position. He appreciates social formalities. He wants to overshadow other people and impress the public with his significance
The writer constantly seeks public acclaim. He hides his insecurity behind a facade of exaggerated assurance. Since this does not come naturally, it often surfaces as arrogance and impudence.

indikator.nama: Signature larger than writing in text
indikator.keterangan: The writer is assuming a role in social life that is not a true representation of himself. He wants to appear more confident, more assured, and more important than he is.
See listing 01-9 on page 6.
See listing 02-10b on page 10.

indikator.nama: Signature shows heavier pressure than writing in text
indikator.keterangan: The writer is trying to prove himself more forceful, energetic and dynamic than he actually is. This is often the case when the person is in a position that clashes with his basic personality.

indikator.nama: Signature with first name emphasized (height, width, pressure)
indikator.keterangan: The writer is egotistical and believes himself to be more important than other members of his family. This affects compatibility negatively, especially between spouses. The writer finds it difficult to take a subservient position, although he may be dependent upon the family or mate in many other respects. He may be excessively sensitive to criticism and harbor feelings of hostility. To the writer, the importance of his personal life is so great that it extinguishes many social considerations. He eagerly displays aspects of his private life in public situations.
See listing 05-4 on page 29.

(Segmentations, distorted or missing letters, or missing letter parts, or transposed letters, would disclose anxiety with resulting disorganization and impaired thinking ability. Lack of this indicator verifies absence of such problems.)

The writer is well integrated and feels comfortable with himself and others. Few personality conflicts interfere with productivity. He handles his life effectively and without feeling frustrated by desires that oppose each other.
He expends his energies productively in an organized, efficient manner. He is convinced of the value of his projects and applies himself wholeheartedly to his tasks.

The writer is consistent in the response he shows in interpersonal relationships. He is predictable in his emotional reaction to the people close to him. He is likely to desire the same degree of openness every time. He is steady in his acceptance of other people’s ideas, working methods and behavior.

The writer is consistent in how far he is willing to cooperate and interrelate. He follows a steady pattern in allowing others to get to know him. He is predictable in how much personal space he demands. He follows a uniform pattern of thinking and is consistent in his ability to discriminate and evaluate.

indikator.nama: Middle zone width equals middle zone height
indikator.keterangan: See listing 11-1a on page 67.
See listing 11-4 on page 68.
See listing 07-3 on page 46.

The writer shows a harmonious balance in his involvements and activities. He displays normal interest in both the material and intellectual world.
He functions more easily in life because he is more relaxed. He is able to place experiences into proper perspective. He rarely harbors emotionally based grudges, unless they are steadily reinforced. Consequently, he suffers less lasting damage from traumatic episodes.
See listing 06-9 on page 42.
See listing 07-4 on page 46.
See listing 11-6 on page 69.

indikator.nama: Signature shows equal emphasis on first and last name
indikator.keterangan: The writer is well integrated. There exists harmony between his feelings of self-worth as an individual and the family’s importance and status. He feels as responsible toward his family as he expects other family members to act toward him.
See listing 11-8 on page 70.

indikator.nama: Signature and ppl without self-protective strokes
indikator.keterangan: See listing 11-9a on page 70.

indikator.nama: Signature and ppl without encircling strokes
indikator.keterangan: The writer functions without self-protective defenses. He deals openly and sincerely with others. He neither resorts to subterfuge nor open hostility.

indikator.nama: Upper zone height/lower zone length balanced
indikator.keterangan: The writer starts from a satisfactory balance between mental and physical energies. He is able to plan his life and his projects and carry them out in action. He has good organizational ability and functions in an orderly manner. He probably budgets his time so that he gets done as much as possible. He knows exactly how much time should be allotted to each task. He derives satisfaction from methodical accomplishment and has little patience with schedules that are wasteful or procedures that lack efficiency.
See listing 08-1a on page 52.
The writer is consistent and emotionally predictable. He displays the same kind of emotional response on two different occasions or under similar circumstances.
The writer is consistent in the display of his emotional reactions. He will show the same degree of response under similar circumstances.

The writer is mentally well-organized. He is able to plan ahead and he has the capacity for working efficiently. He is consistent in his relationships to the world at large and in his attitudes with regard to it. He will be consistent in maintaining a certain degree of contact or distance. He has the inner discipline to maintain boundaries that have been established.
See listing 13-3b on page 83.

indikator.nama: Ductus without corrugations and without excess pastosity
indikator.keterangan:
A corrugated ductus would mean that the writer is exhausted as the result of overindulgence. A breakdown would be imminent.
