His exaggerations are artificial and unnatural; however, he is unaware, most of the time, of how far he is going. The reaction of other people to him is usually disapproving. But the more he feels the negative response, the more he will push for effect. It is a vicious cycle and it may cost him friends and confidence.

The writer may pay extraordinary attention to his appearance. He is preoccupied with his clothes and accessories. Affectation is mirrored in his appearance as well as in his mannerisms.
See listing 02-10b on page 12.

The writer is dramatizing his expressions and behavior. Whatever he feels inside, the outer expression is more spectacular. When he is sad he is VERY, VERY SAD. When he is happy he is VERY, VERY HAPPY. He is not glad to see someone, he is OVERJOYED. He is not sorry about something he COULD JUST DIE.

He tends to exaggerate. It is natural for him. His aim is to enliven discussions and relationships. But he goes too far and makes a discussion appear overdone. Others tend to think of him as phony or insincere.

The writer over-dramatizes his feelings and how he thinks other people feel. He is puzzled by their negative reaction to him since his own view is colored by his exaggerated attitude.

The writer is intense in getting his ideas across and wants to dramatize what he says. Whatever he utters is extremely important to him. Since he distrusts other people’s ability to comprehend the alleged significance of his message, he over-emphasizes it. The result, however, is negative. Other people have trouble discerning what is really important since he puts the same exaggerated emphasis on too many things.

The writer lacks objectivity and perspective in situations and interpersonal relationships. He reacts impulsively to people and intrudes upon others' space without considering the consequences of his acts.

When a long lower extension overlaps an upper, the writer is involved in too many relationships or interests, or in one or two areas that are complex.

When entanglement results from long upper loops, it indicates superficial interest in intellectual pursuits. There may be escape into a fantasy world, day dreaming, etc. The writer tends to confuse facts and chaotic thinking is one of the results.

Such writers are egotistical, adhere to their own standards and feel a general lack of obligation toward other people and the world in general.

With narrow letter spacing, communication is always diminished. One of the underlying causes may be the writer's unconscious desire to thwart communication. He may not want to open himself to others because of the insecurity that doing so arouses. Another reason may be plain disregard for the others (including the reader). The writer simply does not care whether or not he is understood.

indikator.nama: Lower zone loops entangle with following line
indikator.keterangan:
The writer possesses a lot of nervous energy to the point of hyperactivity. He gets involved in too many activities at the same time. Lack of efficiency and confusion are the results.

The writer is quickly physically aroused and tends to be sexually uninhibited.

The writer is often tactless and inconsiderate in social encounters. He will frequently invade the space and rights of others. (This is especially true for writers with aggressive tendencies.)

The writer becomes involved, sometimes over-involved, in everything he does. He lives entirely in the present without planning ahead. He is prone to hasty commitments and rash acts. He will impulsively undertake projects, regardless of whether he has the time or resources. He gets emotionally carried away in relationships and is inconsiderate toward people with a greater need for privacy.

The writer is not in charge of his own expression. Within him, the emotional side is too dominant. He permits himself to wallow in his feelings. He is irritating to others and a liability to himself. He pours out his feelings, positive and negative, indiscriminately and without conscious control.

Basically, the writer is anxious much of the time. He feels inwardly inadequate with the result that he has an exaggerated need to “fit in.” He over-responds or reacts inappropriately. He deals in quantity rather than quality when getting involved in relationships. He may be obtrusive to fulfill his emotional needs. He feels coerced by people he views as superior to him and feels the pressure of those in authority all of the time. He believes that they are trying to drive him continually, whether this is accurate or not.

The writer lacks control to such a degree that his emotions carry him away. He wallows in his feelings and is unpredictable and moody. He easily loses his grip on himself. He is unable to regulate and restrain his feelings toward others. He tends to exaggerate and thus makes an unrealistic assessment of situations and people. His view of others and of circumstances is subjective. He sees things from his own particular perspective and as a result, distorts reality.

The writer has more than average amounts of defensiveness. Basically, he feels inadequate and suffers anxiety all of the time. He tries to lessen the strain through excessive agreeableness, superficial friendliness, self-deception, alibis, submissiveness, or projecting blame on other people.
See listing 03-8a on page 18.

The writer's automatic responses are on the emotional level. He finds it impossible to check his impulsive reactions and it is easy for others to tell what he is feeling just by looking at him. Once he becomes involved, either in love or hate, he gets carried away. He is very much subject to the influence from others. He indulges in self-pity for slights, real or imagined, especially when he reaches out affectionately and is rejected or rebuffed. His overly emotional behavior may easily become an irritant to others who are less emotional. They may treat him like a child and dismiss his displays of feelings as a sign of immaturity. Professionally and personally, this makes for real problems in communication.

He responds with his feelings, not with his mind. Instead of acting on considered thought, he pours out emotions without considering the effect. Emotion is the driving force in most situations and relationships. Since he acts on impulse alone, he often finds himself committed to something he does not want to do or he gets involved in situations he regrets. He is emotionally unpredictable and goes from high to low moods within short periods of time. Emotionally speaking, he is either “all joy” or “all pain.” He cries easily or shows sentiment. And he is just as likely to become part of other people’s negative moods as he will share their positive frame of mind. He judges according to the present mood rather than facts and he tends to have a strongly biased point of view. He sometimes manipulates others by instilling guilt.

The writer is unwilling to forego gratification in the moment for future gains; therefore, he needs immediate or short-term goals. He seeks self-satisfaction at the moment and often cares about no one but himself.

The writer has a warm and sentimental nature and he is spontaneous in how he responds to life. He expresses his feelings, and responds with the heart, not with the head. He will laugh more easily, cry more easily, show anger more vividly, and show devastation or despair more completely; however, where a considered response is required, he is at a disadvantage. It is useless to reason with the writer while he deals with a subject emotionally. Only after his emotional focus is on something else, will he be open to listen to objections or reservations.

This individual gives automatic expression to his first emotional response and his reactions are as impulsive as his deeds. He expresses the same degree of feeling for everything regardless of its real importance to him. He indulges in self-pity for slights, real or imagined, and is extremely vulnerable on the feeling level to the first hint of rejection. It can come from being cold-shouldered, being looked at without interest, not being listened to, a million slights, most of them not even intended. Whenever someone denies or tries to repress his feelings, he turns into an instant enemy.
See listing 27-7b on page 151.

The writer lacks a sense of reality and reacts emotionally in an uncontrolled manner. Basically, he is insecure. To compensate, he applies an excessive amount of mental energy toward his aspirations without actual follow-through.
See listing 28-10 on page 158.

The writer is over-controlled, rigid and tense. He makes an exaggerated effort to maintain his inner equilibrium and deadens his own spontaneity. He attempts to keep order or pretends that order is being kept whereas, in reality, he cannot accomplish this by himself. He needs and searches for support but is hesitant to admit that he needs such assistance. He wants to create a good impression but lacks the inner strength to behave as impeccably as he wants to.

The writer is a follower rather than a leader. He is very uptight about regulating his life according to established rules and about things being done exactly as required. He will try to force his routine on other people too, thereby indicating a degree of selfishness. The writer is unlikely to succeed with projects that occasionally require him to alter routines. He needs somebody else to lay out his work in detail for him, step by step. If an item is left out, the job will either stop at this point or will be done wrong. Any deviation from the norm is devastating to him. On the positive side, he will do routine jobs just as he was taught to do them.

(The diagnosis is especially negative when extremely straight alignment is combined with disconnected lower extensions, short lower zone length or distorted lower zone loops.)
See listing 01-1 on page 3.

indikator.nama: Upper zone loops width angular apexes.
indikator.keterangan: The writer suffers from an undefined inner feeling of dread that he is unable to explain satisfactorily. He cannot understand his apprehension nor can he control his response to it. The apprehension is chronic and illogical, although the writer may be logical otherwise. Because of inner tension, he has trouble making decisions and enthusiasm and optimism are both low.

indikator.nama: Cover strokes in the lower zone
indikator.keterangan: The writer is setting standards beyond reach and reason. He strains compulsively to reach impossible demands. Since he measures his own worth entirely in terms of how he lives up to these self-imposed requirements, he experiences constant tension, insecurity, guilt, and feelings of self-blame. He strives for exactness and error-free performance in order to avoid criticism and is aware of his alleged shortcomings too much of the time. This affects his sex-life negatively and slows down his work.
The writer is tense about present circumstances. He is annoyed with his handling of the situation, specifically, as it pertains to interpersonal relationships.
See listing 01-10c on page 6.

indikator.nama: Diacriticals pressure heavier than rest of writing
indikator.keterangan: See listing 26-4 on page 143.

indikator.nama: Final strokes from middle zone end in lower zone
indikator.keterangan: See listing 01-4 on page 4.

indikator.nama: Initial strokes inflexible from baseline or below
indikator.keterangan:
The writer has a resentful, distrustful attitude. He is under strain because of past negative experiences and biased because of subjective memories. He easily feels taken advantage of by others. Whether such an imposition is real or imagined, he is in a state of preparedness against it. He habitually opposes others and frequently resists by passive means.

The writer has an unreasonable need to justify his beliefs. For every statement by others he immediately knows a contradictory reply. This can go as far as constant bickering or backbiting.

The writer feels under pressure from people in authority. He specifically looks for ways to oppose or criticize them. He has an unreasonable need to resist and have his own way. What he conceives as pressure he rejects. The moment he feels coerced, his guard goes up and he fights back without taking the time to negotiate. He is particularly rebellious when he feels insecure, and he becomes angry when others ignore his antagonism. The need to oppose has become his habitual response. Ironically, he often defies others in ways which are harmful to himself.

The writer suffers tension in interpersonal relationships. He is aware of his limitations and unduly concerned about them. He tries to limit social contacts because he is so self-conscious and timid. It takes a long time before he is at ease in a group, even if the people know him. In public appearances he feels tense and ill at ease. He analyzes every situation in relation to his emotional security. He is prone to inappropriate behavior under stress. His lack of courage holds him back from many possible advances.

The writer feels so vulnerable that he keeps his feelings strictly hidden. He makes himself emotionally inaccessible, even to people close to him. He withdraws on the feeling level and tries to repress emotional displays in others, too. He is tense, over-controlled, and rigid, all due to fear and insecurity.
See listing 08-5b on page 53.

The writer is in a state of abnormal tension. He continually feels agitated. Being in a strained state has become normal for him. Tension for him is caused by something unresolved in either body or mind. He pulls himself along by conscious effort and is driven to accomplish through fear instead of creative energy. He is suffering the negative effects of the strain he is putting on himself and has to exert himself beyond any useful limit just to “hold on.”

The writer lacks control over himself and is in a chronic state of irritability. Being detained or impeded increases the tension even more. He cannot do what must be done easily enough to work productively and effectively. He is trying too hard and exerting too much effort. He puts continuing pressure on himself, regardless of the body's need for nutrition and rest. The writer spends an unreasonable amount of energy fighting what is allegedly wrong. Instead of working for his own progress, he is likely to fight the people who seem to be blocking him. Reasoning with him is useless while he is in such a strained state. He cannot be influenced by anyone or anything.

indikator.nama: Pressure displaced into lower zone upstrokes
indikator.keterangan: See listing 21-8b on page 123.
See listing 27-7a on page 155.

indikator.nama: Score for Self-control (#15) is 6.0 or higher
indikator.keterangan: The writer is an over-controlled, tense personality. He controls himself so rigorously that most of his true self is concealed and he appears detached and unmovable to others. Almost every action is well planned and very conscious. Under prolonged stress, the over-control can break, causing unpredictable, often inappropriate, responses.

indikator.nama: Score for Self-confidence (#11) is 4.0 or less and score for Self-esteem (#12) is 6.0 or higher
indikator.keterangan: The writer is tense, feeling unable to live up to what he has led others to believe about himself. He is uncomfortable, sometimes to the point of being anxious in interpersonal relationships. He cannot relax. He may use a defense system that allows him to escape from interpersonal relationships while at the same time keeping his need for esteem from others intact.
See listing 01-9 on page 6.

indikator.nama: Directional pressure from right in the middle zone
indikator.keterangan:
Directional pressure is not a softly curved form. It is a caved-in letter due to invisible pressure from either left, right, above, or below.

The writer is experiencing pressure from the general problems of everyday life and he is fearful of the future. He is coping to some degree but has given up hope that circumstances will change. He resorts to the defenses of procrastination or withdrawal to avoid emotional strain. He avoids commitments by dodging direct promises. He may withdraw from obligations, or tries to postpone, hoping for a chance to get out of them. He may try to profit from other people's credulity. He may try to outsmart others, particularly his friends and family.

indikator.nama: Directional pressure in the lower zone
indikator.keterangan:
From right: The writer is suffering trauma related to the future. He is experiencing fear of the father, or father figures, or fellow men in general. He may use withdrawal or procrastination as defense maneuvers in the areas of sex and productivity.

From left: The writer has suffered trauma in the past that is still exerting a controlling influence. Unresolved fears from the past are influencing his behavior in the areas of sex and productivity. (There may have been maternal pressure).

The writer feels helpless and dependent. He is weighed down and dispirited due to emotional experiences which have an unusually strong impact on him. Yet he is unable to brace himself against emotional episodes or avoid being affected by them. As a result, he is often exhausted, melancholic, dejected, or depressed.
See listing 03-3 on page 16.

The writer is deeply impressionable. He lacks the ability to resist emotional stimuli coming to him from the outside. He tends to take everything tragically and is unable to free himself from depressive thoughts. Much of the time, he finds himself overwhelmed by feelings he is unable to assimilate. The overload tends to drain him emotionally and makes him feel negative.

indikator.nama: Initial strokes leftward through upper zone loop of capital
indikator.keterangan: The writer is basically fearful and afraid to get involved in unfamiliar activities. His initiative is aborted in its earliest stages. While trying to set something in motion, he suddenly becomes “afraid of his own courage,” so to speak.

indikator.nama: Left tendency in the middle zone
indikator.keterangan: The writer is fearful. He tends to retreat into the past for feelings of security. He is overly cautious and apprehensive in the face of unfamiliar situations. Instead of allowing himself to become involved in risk-taking activities, he will adhere to conforming, traditional and well-established behavior for feelings of safety and stability.

indikator.nama: Left tendency in the lower zone
indikator.keterangan: The writer is fearful in areas related to sex and productivity. He procrastinates and needs much encouragement and help. He tries to withdraw from situations that make him feel apprehensive and insecure and limits himself unnecessarily. He usually performs below the level of his true capabilities. He may use alibis and excuses to explain his avoidance.

The writer is less vigorous in his automatic physical expression. He has restricted energy for physical work and sex. Limited stamina affects his concentration and the degree of perseverance he can muster for the completion of his chores. It has a negative effect on optimism and enthusiasm, hope and motivation. He may need encouragement with projects involving physical work if they are very complex or long lasting. He may work hard, far beyond the capacity of others, but only for a short period of time. He may, for instance, exhaust all his energy resources in order to get a job completed.

Inadequate strength may result in lack of interest in sex or in infrequent sexual activity.

The writer lacks interest in the material-physical side of life. He fatigues easily and endurance is short-lived. He has little energy in reserve. He will engage only in short periods of physical activity. With motivation, he may work somewhat beyond the level of his physical strength, but after an all-out effort, he is exhausted and fatigued. There is little interest in sex or only infrequent indulgence.

The writer lacks determination for long range projects. In fact, where physical work or activity in an unprotected area is required, he is at a real disadvantage. Limited energy affects optimism and enthusiasm and makes him negative. In order to be completed, jobs must be short in duration, easy, or without discouraging elements. He may need encouragement to finish physical work.

indikator.nama: Lower zone loops toward the left
indikator.keterangan: The writer's instinctual sphere is tied to earlier developmental phases. There is mother orientation or infantilism. He is dependent and needs encouragement to perform adequately in the areas of productivity and sex. He is fearful of independent activities. In order to feel more competent, he withdraws from people he considers superior to him. He prefers associates who appear less capable or important than he, himself, seems to be. (He may be unable to function sexually with his wife but may perform satisfactorily with a prostitute.)

With middle zone width narrower than middle zone height, the writer has a poor self-concept. He is self-critical, inhibited, fearful and humble. He feels undeserving of very much in life and is fearful of taking up too much space.

The writer's ego will be reinforced through his work and talent-related achievements rather than through interpersonal relationships. He will strive hard not only to obtain recognition but to deserve it. He is vulnerable to criticism that is directed toward him personally or toward his performance. Much anxiety results from the strain of trying to earn others' approval by meeting or surpassing their standards. His rewards are enjoyed most when they come from others in his own field and are related to his work.

Interestingly, such writers are more open to learning or acquiring new skills. They understand how much they have yet to know, they realize how much they can improve about themselves. They accumulate knowledge because it increases their sense of adequacy in the face of pressures from the outside. What they learn to do well becomes their security. Often, they turn to education because of the security and respect they think it will give them automatically.

The writer's power of concentration is usually well developed and can make him appear like an “absent-minded professor.” He is focusing so exclusively on something that all other thoughts are temporarily gone from his mind. His strong concentration may be used defensively to withdraw into mental work from uncomfortable interpersonal relationships.

With middle zone height proportionate to width, the writer has assurance; however, his interests are geared toward projects not directly involved with people. He works best by himself according to his own time plan. He prefers jobs that require time and attention and once he gets involved in a task, he really becomes immersed, to the exclusion of everything else.

With initial letters on words and sentences emphasized, the writer is intellectually vain. He will make a calculated display of modesty and humbleness. Yet, he clearly possesses a strong sense of rivalry.

The writer is anxious most of the time. The discomfort stems from feelings of inadequacy when he compares himself to those above him in position or ability. While he experiences little pressure from his peers, he feels literally crushed by pressure from superiors or people in authority.

The writer is self-conscious in the face of pressures reaching him from the outside. He appears blocked by them, or inadequate to cope. In any public situation, he seems strained and ill at ease. He feels inept and does not know what to do. He is instinctively wary and feels best when he is reassured and supported in what he has to do. He is overly cautious and inclined toward unjustified anxiety. Because of the discomfort he experiences, he will try to withdraw from threatening situations, or he may retire “into himself.” When none of these alternatives are open to him, he conforms to whatever others in his group are doing to avoid criticism or drawing attention to himself.

The writer tries hard not to rock the boat. He refuses to take a stand on anything that is bound to offend or cause strife. In every area of his life, he dwells on his inadequacies. His self-abasement makes him undersell himself. He is afraid to start things on his own. He is painfully aware of past failures and mistakes. He tends to base future plans on what has worked for him before. Lack of courage holds him back from growing personally or vocationally. Other people are inclined to overlook his talents and just take over authority. He finds himself passed over in many situations because he cannot assert himself.

The writer feels insignificant. Most of the time, he presumes his own inadequacy too much. He finds it difficult to accept his good qualities or aptitudes. In comparing himself with others he sells himself short. He berates his deficiencies and belittles his own self-worth. Because he feels unworthy, he expects to be ignored by others, or put down. He often feels censured when no criticism is intended. As a result, he feels resentful. Communication breakdowns may ensue.

The writer has a low fear threshold. It is difficult for him to cope with everyday problems. He is quick to retire from conflicts. His behavior is self-defeating because it prevents him from getting ahead. He is inhibited and stays with what is familiar because change of any kind is threatening to him.

He is able to perform adequately as long as he is doing what he knows well. Therefore, he works best in support of stronger personalities. A new situation, especially one that involves meeting the public, frightens him off. He assumes that because he feels uncomfortable under emotional stress, he is unable to deal with it. He is wary of consequences and proceeds with caution and humility.

In a state of tension, the writer's mind cannot operate as fully as it can in times of relaxation. His sense of inadequacy limits his ability to comprehend a given situation. This is due to tension arising from feelings of inferiority. He seems more eager to hear what others are saying rather than voice opinions himself. He depends on the counsel of others instead of relying on his own judgment and resourcefulness. He holds back because he always feels that there is someone better qualified than he considers himself to be.

With the personal pronoun “I” height restricted to the middle zone, the writer feels pity for himself. He feels helpless in his situation and tries to over-compensate as an ego-saving defense measure. He may overdo something that either benefits society or that is directed against the establishment.

The writer thinks little of himself. He has grown up feeling inadequate, self-critical and unsure of what he is capable of doing. As a result, he feels unworthy and expects to be regarded as less important than other people. He is filled with self-doubt and has a harder time coping with the problems of life. His fearful behavior is self-defeating. It affects his ability to handle daily life situations and relationships effectively. Since he does not feel good about himself, he either tries to beat others in retaliation, or he acts indifferent toward them. He may be stubborn, intolerant, or narrow-minded. He uses these defenses to maintain at least a degree of self-respect.

A curved personal pronoun “I” signifies mother or female influence on the personality. It is normal in female writings. Such individuals are impressionable and more sensitive, even on the physical level. In male writing, it implies strong mother influence, resulting in a confusion of cultural roles. Such writers give up easily to intellectual and/or physical pressure.

The writer feels helpless and has a strong need for protection. His life is characterized by trying to avoid discomfort and stress. It is almost impossible for him to do anything that causes conflicts. He finds it hard to discipline himself. Likewise, he cannot discipline others because it requires too much energy. If asked to do something, the writer will neither argue about it nor exert himself in the moment. He will agree when face to face with the person demanding the task, but may not follow through. He finds it difficult to take a stand or say “yes” or “no” unequivocally.

Important! Any weakness in the form of the personal pronoun “I” corresponds to a deficiency in the writer's self-esteem.

The writer has an inadequate self-image. He is self-effacing and unable to appreciate his own aptitudes. He under-values his worth to himself and to others. He is inhibited and tense in interpersonal relationships. He is more comfortable working by himself or in the background in support of stronger individuals.

If width in the signature is proportionate to height, the writer is assured when dealing with his peers or in situations where he has had previous success experiences.

The writer has an inadequate self-image. He is self-effacing and unable to appreciate his own aptitudes. He under-values his worth to himself and to others. He is inhibited and tense in interpersonal relationships. He is more comfortable working by himself or in the background in support of stronger individuals.

If width in the signature is proportionate to height, the writer is assured when dealing with his peers or in situations where he has had previous success experiences.
See listing 15-4b on page 93.
See listing 30-8b on page 172.

With copybook arcades retained, the writer conforms to conventional standards in his day-to-day activities and in his associations with people.

With arcades more frequent than copybook style, the writer lacks spontaneity. He adapts himself to the outside world but rarely discloses his inner self. His adaptability is not a natural expression, it is a sham attitude which he forces upon himself. He stresses form and deportment, socially as well as in his personal life.

By nature, the writer is reserved and secretive and shuns emotional contact with the outside world. Reticent about himself and his private thoughts he responds to personal questions with great reserve and reticence.

The writer is hesitant to display feelings, either of sorrow or joy. He is unreceptive to friendly overtures from others and often intolerant. When he seeks contact, it is often for egotistical reasons. He can be cautious, calculating and wary of possible consequences in situations and relationships.

The writer lacks assurance in interpersonal relationships. He is timid, self-conscious and insecure. He is aware of his alleged limitations and worries about them all the time. As a result he limits his field of social activities and withdraws from unfamiliar people and new relationships. Because of his fear of appearing foolish, he resists sharing his feelings and thoughts. His excessive sensitiveness inhibits intimate communication, further depriving him of the warmth and acceptance he craves but will not give or accept.

The writer is easily fearful of the demands of daily life and apprehensive about contact with people.

The writer often displays more than average defensiveness. He is extremely cautious, evasive and suspicious. He may try to conceal certain things, either through evasiveness or secretiveness. He contemplates possible involvements from the aspect of whether his security will be improved or threatened.

The writer may have a tendency toward ultra-conservative conduct due to fear. He either withdraws from “unsafe” situations or he will behave inappropriately under stress.
See listing 26-1a on page 148.
See listing 26-1b on page 148.
See listing 26-1c on page 148.
See listing 26-1d on page 148.
See listing 12-2a on page 76.
See listing 12-2b on page 76.
See listing 12-1a on page 76.
See listing 12-1b on page 76.

The writer is fearful and isolates himself to avoid the discomfort in interpersonal relationships. He shuns involvement due to self-protectiveness.

Details, planning and logic may interest him. He may be interested with anything requiring the use of logic, organization, structure, or analysis. Ordinary social interaction, on the other hand, is disquieting to him. He feels out of his element and often, uncomfortable and tense.

The writer makes a better observer than a participant. He is also more inclined toward introspection than is the majority of people.

The writer is out of touch with reality and the world around him. Due to insecurity, he separates himself from his environment.

Because of his discomfort in interpersonal relationships, the writer may escape into idealism or isolation from interpersonal and social activities. Such escape may be oriented toward mental orientation (it could be paranoia).

Basically, the writer separates himself from the world around him. He works well alone or with very few others. The writer may be yearning for some degree of clarity because he, himself, is disorganized. In this case, extremely broad spacing is a kind of over-compensation.

The writer lives primarily for the present. He prefers activities that are short-term and take place in the present rather than planning ahead. This includes such things as making social arrangements, dates, etc.

The writer moves within self-imposed limits. He restricts himself due to feelings of inadequacy. He is aware of what he can do and does not extend himself beyond his capacities. He is cautious in his undertakings and in how far he commits himself, sometimes overly cautious. He paces himself, always conscious of the limitations he has imposed upon himself.

In dealing with people, he is unspontaneous. He needs much space around himself and restricts the extent to which he allows himself to become involved. He dislikes people who stand too close or who try to touch and hold. He can be with a group and yet not hear or see much of what is going on, for he has a highly developed mechanism for staying inwardly aloof.

The writer is apprehensive about unfamiliar things and people he does not know. He is introverted and fearful.

He may be distrustful of others because of his own lack of assurance and shyness.

The writer carefully restricts the extent to which he becomes involved and will not enter into anything that could be unsafe. He avoids getting mixed up in anything that might cause him to extend himself too far beyond what he knows he can handle.

The need to control himself is a major concern in his life.

The writer often lacks the firmness and fortitude to finish projects he has begun.

The writer is afraid of the future because of the uncertainties it represents. He feels that he is incapable of dealing with life and its everyday exigencies. In interpersonal relationships, he is fearful and inhibited. He is distrustful of people he does not know.

He has a closed mind and rejects progressive concepts outright. He automatically fears anything with which he has little or no familiarity and severely limits his participation in new projects and relationships.

The need to control himself and his involvements is of paramount importance in his life. He cannot be expected to bring projects in which he is involved to a satisfying finish.

The writer is insecure, and dependent. He is also indecisive and inhibited. For that reason, he limits himself to things and people he knows. He seeks security through maintaining the status quo, the familiar, the traditional.

He withdraws from projects and relationships that increase his tension and make him uncomfortable.

The writer's emotional display is strictly limited. Most of the time, he is introverted and restrained. He has a natural aversion to expressed emotion. He distrusts people who are too demonstrative. He has learned early in life to keep to himself what is going on inside, his joys as well as his suffering. Control has come to mean more to him than sharing relationships. He is uneasy when feelings are shown by others. Tears, uninhibited laughter or overt responses to hurts and pains are frowned upon. If others indulge in such displays, he tends to become cold, angry and withdrawn. He has paid a big price for his emotional reserve and expects the same from others. He does not relate well to emotional appeals. He deals with realities and expects facts and figures, bare of emotional overtones. He deals dispassionately with others and makes few excuses for those around him because he “likes” them or “pities” them.

There is only one group of people he can feel comfortable with, and these people are as unresponsive as he is. But when he is with them, he still cannot express what means the most to him, because that would mean abandoning the control he has built up for his own feelings. He may speak less because talking at length would mean to reveal himself more. Gestures may be reduced, too.

Any job that demands restraint of emotion profits by persons who are unresponsive. Surgeons, executioners, professional gamblers, bill collectors, traffic enforcers, are examples of such professions.

The writer is emotionally withdrawn and isolated. He recoils from involvement and is suspicious of relationships that become too intimate. He wants to keep distance between himself and others. He is afraid of life itself and of the future. He discovered early in life that natural responsiveness was not acceptable and it was safer to hide his emotions whenever he could. He began to mask his feelings and put on a face that others found acceptable. In later life, that mask became his face and he learned to think of his lack of response as an accomplishment. He felt he was more in control if he did not allow himself to “feel.” He may even have stopped using the language of emotions. He may say “I think” instead of “I feel.” He spent a lot of time and energy suppressing emotions and control finally became more important than acceptance and responsiveness. The fallacy is that denying his feelings did not stop the hurt and fear inside. Unfortunately, he can no longer reach out to anyone, nor can they reach out to him. Suppressed feelings mean lack of communication, antagonism and, eventually, a sense of real separation. By suppressing his feelings, the writer hurts himself. He also continues to hurt the feelings of others who believe he does not need or want relationships or their support. Since they assess him only from what they can see, they may be judging him incorrectly or miss his true feelings entirely.

The writer consciously restricts any emotional display. He holds back the instinct to sympathize with others, to embrace, comfort, share, or love. Most of the time, he is introverted and restrained. He expects the same controlled behavior from others. He may act spontaneous and extroverted when it seems the expedient thing to do. However, such behavior is spurious and calculated. The inward personality remains introverted and self-protective at all times.

The writer is defensive and self-protective. He lacks spontaneity and finds it difficult to communicate naturally. He consciously maintains distance in his relationships to hide his vulnerabilities. To others, he may appear unresponsive and aloof. (This does not mean that he really feels this way. On the inside, he may feel a very strong response.) When his ego is threatened, he may resort to whatever behavior seems expedient at the time to get him out of the difficult situation.

Left slanted downstrokes with right slanted upstrokes are so-called braced strokes. They reveal conflict and betray the writer's fearfulness. The writer will always act defensively when stressed, or when the unfamiliar is forced on him.

With left slant less than 50°, the writer has a distorted view of the realities of life and his adaptability is seriously impeded. Since he distorts the true nature of things, it is harder for him to act realistically and the consequences may be far-reaching. He has convinced himself that people are his antagonists who want to inconvenience and embarrass him. He believes they will manipulate him or take advantage of him, if he shows his emotions. He withdraws from emotional relationships to prevent others from hurting him further. With him, there is always the danger that, when his defense of emotional isolation does not work, he will be overwhelmed by anxiety.

The writer is insecure and fearful in normal daily encounters. While his need for contact may be strong, his fears are more intense. Defensive and self-protective, he is apprehensive about physical contact. He is afraid to permit others to get close to him. His tension and lack of spontaneity may be taken as aloofness by others. He is most comfortable working alone or in intellectual occupations. On the positive side, he is able to handle more than one task at once because his field of consciousness is enlarged, so to speak. On the negative side, he is easily sidetracked. (Musical or artistic ability is often evident in writers with broad word spacing.)

The writer needs an inordinate amount of space to surround him to feel secure. With an exaggerated need for solitude, he is unwilling to interrelate on the social level. He is withdrawn, self-protective and uncommunicative. He has erected an invisible wall which others cannot penetrate. He has difficulty with people who make demands or cling to him. His life is isolated, only few people are allowed to share personal experiences. In a sense, he is an onlooker rather than a participant in active living. He is extremely uncomfortable and tense in the pressure of large crowds or in heavy traffic, for that matter. (The fact that the writer demands for himself so much extra space at the expense of others implies a tendency toward egotism and conceit.)

The writer lacks objectivity in thinking. He is overly concerned with details and unable to correlate and integrate information. Often, he loses sight of the big picture. Details become ends in themselves. Whole situations may get out of hand while he wastes time haggling over trivia. He is easily sidetracked. In conversations, he is likely to meander and digress to ideas totally unrelated to the subject under discussion. (This tendency is especially pronounced if the writing is otherwise connected.)

The writer suffers extreme anxiety related to dangerous (usually hostile or sexual) urges. Unconsciously, he feels compelled to leave an inordinate amount of space between himself and others to protect himself from acting out the unacceptable impulses. He may not recognize the irrationality of such behavior but does not seem to be able to stop it. While isolating himself by an exaggerated distance seems to reduce anxiety to some degree, there is a compulsive need to persist in the ritual. (Consequently, in writing, the peculiar spacing is repeated through a number of lines.)
See listing 32-1b on page 186.

indikator.nama: Final strokes are left tending half ovals
indikator.keterangan: See listing 26-5 on page 149.

The writer has had bad experiences in the past. He cannot free himself of these recollections that have taken hold of him and keep him worrying and brooding. One of the effects is extreme caution. He is suspicious of other people and expects that they will try to take advantage of him again. Out of fear, he defers decisions. He needs time to thoroughly consider all ramifications of the matter first.

indikator.nama: Final horizontal strokes with two dots
indikator.keterangan: The writer suffers from extreme suspicion. This may be pathological.

indikator.nama: Initial strokes inflexible from baseline or below
indikator.keterangan: See listing 30-5b on page 168.

The writer may (a) intentionally create illegibility and confusion, for instance by misplacing an i-dot over another letter or writing a “u” for an “n;” or (b) write carefully and meticulously with infrequent illegible letters or words; or (c) insert corrections that do not improve legibility and instead make the word totally illegible. Too defensive to share his honest reactions, he is distrustful of others and does not want to “put his cards openly on the table.”

The writer is thoughtless and indifferent. In practical life, he is careless and accident prone. As a worker, he may liable to mishaps and a security risk. Where safety is a factor, he works to disadvantage. He is apt to blunder into many situations, causing inadvertent harm to others and himself.

The writer has suffered stress beyond his coping resources. As a result, he has erected a complex and deeply entrenched defense system. He is self-protective, suspicious, jealous, rigid and hypersensitive. His lack of trust interferes with the ability to test reality. While his thinking remains logical, it is based on false premises. He reconstructs facts to fit his misconceptions and afterwards, seeks additional data to support his fabricated conclusions. Not surprisingly, interpersonal relations for the writer are poor. As a defense, he rationalizes why he should be suspicious of others' behavior toward him.

Important! Malformations in the upper zone may indicate low mental energy and possible problems with the writer's health.

The writer is egocentric and mentally inefficient. He lacks a sense of reality and responds with fear and confusion when faced with the realities of life. He may have unjustified feelings of euphoria or be paranoid.

indikator.nama: Margin on left narrowing toward bottom of page
indikator.keterangan: The writer commences projects and relationships with at least a measure of courage. As he becomes more involved, doubts assail him. He becomes distrustful of the people or the situation. If circumstances allow it, he may abandon the project altogether. Others will find that over and over again, the writer promises more than he is able to do.

The writer is afraid of the future because of the uncertainties it represents. He feels that he is incapable of dealing with life and its everyday exigencies. In interpersonal relationships, he is distrustful and insecure, especially with people he does not know.

The writer automatically fears anything with which he is unfamiliar. He has a closed mind and rejects progressive concepts outright. He severely limits his participation, both in projects and relationships. The need to control himself and his involvements is of paramount importance in his life. He cannot be expected to bring projects in which he is involved to a satisfying finish.

The right margin is the hardest to regulate. A certain amount of irregularity is to be expected due to variable word length.

The writer is very distrustful; he worries that people will try to manipulate him or take advantage of him if he allows himself to become spontaneously involved in situations and relationships. He tries to work strictly according to method and routine. He feels that this protects him from becoming involved in challenges which would tax his abilities. Once he has set up his schedule, he refuses to change. Lack of spontaneity makes him rigid in unfamiliar situations.

In evaluating legibility of the signature, it must be taken into account that writers who have to sign their name many times every day may simplify or neglect it without negative intent.

The writer seems to be distrustful of other people. He is afraid that someone may try to copy his signature for illegal purposes. Through illegible letter formations, he wants to forestall imitation of his name.

With signs of insecurity (self-confidence low, inhibitions), the writer may be distrustful toward himself. He doubts his ability to assume responsibility for the document he has signed. Disguising his signature to the point of illegibility, he instinctively tries to evade accountability.
See listing 02-10b on page 13.

Through exaggeration the writer wants to cover up the lack of inner assurance. He tries to delude himself and others that he is very impressive. In reality, he is overbearing and crude. He is self-centered and constantly aware of other people's opinion of him. Circumstances and other people rule his life.

He displays a superficial interest in intellectual matters and tries to mislead others with his “intellectual” bend of mind. In actuality, he suffers from scattered, unresolved thinking. He needs plenty of time to think matters through and is unable to differentiate what is or is not essential. He dwells on details, and makes much of unimportant concerns. He is poor in communicating his ideas and in every-day matters, he is highly impractical.

Most of the time, has a very poor sense of reality and lives in a fantasy world of his own. He is subjective and sees things only from his own particular point of view. Distrustful and defensive, it is nearly impossible for him to share his honest reactions with others.

Convex alignment indicates temporary inability to maintain control. The writer alternates between feelings of exhilaration and doubt. He cannot keep himself from becoming enthusiastic about a project or relationship; however, he cannot sustain this hopeful attitude for any length of time. Such mood swings may not be obvious to outsiders but will be noticeable to family and close associates.

The writer starts projects with cheerfulness and zeal. Temporarily, he grows increasingly enthusiastic. Soon, however, his ardor diminishes. Having started with much, perhaps too much confidence, his optimism wanes and he becomes discouraged. If the situation allows him to drop the undertaking, he will do so before it is completed. If the process occurs repeatedly, a negative pattern may be established. If through outside forces or circumstances the writer is forced to continue, he will do so; however, inner tension and anxiety prevail.

The writer consistently maintains the image of his goals. However, the pursuit of his purposes entails a constant struggle against overpowering feelings of melancholy. He tries to counter such feelings by sheer will and usually succeeds in overcoming his depressive mood temporarily, only to be defeated again. The ongoing struggle causes inner conflict with subsequent frustration.

In every case, the writers' efforts surpass their available energy. Moreover, the continuing effort for self-control greatly inhibits their spontaneity.

The more frequently the process repeats itself, the more the individuals become discouraged and physically fatigued. Feelings of dejection become a serious drain on their mental and physical resources. Roman sees the step-down alignment as evidence of the struggle against depression by individuals who “seek to overcome fatigue and low spirits. The stepped lines,” she says, “indicate that the fight against weariness is supported by a strong feeling of responsibility.”³

Extreme step-down alignment corroborates that the writer is severely depressed. Suicidal tendencies may be present. (Mental disturbance is possible).

The writer suffers from lack of energy. He is discouraged and in a dejected mood most of the time. More than the usual strain has been placed on him for a long period of time. Susceptible to gloomy people and thoughts, he is more likely to create negative pictures in his mind. He focuses on the dark side of things and anticipates what he does not want to happen instead of success. His general disposition is pessimistic and he lacks confidence in the future and in himself. The writer's vocabulary is likely to include such words as can't, won't, if, but, should, shouldn't, perhaps, maybe, etc. With each obstacle, the feeling of pessimism grows and he finds it difficult to follow a definite line of action. He is discouraged before he starts.

Because pessimism develops gradually, the writer may still think of himself, in many cases, as being positive. He may not be fully aware of how pessimistic he looks, sounds, and really is. He may not realize how much he has been taken over by his own negative feelings.

Important! Not only depression, but also physical or mental tiredness can cause descending words and lines. If sinking alignment is due to a general state of exhaustion or a poor state of mental or physical health, there will be additional indicators such as smeariness, low placement of diacriticals, lack of pressure, stunted or incomplete letters, or wavering or broken strokes. The writer may be under the influence of drugs or a chronic alcoholic. It is prudent to check the possibility of the above conditions first.

Frequently, downslanted alignment is found in people who are in the wrong vocation. There is an unpleasant inner feeling, which may be one of sadness or remorse about having made the wrong choice in life.

indikator.nama: Dry spots on the writing line
indikator.keterangan:
An indentation in the ductus that is devoid of ink is a serious indicator. It usually occurs in initial strokes.

The writer has an extremely low state of energy which makes him negative and discouraged. This condition may result from ill health, stress, or exhaustion. If the writer continues to drive himself despite this warning, he may soon deplete his energies completely.

Important! Dry ductus may be the result of a faulty pen. If that is the case, it will happen only once at the beginning of the manuscript. Dry ductus due to physical causes will occur repeatedly.

indikator.nama: Final garlands pushed into the lower zone
indikator.keterangan: The writer has a melancholic and despondent outlook. He may be extremely fatigued and ceases efforts too soon before reaching his goals. He has problems that weigh on his mind. He feels more and more that he is unable to deal with the situation. Because of his dilemma, he has little time to think of anything else, including his job. He is unable to devote his full attention to anything except his predicament.

indikator.nama: Final strokes dipping down and returning to baseline
indikator.keterangan: The writer experiences chronic dissatisfaction hidden behind a mask of pseudo-joviality.

indikator.nama: Final strokes curving downward in the lower zone
indikator.keterangan: The writer suffers from constant dejection and a deep-seated negative attitude. Discouragement undermines self-direction and motivation and, in extreme cases, means fatalism or apathy. He feels as if it is useless to make an effort since nothing is going to work out anyway.
See listing 31-2a on page 177.

indikator.nama: Initial strokes leftward through upper zone loop of capital
indikator.keterangan: See listing 31-3 on page 178.

indikator.nama: Initial strokes crossing out all or part of signature
indikator.keterangan:
“An initial stroke crossing out the signature is a ‘stroke through the writer’s life.’ It is a ‘sign fixe’ of the old graphological school. According to Pfanne, a German graphologist, it still occurs frequently, especially with older people. ‘Experience has shown,’ he states, ‘that one cannot deny its accuracy. And since the crossing out occurs before the letter is actually written,’ he clarifies, ‘the writer is taking something back before he expresses it.’

The writer has experienced trauma which has resulted in very negative feelings about himself. He has a sense of utter insignificance. Subconsciously, he feels so worthless that he denies himself the right to exist. He either wants to become an entirely different person or he may even contemplate suicide.

The writer’s negative state of mind affects every area of his personality. Before giving himself a chance to express a valuable part of himself, either creatively, emotionally, or intellectually, he negates the rightfulness of such expression.

The writer may possess strong innate potentials, yet may display a bizarre inability to use them productively. Anything he does to function effectively makes him anxious. He may suffer fatigue or other signs of inhibition when he makes a try at self-expression. To avoid anxiety-producing situations and activities, he subconsciously limits his ability to perform. This may occur on different levels. The more superficial inhibitions may curtail his ability to act upon his wishes, or to ask for something which is in his own interest.

The more profound inhibitions occur on the inner level, so that the writer no longer knows clearly what he wants or thinks.

indikator.nama: Initial and final strokes cross each other below the baseline
indikator.keterangan:
The writer suffers from extreme discouragement. He has self-destructive inclinations and may be suicidal.

Important! The above findings need to be confirmed by additional indicators in the writing.

The writer has suffered from a severe emotional or physical crisis in his life. He has been permanently traumatized. He buries himself in the past because he sees no hope for the future and the present has nothing to offer.
See listing 15-4b on page 93.

indikator.nama: Pressure lighter toward end of word or end of text
indikator.keterangan: The writer has only a limited amount of energy at his disposal and becomes easily discouraged and fatigued. Rather than pacing himself carefully, he uses most of his strength during the initial phase of a project. For tasks to be completed, they have to be of short duration, otherwise his stamina will drastically decrease after an initial all-out effort.

The writer experiences discouragement of a personal nature. His attitude toward himself or his accomplishments is negative. He may find it increasingly difficult to work in stressful situations or under pressure.

The speed of writing corresponds to the speed of a personality in all its aspects.

The writer is self-controlled and deliberate in thinking and acting. He wants to consider a matter from all sides before becoming involved. He may become very negative when forced to deal with faster individuals. He feels irritated when other people want him to speed up because under pressure his mind tends to go blank.

The writer works best by routine. He enjoys creating a method and following it. He feels this is the best way of being sure to accomplish what he sets out to do. He emphasizes order, schedules, and procedures and gets satisfaction from methodical accomplishments. This tendency slows him down in unfamiliar situations and activities and makes him inflexible. Once he has set up his routine, it is hard for him to adjust to last minute changes. He lacks variety in approach, particularly in intimate human relationships. When he does something on impulse it is usually an emotional response and he regrets his impulsive behavior later.

The writer has a slower pace of learning but he retains what he has learned excellently and can use it effectively in all similar areas and relationships.

The tempo of the writer's sex life corresponds to his basic speed. He wants to organize his sex life so he has the time to enjoy it, and he feels most comfortable having sex at his own speed, in his own bed or in surroundings that are relaxing and familiar to him. His sexual ritual seldom varies once it has proven satisfactory to him.

Important! Compatibility between fast and slow writers in the sexual area is difficult. Out of consideration, the fast writer may check his tempo for a while to match the partner's rhythm, but eventually he is bound to become impatient. And because he moves faster, he is prone to miss many things that have real meaning to his mate. The slow writer may try to speed up his reactions to make the partner more comfortable but inside he will still feel rushed. He will take the partner's quicker reaction pattern as criticism and will feel hurt by it.

indikator.nama: Final strokes fading in slow writing
indikator.keterangan:
Because he is insecure, the writer fears the finality of a hard and fast decision. Unsure of his judgment, he vacillates, procrastinates, or in other ways hesitates to decide. Afraid of the consequences, he does not want to make unjust or unpopular decisions nor does not wish to commit himself to agreeing or disagreeing. Especially in unfamiliar areas will he be cautious and hesitant.

Decisions that could be made speedily may be delayed pending the development of more and more data, most of which frequently reconfirms what the writer already knows.

As a supervisor, insecurity may so immobilize the writer that he is prevented not only from making decisions himself but also from delegating them, afraid that mistakes made by subordinates will reflect on him.

The writer finds a sort of negative security in temporizing. Refusing to take a stand, he goes back and forth and tends to change his mind frequently.

His instinctive inclination is to wait for someone else to tell him what to do. He often spends so long weighing each side that the decision is usually made by default or by the other persons involved. Unable to rely on his own judgment, he lets others make the choices he should make for himself. He waits to see what people want before airing his position and quickly accedes if he thinks someone else knows better (which is most of the time).

Indecisiveness is a handicap because it delays action and wastes time. Instead of making definite decisions and acting on them, the writer tries to keep too many options open. He may even alter plans because of doubts after work has commenced.

indikator.keterangan:

indikator.nama: Initial loops on M's, N's, H's, or on the ppl
indikator.keterangan:
(Jealousy is a complex emotion compounded by feelings of insecurity, apprehension, self-blame, and hostility toward an alleged rival. Foremost, it is rooted in low self-esteem and insecurity about self-worth.)

The writer suffers from the fear of not being loved. He is afraid of competition or not measuring up.

He experiences intense emotions when his relationships are threatened by a rival. He fears losing the affection of a loved person as well as the loss of that relationship. Any other interest his partner may have is considered a potential threat.

Jealousy may destroy any chance of a happy relationship. Because he feels unloved, he often acts unloving toward the person he needs love from the most. He strives to possess rather than love and his affections can be smothering. He is definitely the taker in a relationship and a partner belongs to him - body, mind, and soul. This can make a relationship complicated at times. His possessiveness and tendency to take over the other person will definitely cause many disputes.

Being distrustful, he depends upon continuing demonstrations of affection. He cannot believe someone could possibly love only him. Constantly on the watch for indications that his jealous suspicions are justified, he may manufacture evidence if he does not find it. He may then turn with bitterness against a real or imagined rival. Even in his most secure moments, he suffers from the unconscious fear of losing love.

Fear of rejection inhibits his urge to make advances to a person he likes, as long as he cannot be absolutely certain of not meeting with rejection.

On the job, the writer deeply fears to compete with others. It may be in skills, or in some other area. Jealous of what others accomplish, he resents the success of his peers.

As a boss, despite the authority of his position, he fears rivalry from younger executives.

As an employee, he fears being outshone by those who are more popular, or more successful, or more gifted than he, himself, is. Unable to give praise where it is due, he is rarely capable of a complimentary word to somebody else.

Jealousy may also operate as a spur to achievement. The writer may try to outrank others and so makes realistic attempts to earn promotion.

indikator.nama: Tightly retraced strokes on m's and n's
indikator.keterangan:
Repression in the writer is a defense mechanism with which painful or threatening thoughts are automatically excluded from consciousness.

He bottles up a lot inside of him and his emotions are subject to strict repression. Emotional survival in the past may have depended upon isolating himself from his feelings. As a result, today, his emotions are consistently and strongly repressed.

Likewise, the writer excludes painful experiences and unacceptable impulses automatically from his consciousness. Excessive restraint is exerted to prevent “bad” behavior.

But even though these impulses are banished from awareness, this does not deprive them of their dynamic force. They may express themselves in many indirect ways, as in dreams, jokes, slips of the tongue, vague feelings of guilt, and uneasiness.

Repression may have its advantages and liabilities. It may protect the writer against the memory of traumatic experiences until he is better prepared to assimilate them. On the other hand, repression of threatening impulses is not a thing done only once and thereby completed. Rather, it requires continuous output of energy. Thus, repression is costly to the individual, being a steady drain on his energy. But since he is not aware of his repressed impulses, he often cannot deal with them in a logical and reasonable manner. They are now part of his unconsciousness but continue to play a role in his life, though they are beyond the range of his direct control.

Because repression renders the writer incapable of consciously dealing with his desires, he may expose himself to potentially tempting situations, thereby increasing the very discomfort that repression was meant to diminish.

indikator.nama: Final strokes turning leftwards over the previous word
indikator.keterangan:
The writer suffers from self-blame and subconsciously seeks self-punishment. He apparently finds satisfaction for a deep need in this way; it seems as if he takes pleasure in his own misfortune.

The writer habitually blames himself for mistakes or misdeeds. Often, he reproaches himself for negative situations over which he has no control. He finds it difficult to forgive himself and put such incidents out of his mind.

The writer is his own worst enemy and makes himself court his own disadvantage. With an unconscious wish to suffer, he continually falls into pits he could have easily avoided. This appears to be an unconscious way of setting himself up for failure, since he does not really believe he deserves success.

Self-castigation may be revealed in destructive behavior such as nail-biting, overeating, alcoholism, use of dangerous drugs, hazardous sports, or self-humiliating acts of all kinds. Or the writer may be involved in difficult or abusive relationships. He seems to seize upon every opportunity there is to achieve a state in which he will be miserable. The writer is quick to condemn his own shortcomings without making a positive effort to correct them. As an employee, he would need an understanding superior who will not pile criticism upon self-criticism but take a calm constructive approach when improvement is necessary.

The writer often makes himself vulnerable and provokes others into abusing him. Although he may perceive that a particular way of behaving toward people will incite abuse, he persists and exposes himself to humiliation.

Subconsciously the writer subverts his own efforts. His capacity for success is undermined by a drive to make himself pay for his sins. Suffering pain or humiliation seems to be seen as a form of atonement.

Temporarily, the self-inflicted punishment eases his guilt. For a time the writer can make more constructive efforts on his own behalf until anxiety builds anew and the ineffective behavior is repeated.

indikator.nama: Final strokes in M's and N's or m's and n's higher than previous strokes
indikator.keterangan:
The writer suffers from fear of ridicule or humiliation. He is ill at ease in the presence of strangers, particularly with people he perceives as superior. Acutely aware of his shortcomings, he is afraid that he will not pass muster with his peers and associates.

He is so concerned about the impression he makes on others that all spontaneous reactions are kept under wraps. Because he believes that others are constantly assessing him he cannot gather the inner resources to make easy conversation. His communications are composed mostly of agreement with others or silence. When someone draws him out in a discussion, he seems to be grateful for the attention and begins to brighten perceptibly.

Anything that makes him feel conspicuous can engender self-consciousness; he is very much afraid of being singled out for attention, especially when it is negative. For that reason, he carefully avoids behavior that attracts attention, or creates a scene.

In a large gathering, he feels strained and ill at ease. Easily embarrassed, he tends to drift off to the fringe of any crowd, and tries to attract as little attention as possible.

Naturally shy, the writer is always more comfortable among established friends and in familiar surroundings. It takes a long time for him to feel at ease in a group or with unfamiliar people.

Self-consciousness may hold him back vocationally. It ties him to the familiar and prevents him from taking chances with unfamiliar activities. Also, supervision makes him nervous. While he probably wants to do the best job of which he is capable, he cannot do it easily with someone looking over his shoulder. This hampers his performance by making him feel inept and awkward.

Socially, he is also restricted slightly by self-consciousness. Since he feels uncomfortable, chances are that it will show and his discomfort will make others uncomfortable, too.

The writer underestimates his abilities. As a result, he restricts himself and sets his goals at a low level. Often, he does not aspire higher than where he presently is. He is afraid to fail and, therefore, fearful to try.

Failure to him is a crushing experience. It proves what he secretly believes to be true of himself, namely, that he is a worthless being. And should he succeed, he often feels that he was just lucky that time, but that next time he may not be so fortunate again.

He has a tendency to ignore his successes and is instead on the alert for his failures. He finds it difficult to aspire higher than where he is because higher goals are creating more stress than his powers of adaptation are able to cope with.

Because of the tension he feels in unfamiliar undertakings, he seldom makes an effort to get ahead.

He misses opportunities because he does not demand enough of himself. Because he is afraid to reach up or take a chance with what he may not be able to accomplish, he fails to develop his innate talents.

In many instances, he is prepared to take a back seat and allow others to receive the acknowledgment that is rightly due him.

indikator.nama: Signature smaller than writing in text

indikator.keterangan:
The writer is sensitive to criticism. It seems that at some time in his life, he has been hurt by someone or by people close to him. These hurts have left deep emotional scars.

Today, he has come to anticipate criticism, often when no censure is intended. He finds it hard to put his trust in others because he is so afraid of being hurt.

Others may feel it is difficult to discuss a contentious subject with him since he takes differences of opinion as a personal attack.

Easily hurt, he is afraid to enter into any situation or relationship where a chance exists that he could be rebuffed or snubbed. But in avoiding criticism he may also miss out on praise. If given the opportunity, persons who know his good qualities would surely voice their favorable opinion in comments that could bring him much pleasure and encouragement.

Sensitiveness to criticism can hinder the writer vocationally; he may not attempt certain things because of the potential threat of criticism. Fearful of giving offense, he hates to admit a mistake. It matters a great deal to him what his superiors think of him, and he takes their disapproval seriously.

Being so sensitive, he needs to be surrounded by supportive, positive people. Susceptible to both flattery and criticism, he is at the mercy of anyone who happens to make a personal remark. But on the other hand, a kind, uplifting comment can pick him right up.

The writer does not take teasing lightly. In fact, he finds it almost impossible to see the joke when he is the victim.

It is true that the writer wants approval, but because of insecurities developed from previous experiences, he fears more disapproval. He probably would rather hear a flattering lie that feels good than the truth that might hurt. Others should remember to reproach him tactfully and privately, lest criticism will never accomplish its intended purpose with him.

With sensitiveness very high, the writer’s feelings are easily bruised. He is vulnerable to even unintended slights regarding his performance, mannerisms, ideas, and beliefs. A hint of displeasure, a word, a nuance, a silence, or a gesture can hurt him.

It is difficult for the writer to deal with others because he is affected by what they say, and even by the way they say it.

His magnified fear may lead to the development of various forms of defenses, among them secretiveness, or procrastination, or withdrawal.

Due to his sensitiveness, he would find it difficult to accept closely supervised situations. He is suspicious of those around him, believing they are out to hurt him in some way. He believes that others are saying spiteful things on purpose, strictly to provoke or irritate him.

He not only exaggerates trivial incidents, he fabricates painful episodes in his mind and imagines reasons that others may not like him or disapprove of his actions.

With d/t loops leaning more toward the right than the rest of the writing, the writer overreacts when criticized. He feels extremely hurt and plunges immediately into a depressed or angry mood.

With d/t loops leaning more toward the left than the rest of the writing, the writer becomes withdrawn when he is hurt. He may keep to himself and hope to hide his hurt from others. Often he becomes morose and sullen. 

Sensitiveness positive: Sensitiveness to criticism makes the writer more sympathetic to others’ feelings in this regard. Because of his own fears, he will go to great lengths not to blame others. He will not dish it out nor does he try to hurt others unnecessarily. Personal sensitivity makes him compassionate because he understands how criticism hurts. Likewise, he is more considerate of the feelings of those close to him. Fear of criticism makes him try hard so as to be above reproach. He probably works hard to do a good job so as to avoid negative comments. One of his advantages is his ability to deal with other equally “thin-skinned” people. Because of his own sensitiveness he can understand them and their fear of being criticized. He will not needlessly censure and he will word criticism tactfully and diplomatically.
